Nina's absolute advantage in both goods (200 > 120 and 100 > 90) is irrelevant — it never determines the pattern of specialisation.

quiz.q: Country X needs 4 labour hours to make one shirt and 24 labour hours to make one bicycle. What is the opportunity cost of one bicycle, measured in shirts?
quiz.explain: With hours-per-unit data the opportunity cost is a ratio of the country's own two numbers: $24/4 = 6$ shirts. Building one bicycle uses 24 hours, and those same 24 hours would have produced 6 shirts. The usual mistake is to compare the 24 hours with another country's figure — comparative advantage is only revealed after each country's internal ratio has been computed.

quiz.q: Ada can produce 90 units of good A or 30 units of good B; Ben can produce 40 of A or 40 of B. In autarky each splits their time equally between the two goods. After full specialisation according to comparative advantage, by how many units does total output of good A rise?
quiz.explain: Opportunity cost of A: Ada $30/90=1/3$ of B, Ben $40/40=1$ of B → Ada specialises in A, Ben in B. Autarky: Ada 45 A + 15 B, Ben 20 A + 20 B, so totals are 65 A and 35 B. Full specialisation: Ada 90 A, Ben 40 B. Good A rises from 65 to 90, i.e. by 25 units — and B rises from 35 to 40 as well, so the reallocation raises output of both goods.

quiz.q: Czechia's opportunity cost of a car is 2 software modules; Germany's is 3 modules. At which price would trade take place with both countries gaining?
options: 1.5 modules per car
2 modules per car
2.5 modules per car
3.5 modules per car
quiz.explain: The price must lie strictly between the two opportunity costs, $2 < p < 3$. Only 2.5 qualifies. At $p=1.5$ Czechia would rather build its own cars (they cost it only 2 modules, but selling one earns just 1.5). At exactly $p=2$ Czechia is indifferent and captures none of the gain; at $p=3.5$ Germany would rather build its own. Note that all prices in $(2,3)$ produce the same total gain — the price only decides how it is split.

quiz.q: Which statements about comparative advantage are true?
options: A producer with an absolute advantage in both goods can still gain by specialising and trading.
With two producers and two goods, one producer can have a comparative advantage in both goods.
A producer's two opportunity costs are reciprocals of each other.
If two producers have identical opportunity costs, there are no gains from trade between them.
Free trade guarantees that every individual within a trading country is made better off.
quiz.explain: (1) is the whole point of the model — Greta beats Carlos at both goods and both still gain. (3) is a useful check: if a tonne of wheat costs 25 apples, an apple costs $1/25=0.04$ tonnes. (4) is right: gains come from differences in opportunity cost, so with identical ratios the joint frontier is a straight line and reallocation achieves nothing. (2) is false — a lower ratio in one good forces a higher ratio in the other. (5) is false: the model shows aggregate gains, and says nothing about how they are distributed; workers in a shrinking industry can lose.

quiz.q: Greta and Carlos specialise fully: Greta produces 50 tonnes of wheat, Carlos 1 000 apples. Greta sells Carlos 10 tonnes of wheat at 42 apples per tonne. Her autarky bundle was 40 tonnes of wheat and 250 apples. By how many apples is Greta better off?
quiz.explain: After the trade Greta keeps $50-10=40$ tonnes of wheat — exactly her autarky level — and receives $10 \times 42 = 420$ apples instead of 250. Her gain is $420-250 = \mathbf{170}$ apples. Carlos ends with 10 tonnes of wheat and $1000-420=580$ apples, a gain of 80 apples. The two gains sum to $170+80=250$: the total efficiency gain from specialisation, which is the same at any price in $(25,50)$.

quiz.q: Two countries each have 6 000 labour hours. Alfa needs 30 hours per tonne of steel and 10 hours per tonne of grain. Beta needs 20 hours per tonne of steel and 20 hours per tonne of grain. (a) Determine absolute and comparative advantage. (b) Compute total output if each country splits its hours evenly, and after full specialisation. (c) State the range of terms of trade. (d) Give one reason why the country losing its steel industry might oppose this trade despite the aggregate gain.
quiz.solution:
(a) Absolute advantage. Beta needs fewer hours per tonne of steel (20 < 30), Alfa fewer per tonne of grain (10 < 20). Absolute advantage is split.

Comparative advantage. Opportunity cost of 1 tonne of steel, in grain: Alfa $30/10 = 3$; Beta $20/20 = 1$. Beta's cost is lower → Beta specialises in steel. Opportunity cost of 1 tonne of grain, in steel: Alfa $10/30 \approx 0.33$; Beta $20/20 = 1$ → Alfa specialises in grain. (Check: the two costs within each country are reciprocals, 3 and 1/3 for Alfa, 1 and 1 for Beta.)

(b) Autarky, 3 000 hours each way. Alfa: $3000/30 = 100$ t of steel and $3000/10 = 300$ t of grain. Beta: $3000/20 = 150$ t of steel and $3000/20 = 150$ t of grain. Totals: 250 t of steel, 450 t of grain.

Full specialisation. Alfa uses all 6 000 hours on grain: $6000/10 = 600$ t. Beta uses all 6 000 hours on steel: $6000/20 = 300$ t. Totals: 300 t of steel, 600 t of grain — an increase of 50 t of steel and 150 t of grain, with no extra labour or technology.

(c) Terms of trade. One tonne of steel must exchange for between 1 and 3 tonnes of grain (Beta will not sell below its own cost of 1; Alfa will not buy above its own cost of 3). At exactly 2 tonnes of grain per tonne of steel the gain is shared roughly evenly; at 1 the whole gain goes to Alfa, at 3 it all goes to Beta.

(d) Why opposition can be rational. The gains are aggregate and diffuse — spread thinly across all consumers as lower prices — while the losses are concentrated and immediate: steelworkers in Alfa lose their jobs, their industry-specific skills lose value, and whole regions can decline, often permanently, since labour is far less mobile than the model assumes. The model compares two static equilibria and is silent about the transition. Unless Alfa compensates and retrains the losers, a majority of the people directly affected are genuinely worse off, so their opposition is not economic illiteracy but a distributional objection the model cannot answer. A second, dynamic argument: giving up steel may also give up the learning-by-doing and supplier networks that would have generated future comparative advantage.

lessons.html:
The spinning jenny was invented in England in 1764 and spread across Britain within a decade — but French firms, who knew all about it, largely ignored it for another fifty years. The technology was the same on both sides of the Channel. What differed were the relative prices of labour and energy. This lesson gives you the tool that makes that argument precise: the isocost line, and cost-minimising choice of technology.

🎯Learning objectives
  • Read a technology set as points in labour–energy space and spot dominated technologies.
  • Write the equation of an isocost line, find its intercepts, and interpret its slope as $-w/p$.
  • Find the cost-minimising technology as the point touched by the lowest attainable isocost.
  • Recompute the choice when relative prices change, and find the exact switching price.
  • Explain Britain's early mechanisation with the model, and define induced innovation.

1 · The technology set

A technology is a recipe: a list of inputs that together produce a given output. Consider five ways of producing 100 metres of cloth, each using some number of workers and some tonnes of coal:

TechnologyWorkersCoal (tonnes)Character
A16energy-intensive, labour-saving
B42balanced
C37wasteful
D55wasteful
E101labour-intensive, energy-saving

Two of these can be eliminated straight away, before you know a single price.

📐Definition — dominated technology

Technology X dominates technology Y if X uses at least as little of every input and strictly less of at least one. A dominated technology is never cost-minimising, whatever the prices.

A (1 worker, 6 tonnes) dominates C (3 workers, 7 tonnes): fewer workers and less coal. B (4, 2) dominates D (5, 5) for the same reason. C and D can be dropped permanently. What remains — A, B and E — form a downward-sloping frontier: to use less coal you must use more labour. Choosing among them requires prices.

2 · Isocost lines

Let $w$ be the wage per worker and $p$ the price of a tonne of coal. A technology using $L$ workers and $R$ tonnes of coal costs

$$c = wL + pR.$$
📐Definition — isocost line

An isocost line is the set of all input combinations costing the same amount $c$. Rearranging $c=wL+pR$ for $R$: $$R = \frac{c}{p} - \frac{w}{p}\,L.$$ It is a straight line with vertical intercept $c/p$, horizontal intercept $c/w$, and slope $$\text{slope} = -\frac{w}{p},$$ the relative price of labour in terms of coal.

Three facts about the picture are worth memorising. Isocost lines for different values of $c$ are parallel — the slope depends only on prices, not on $c$. Lines closer to the origin mean lower cost. And the slope is a pure statement about the market, containing no information whatsoever about what the firm can technically do.

💡How to read the slope

The slope $-w/p$ answers: how many tonnes of coal can I buy with the money saved by firing one worker? If $w=10$ and $p=20$, firing a worker saves 10, which buys half a tonne — slope $-0.5$, a shallow line. If coal collapses to $p=5$, that same 10 buys two tonnes — slope $-2$, a steep line. Steep isocosts mean labour is expensive relative to energy.

3 · Cost-minimising choice

ΣRule — the cost-minimising technology

The firm chooses the technology touched by the lowest isocost line that still reaches the technology set. Equivalently: compute $wL+pR$ for every non-dominated technology and pick the smallest number.

Take $w=10$ and $p=20$ (labour cheap relative to coal, $w/p=0.5$):

TechnologyWorkers × 10Coal × 20Total cost
A (1, 6)10120130
B (4, 2)404080
C (3, 7)30140170
D (5, 5)50100150
E (10, 1)10020120

B is cheapest at 80. Graphically, the isocost line $R = 4 - 0.5L$ passes exactly through B, and every other technology lies above it — above meaning "on a higher isocost", i.e. more expensive.

⚠Common mistake — mixing up technology and prices

The points are technology (engineering); the lines are prices (markets). When the wage changes, the points do not move — only the slope of the lines does, which is why a different point gets touched. Students who redraw the technology set when a price changes have misunderstood the whole diagram.

⚠Common mistake — "the cheapest technology uses the fewest inputs"

E uses the least coal; A uses the fewest workers. Neither is cheapest at these prices. Being un-dominated only means a technology could be chosen at some price — which one actually is chosen depends entirely on $w/p$. Always compute $wL+pR$; never eyeball the input quantities.

4 · When relative prices change, the choice switches

Now suppose coal becomes cheap: $p=5$, with the wage still $w=10$, so $w/p=2$ and the isocosts become four times steeper.

TechnologyCost at $w=10,\ p=20$Cost at $w=10,\ p=5$Cost at $w=2,\ p=20$
A (1, 6)13040122
B (4, 2)805048
E (10, 1)12010540
ChosenBAE

Read the row of chosen technologies from right to left, in order of a rising relative price of labour: $w/p = 0.1 \Rightarrow$ E, $w/p = 0.5 \Rightarrow$ B, $w/p = 2 \Rightarrow$ A. The more expensive labour becomes relative to energy, the more labour-saving the chosen technology. That single sentence is the whole model.

ΣFinding the switching price

The firm is indifferent between two technologies when their costs are equal. For A $(1,6)$ and B $(4,2)$: $$w\cdot1 + p\cdot6 = w\cdot4 + p\cdot2 \;\Longrightarrow\; 4p = 3w \;\Longrightarrow\; \frac{w}{p} = \frac{4}{3}.$$ For $w/p > 4/3$ the firm chooses A; for $w/p < 4/3$ it prefers B. Comparing B and E in the same way gives $w/p = 1/6$: below that, E wins.

5 · Why Britain mechanised first

In the eighteenth century Britain had, by European standards, high wages and very cheap coal — coal was mined domestically and moved cheaply by water, while wages had risen after centuries of labour scarcity. France, and still more India and China, had abundant cheap labour and expensive energy. On the diagram: Britain sat at a steep $w/p$, France at a shallow one.

The spinning jenny was a labour-saving, capital- and energy-using technology — a point far to the upper left of the technology set. It was profitable exactly where the isocosts were steep. Robert Allen's argument, which CORE follows, is that British firms adopted it not because they were cleverer or more entrepreneurial, but because at British relative prices it lowered costs, while at French relative prices it did not. Same technology set, different price ratio, different choice.

📌Note — induced innovation

The story does not stop at adoption. Because a labour-saving invention is worth more where labour is expensive, the innovation rent from creating one is also larger there — so inventors direct their effort towards saving the expensive input. This is induced innovation (Hicks, 1932): relative prices shape not only which technologies are chosen from an existing set, but which new technologies get invented in the first place. It is why a high carbon price is expected to produce not just less coal use, but more low-carbon inventions.

Adopting a new technology below the current lowest isocost yields an innovation rent, exactly as in Lesson 4: the difference between the old minimum cost and the new one, on every unit produced, for as long as competitors have not followed.

📊Where this shows up in data work

"Minimise $wL+pR$ over a finite set of feasible points" is a tiny linear programme — the same structure as the transport and blending problems in your optimisation course, and identical to the cost-minimisation step inside energy-system models. Empirically, the model's prediction is testable: the labour share of production costs should fall where wages rise fastest, and firms in countries with high electricity prices should adopt more energy-efficient equipment. Eurostat publishes both labour cost indices and industrial energy prices by country, so the correlation can be checked directly.

Worked examples

Example 1Eliminate, then compute

Problem. Using the five technologies above with $w=10$ and $p=20$: which technologies are dominated, and which is cost-minimising?

1

Dominance check — compare every pair on both inputs. A (1,6) vs C (3,7): A uses fewer workers and less coal → C is dominated. B (4,2) vs D (5,5): B is lower on both → D is dominated. A, B, E are mutually non-dominated (each is lower on one input and higher on the other).

2

Compute costs for the survivors: A $=10(1)+20(6)=130$; B $=10(4)+20(2)=80$; E $=10(10)+20(1)=120$.

3

Sanity check on the losers: C $=170$ and D $=150$, both above their dominators, as dominance guarantees.

Answer: C and D are dominated; B is cost-minimising at a cost of 80 per 100 metres of cloth.
Example 2Coal becomes cheap — Britain

Problem. The wage stays at $w=10$ but coal falls to $p=5$. Recompute and explain the switch geometrically.

1

A $=10(1)+5(6)=10+30=\mathbf{40}$; B $=10(4)+5(2)=40+10=50$; E $=10(10)+5(1)=100+5=105$.

2

A is now cheapest. The firm switches from B to A — from 4 workers to 1, from 2 tonnes of coal to 6.

3

Geometry. The relative price of labour rose from $w/p=0.5$ to $w/p=2$, so the isocosts became four times steeper. Steep lines reach furthest to the upper left of the diagram, which is where the labour-saving technologies sit.

Answer: cost falls from 50 (using B) to 40 with technology A. Cheap energy plus expensive labour makes the labour-saving, energy-hungry technology profitable — the spinning-jenny logic.
Example 3Cheap labour, expensive coal — France

Problem. Now $w=2$ and $p=20$. Which technology is chosen, and what is the cost?

1

A $=2(1)+20(6)=2+120=122$; B $=2(4)+20(2)=8+40=48$; E $=2(10)+20(1)=20+20=\mathbf{40}$.

2

The relative price is $w/p=2/20=0.1$ — very shallow isocosts, which reach furthest to the lower right, where the labour-intensive technologies are.

3

Sense check against the switching rule: E beats B when $w/p < 1/6 \approx 0.167$, and $0.1 < 0.167$ ✔.

Answer: E is chosen, at a cost of 40. A firm facing these prices would look at the spinning jenny (a technology like A, costing 122 here) and rationally reject it — three times the cost of hand spinning. It is not backwardness; it is arithmetic.
Example 4The switching wage

Problem. Coal costs $p=20$. (a) At what wage does the firm become indifferent between B and A? (b) Between E and B? (c) Describe the full choice as a function of $w$.

1

(a) Set costs equal: $w(1)+20(6)=w(4)+20(2)$, i.e. $w+120=4w+40$. Then $80=3w$, so $w=\tfrac{80}{3}\approx 26.67$.

Check: A $=26.67+120=146.67$; B $=106.67+40=146.67$ ✔.

2

(b) $w(10)+20(1)=w(4)+20(2)$ gives $10w+20=4w+40$, so $6w=20$ and $w=\tfrac{10}{3}\approx3.33$.

3

(c) With $p=20$: for $w<3.33$ choose E; for $3.33<w<26.67$ choose B; for $w>26.67$ choose A. In ratio form these thresholds are $w/p=1/6$ and $w/p=4/3$, exactly as derived earlier — the thresholds depend only on the ratio, so doubling both prices changes nothing.

Answer: switch B→A at $w\approx26.7$, E→B at $w\approx3.3$. A rising wage pushes the firm stepwise towards labour-saving technology.
Example 5Innovation rent from a new technology

Problem. At $w=10$, $p=20$, an engineer develops technology F using 2 workers and 2 tonnes of coal per 100 metres. (a) Is F worth adopting? (b) The firm produces 200 000 metres a year. What is the annual innovation rent while rivals still use B? (c) What happens to that rent over time?

1

(a) Cost of F $=10(2)+20(2)=20+40=60$, against the previous minimum of 80 with B. F also dominates B (2 < 4 workers and 2 = 2 tonnes), so it is cheaper at every pair of prices. Adopt it.

2

(b) Saving per 100 metres $=80-60=20$. Annual output is $200\,000/100 = 2\,000$ batches of 100 metres, so the rent is $20\times2\,000=\mathbf{40\,000}$ per year.

3

(c) As rivals copy F, competition drives the price of cloth down towards the new cost of 60 and the rent falls to zero — the S-curve of Lesson 4. Firms still on B then face a negative rent and must switch or exit.

Answer: adopt F; innovation rent 40 000 per year initially, competed away as the technology diffuses.

Practice

Problem 1

Write the equation of the isocost line for a cost of 120 when $w=15$ and $p=30$. Give both intercepts and the slope, and state which technologies from the table (A, B, E) lie on or below it.

Solution

Equation: $15L+30R=120$, i.e. $R = \dfrac{120}{30} - \dfrac{15}{30}L = 4 - 0.5L$.

Intercepts: vertical $c/p = 120/30 = 4$ tonnes of coal (if all money goes on coal); horizontal $c/w = 120/15 = 8$ workers. Slope $-w/p = -0.5$.

Which technologies? Costs: A $=15+180=195$; B $=60+60=120$; E $=150+30=180$. Only B lies exactly on the line; A and E are above it (more expensive). B is therefore the cost-minimising choice at these prices — unsurprising, since $w/p=0.5$ is the same ratio as in the $w=10,p=20$ case, and only the ratio matters for the choice.

Problem 2

A firm can produce one unit of output with any of: T1 = (2 workers, 9 tonnes), T2 = (5, 4), T3 = (9, 2), T4 = (6, 6). (a) Is any technology dominated? (b) Find the cheapest at $w=8$, $p=3$. (c) Find the cheapest at $w=3$, $p=8$.

Solution

(a) T4 (6,6) is dominated by T2 (5,4), which uses fewer of both. T1, T2 and T3 are mutually non-dominated.

(b) $w=8$, $p=3$ (labour dear, $w/p\approx2.67$): T1 $=16+27=43$; T2 $=40+12=52$; T3 $=72+6=78$; T4 $=48+18=66$. Cheapest: T1 at 43 — the labour-saving one.

(c) $w=3$, $p=8$ (energy dear, $w/p=0.375$): T1 $=6+72=78$; T2 $=15+32=47$; T3 $=27+16=43$; T4 $=18+48=66$. Cheapest: T3 at 43 — the energy-saving one.

Pattern: exactly reversing the prices reverses the choice. Note T4 is never chosen, as dominance guarantees.

Problem 3

Using T1 = (2, 9) and T2 = (5, 4) from Problem 2, find the relative price $w/p$ at which the firm is indifferent between them. For which values of $w/p$ is T1 chosen?

Solution

Set the costs equal: $2w + 9p = 5w + 4p$, so $5p = 3w$ and $\dfrac{w}{p} = \dfrac{5}{3} \approx 1.667$.

Which side? T1 uses less labour, so it becomes relatively more attractive as labour becomes more expensive: T1 is chosen when $w/p > 5/3$, T2 when $w/p < 5/3$.

Check with Problem 2(b): there $w/p = 8/3 \approx 2.67 > 1.667$ and T1 was indeed cheaper ✔. In 2(c), $w/p=0.375 < 1.667$ and T1 was the most expensive ✔.

Problem 4

The wage doubles from 10 to 20 and the coal price doubles from 20 to 40. Does the firm's chosen technology change? Does its cost change? Explain what this tells you about the model.

Solution

Choice: unchanged. The slope of the isocosts is $-w/p$, and $20/40 = 10/20 = 0.5$ — the relative price is identical, so the same isocost line orientation touches the same point, B.

Cost: doubles. B now costs $20(4)+40(2)=160$ instead of 80. Every isocost has shifted, but they are all parallel to their old positions.

Interpretation: technology choice depends only on relative prices, not on the price level. A general inflation that raises all input prices equally changes nominal costs but not the technique. This is why the model's historical claim is about the British wage-to-coal ratio, not about British wages being high in absolute terms.

Problem 5

Explain, using the model, why a carbon tax that raises the price of coal from 20 to 60 (with $w=10$) changes the firm's behaviour. Compute the new choice from technologies A, B, E and the cost increase.

Solution

New costs: A $=10+360=370$; B $=40+120=160$; E $=100+60=\mathbf{160}$. B and E tie at 160, so the firm is exactly indifferent; any further rise in $p$ tips it to E.

Check with the switching rule: B and E are indifferent at $w/p = 1/6$, and here $w/p = 10/60 = 1/6$ ✔.

Interpretation. Two things happen. First, a substitution effect: the isocosts flatten, so the firm moves towards the energy-saving technology E, cutting coal use from 2 tonnes to 1 per 100 metres. Second, costs rise from 80 to 160, which will reduce output and hence coal use further. The model also predicts a third, slower effect — induced innovation: with energy now expensive, the rent from inventing an energy-saving technology has grown, so R&D will be redirected towards it.

Problem 6

A firm currently uses B (4 workers, 2 tonnes) at $w=10$, $p=20$. A consultant offers technology G = (3 workers, 3 tonnes) for a one-off fee of 25 000. The firm produces 500 000 metres of cloth per year. Should it buy?

Solution

Step 1 — is G cheaper? G $=10(3)+20(3)=30+60=90$, against B at 80. G is more expensive at these prices, so the fee is irrelevant: the firm should not buy. (Note G does not dominate B, and B does not dominate G — G uses fewer workers but more coal — so the answer depends on prices.)

Step 2 — when would it be worth it? G beats B when $3w+3p < 4w+2p$, i.e. $p < w$. At the current prices $p=20 > w=10$, so no. If the wage rose above 20 (with coal unchanged), G would become the cheaper of the two — although A would then also need to be checked, since $w/p>4/3$ makes A a candidate too: at $w=25$, A $=25+120=145$, B $=100+40=140$, G $=75+60=135$, so G would win.

Result: do not buy at current prices; the deal is only worth revisiting if wages rise substantially relative to coal.

Problem 7

"British industrialists in 1780 adopted machines because they were more entrepreneurial than the French." Evaluate this claim using the model, and explain what induced innovation adds to the story.

Solution

The model's answer. Both countries faced the same technology set — the spinning jenny was published, described and copied, and the French knew about it. What differed was the isocost slope. Britain had high wages and cheap coal (steep isocosts, high $w/p$), so a labour-saving, energy-using technology minimised cost there. France had cheap labour and dearer energy (shallow isocosts), so the same machine raised costs. Both sets of firms were doing the same thing: choosing the lowest attainable isocost. No difference in culture or entrepreneurship is needed to explain the divergence, and invoking one is unfalsifiable.

What induced innovation adds. The argument so far only explains adoption from a fixed set. Induced innovation says the set itself is endogenous in the long run: because a labour-saving invention earns a larger innovation rent where labour is expensive, inventors in high-wage Britain had a stronger incentive to work on labour-saving machines in the first place. Relative prices thus shape both the choice among existing technologies and the direction of technical change — which is the mechanism behind modern arguments for carbon pricing as an innovation policy.

Caveat. The model is not the whole story: property rights, patents, access to capital, coal transport by canal, and scientific institutions all mattered. But relative prices are the part the model can make precise and test.

Summary

A firm's technology set is a list of input combinations that each produce the same output; dominated combinations — those using at least as much of everything — can be discarded before any prices are known. Cost is $wL+pR$, and the set of combinations with equal cost is an isocost line with slope $-w/p$ and intercepts $c/p$ and $c/w$. The firm picks the technology touched by the lowest attainable isocost, which is the same as computing $wL+pR$ for each survivor and taking the minimum. Because the slope depends only on relative prices, the choice switches at well-defined price ratios: expensive labour pushes the firm towards labour-saving technologies. Applied to the eighteenth century, that gives Allen's explanation of why Britain, with high wages and cheap coal, mechanised first — and, through induced innovation, why relative prices also steer which technologies get invented.

📌Key takeaways
  • Isocost: $c=wL+pR \Rightarrow R = c/p - (w/p)L$. Slope $-w/p$; intercepts $c/p$ (coal axis) and $c/w$ (labour axis).
  • Isocosts are parallel; lower lines are cheaper. Slope = markets, points = technology. Prices move the lines, never the points.
  • Discard dominated technologies first, then compute $wL+pR$ for the rest and take the minimum.
  • The switching ratio between two technologies comes from setting their costs equal and solving for $w/p$.
  • Only relative prices matter: doubling all prices changes cost but not the technique.
  • High $w/p$ (Britain: high wages, cheap coal) → labour-saving technology; low $w/p$ (France) → labour-intensive technology.
  • Induced innovation: relative prices also determine which new technologies it pays to invent.

quiz.q: Four technologies each produce one unit of output: P = (2 workers, 8 tonnes of coal), Q = (4, 4), R = (8, 2), S = (5, 9). Which is dominated?
options: P
Q
R
S
quiz.explain: S uses 5 workers and 9 tonnes, while Q uses 4 workers and 4 tonnes — less of both inputs. S is therefore more expensive than Q at every possible pair of prices and can never be cost-minimising. P, Q and R are mutually non-dominated: each uses less of one input and more of the other, so which one wins depends on the price ratio $w/p$.

quiz.q: Using P = (2, 8), Q = (4, 4), R = (8, 2) from the previous question, the wage is $w=4$ and coal costs $p=4$ per tonne. What is the minimum cost of producing one unit?
quiz.explain: P $=4(2)+4(8)=8+32=40$; Q $=4(4)+4(4)=16+16=\mathbf{32}$; R $=4(8)+4(2)=32+8=40$. The balanced technology Q wins, at a cost of 32. With $w/p=1$ the isocost has slope $-1$, and it is the middle technology that the lowest such line touches — neither extreme is cheapest when the two inputs cost the same.

quiz.q: The wage is 12 per worker and coal costs 4 per tonne. In a diagram with workers on the horizontal axis and coal on the vertical axis, an isocost line for a total cost of 96 has:
options: slope −3, vertical intercept 24, horizontal intercept 8
slope −1/3, vertical intercept 8, horizontal intercept 24
slope −3, vertical intercept 8, horizontal intercept 24
slope −1/3, vertical intercept 24, horizontal intercept 8
quiz.explain: Rearranging $96 = 12L + 4R$ gives $R = 96/4 - (12/4)L = 24 - 3L$. So the slope is $-w/p = -3$, the vertical (coal) intercept is $c/p = 96/4 = 24$ tonnes, and the horizontal (worker) intercept is $c/w = 96/12 = 8$ workers. A steep line like this means labour is expensive relative to coal: firing one worker frees up enough money to buy three tonnes of coal.

quiz.q: Technologies P = (2 workers, 8 tonnes) and Q = (4 workers, 4 tonnes). At which relative price of labour $w/p$ is the firm exactly indifferent between them?
quiz.explain: Set the two costs equal: $2w + 8p = 4w + 4p$, so $4p = 2w$ and $w/p = \mathbf{2}$. Check with $w=4,\ p=2$: P $=8+16=24$ and Q $=16+8=24$ ✔. For $w/p > 2$ the labour-saving technology P is cheaper; for $w/p < 2$ the more balanced Q wins. Only the ratio matters — $w=40,\ p=20$ gives exactly the same indifference.

quiz.q: Which statements about the technology-choice model are true?
options: Isocost lines for different cost levels are parallel to each other.
When the wage rises, the points of the technology set move to the left.
Doubling both the wage and the price of coal leaves the chosen technology unchanged.
A technology that is not dominated is chosen at some relative price.
The cost-minimising technology is always the one using the fewest total physical units of input.
quiz.explain: (1) True — the slope is $-w/p$, which does not depend on the cost level $c$. (3) True — only the ratio $w/p$ determines the slope, so proportional price changes raise cost but leave the technique unchanged. (4) True in this setting: each point on the non-dominated frontier is touched by the lowest isocost for some range of $w/p$. (2) is false and is the classic confusion: prices move the lines, while the technology set is engineering and stays put. (5) is false — adding workers and tonnes together is meaningless, since they have different prices; you must compute $wL+pR$.

quiz.q: Why, according to the model, did British firms adopt the spinning jenny while French firms mostly did not?
options: The French did not know about the technology
British firms were larger and could afford the machines
Britain had a high wage relative to the price of coal, making a labour-saving technology cost-minimising there
British workers were more productive than French workers
quiz.explain: The technology set was the same on both sides of the Channel — the machine was described, copied and well known. What differed was the isocost slope: Britain's high wages and cheap domestic coal meant a steep $w/p$, so a labour-saving, energy-using technology sat on a lower isocost there. At French relative prices (cheap labour, dearer energy) the same machine raised costs, so rejecting it was the cost-minimising decision, not a failure of enterprise. This is Robert Allen's argument, and it needs no assumption about culture or ability.

quiz.q: A textile firm can produce 100 metres of cloth with technology A = (1 worker, 6 tonnes of coal), B = (4, 2) or E = (10, 1). Currently $w=10$ and $p=20$. (a) Find the cost-minimising technology and its cost. (b) The government introduces a carbon tax that raises $p$ to 60. Recompute and describe both effects on coal use. (c) Instead of the tax, suppose a trade union raises the wage to 30 with $p=20$. Which technology is chosen, and what does this predict about the effect of high wages on technology? (d) Explain what induced innovation would add to your answer in (b).
quiz.solution:
(a) At $w=10$, $p=20$. A $=10(1)+20(6)=130$; B $=10(4)+20(2)=80$; E $=10(10)+20(1)=120$. The cost-minimising technology is B, at a cost of 80 per 100 metres. Geometrically, the relative price is $w/p=0.5$, so the isocosts have slope $-0.5$, and the lowest such line that reaches the technology set touches B.

(b) Carbon tax, $p=60$. A $=10+360=370$; B $=40+120=160$; E $=100+60=160$. B and E now cost the same, so the firm is exactly at the switching point $w/p = 10/60 = 1/6$; any further rise in $p$ makes E strictly cheapest. Two effects on coal use: (i) a substitution effect — the isocosts flatten and the firm moves towards the energy-saving technology, cutting coal from 2 tonnes to 1 tonne per 100 metres while raising employment from 4 to 10 workers; (ii) a scale effect — the minimum cost has doubled from 80 to 160, so at any given price of cloth the firm produces less, reducing coal use further. Both push in the same direction, which is why the tax works.

(c) Wage rises to 30, $p=20$. A $=30(1)+20(6)=150$; B $=30(4)+20(2)=160$; E $=30(10)+20(1)=320$. The firm switches to A, at a cost of 150. Check with the switching rule: A beats B when $w/p > 4/3$, and here $w/p = 1.5 > 1.33$ ✔. Prediction: expensive labour makes firms adopt labour-saving technology — employment per 100 metres falls from 4 workers to 1, while coal use triples. This is the mechanism behind the historical argument that high wages, rather than obstructing industry, caused mechanisation.

(d) Induced innovation. Parts (a)–(c) treat the technology set as fixed and exogenous; the firm only chooses among given points. Induced innovation makes the set itself endogenous over the longer run. Because the innovation rent from a new technology is proportional to the cost it saves, and cost savings are largest on the input that has become expensive, a high carbon price raises the payoff to inventing energy-saving technologies specifically. So the tax has a third effect beyond substitution and scale: it redirects research effort, adding entirely new points below the existing frontier — and specifically points that economise on coal rather than on labour. This is why economists argue that a credible, long-lasting carbon price is not merely a way of rationing existing coal use, but an innovation policy — and equally why a tax that is expected to be repealed produces much less innovation, since the expected rent is small.

test.sub: Summative test for Block 2 (Lessons 4–6): economic models, exogenous and endogenous variables, opportunity cost and economic cost, economic rent and reservation options, incentives, innovation rents and diffusion; absolute vs. comparative advantage, gains from specialisation and the terms of trade; technology sets, isocost lines, cost-minimising technology choice and switching prices. One step harder than the lesson quizzes — this is the material the midterm test is built from.

questions.q: In the model of Lesson 6, a firm chooses a technology given the wage and the price of coal. Which combination is correct?
options: The wage is endogenous; the chosen technology is exogenous
The wage is exogenous; the chosen technology and the firm's cost are endogenous
Both the wage and the technology are exogenous, since the firm cannot influence either
Everything in the model is endogenous, otherwise the model would not predict anything
questions.explain: The firm takes input prices as given from outside the model — they are exogenous — and the model explains which technology is picked and what production then costs, so those are endogenous. Option 3 confuses "the firm cannot influence it" with "the model does not explain it": the firm cannot influence the wage, but it certainly does choose the technology. Note also that the same variable can switch roles: in a model of the labour market, the wage becomes endogenous.

questions.q: Eva gives up a job paying 540 000 CZK per year to open a bakery. In its first year the bakery has revenue of 1 750 000 CZK and pays out 1 100 000 CZK for flour, rent, energy and staff. She also invests 400 000 CZK of her own savings, which would otherwise have earned 3 % interest. What is her economic profit in CZK?
questions.explain: Opportunity costs: forgone salary 540 000 plus forgone interest $0.03 \times 400\,000 = 12\,000$, so 552 000 CZK. Economic cost $= 1\,100\,000 + 552\,000 = 1\,652\,000$ CZK. Economic profit $= 1\,750\,000 - 1\,652\,000 = \mathbf{98\,000}$ CZK. Her accounting profit is 650 000 CZK — more than six times larger — because it ignores the two inputs she supplies herself and is never invoiced for.

questions.q: You bought a non-refundable theatre ticket for 900 CZK; you value the performance at 1 100 CZK. A friend then invites you to a concert the same evening; a ticket costs 700 CZK and you value the concert at 1 500 CZK. The theatre ticket cannot be resold. What should you do?
options: Go to the theatre, because you already paid 900 CZK and it would otherwise be wasted
Go to the concert, because its net benefit of 800 CZK is positive
Go to the theatre: its net benefit of 1 100 CZK exceeds the concert's 800 CZK, and the 900 CZK already paid is irrelevant to the comparison
Go to the concert: once the sunk 900 CZK is added, the theatre effectively costs 2 000 CZK
questions.explain: The 900 CZK is sunk: unrecoverable and identical under every option, so it drops out entirely. Looking forward, the theatre delivers a net benefit of 1 100 CZK (nothing more to pay) and the concert $1\,500-700 = 800$ CZK, so the theatre wins, 1 100 > 800. Its economic cost is $0 + 800 = 800$ CZK (out-of-pocket zero plus the forgone concert), giving a rent of $1\,100-800 = +300$ CZK. Option 1 reaches the right conclusion by the wrong route — the sunk-cost fallacy — which earns no marks in an exam; options 2 and 4 both let the sunk 900 CZK distort the comparison.

questions.q: A country needs 6 labour hours to produce one tonne of steel and 2 labour hours to produce one tonne of grain. What is the opportunity cost of one tonne of steel, measured in tonnes of grain?
questions.explain: With hours-per-unit data, divide the country's own two numbers: $6/2 = \mathbf{3}$ tonnes of grain. The six hours spent on a tonne of steel would have produced three tonnes of grain. The reciprocal check: one tonne of grain costs $2/6 = 1/3$ tonne of steel ✔. Never compare the 6 hours with another country's hours — comparative advantage only emerges after each country's internal ratio has been computed.

questions.q: Producer X can make 300 units of good 1 or 100 units of good 2 per week. Producer Y can make 120 units of good 1 or 60 units of good 2. Which statement is correct?
options: X should produce both goods, because X has an absolute advantage in both
X has a comparative advantage in good 1 and Y in good 2
Y has a comparative advantage in good 1 and X in good 2
There are no gains from trade, since X is better at everything
questions.explain: X has an absolute advantage in both (300 > 120 and 100 > 60), which decides nothing. Opportunity cost of one unit of good 2: X gives up $300/100 = 3$ units of good 1; Y gives up $120/60 = 2$. Y's cost is lower → Y specialises in good 2. Opportunity cost of one unit of good 1: X $= 100/300 \approx 0.33$ of good 2, Y $= 60/120 = 0.5$ → X specialises in good 1. Absolute advantage in both goods is always compatible with mutually profitable specialisation — that is the entire point of the model.

questions.q: Ivo can make 60 chairs or 20 tables per month; Jana can make 30 chairs or 30 tables. In autarky each splits their time evenly between the two. After full specialisation according to comparative advantage, by how many chairs does total chair output rise?
questions.explain: Opportunity cost of a table: Ivo $60/20 = 3$ chairs, Jana $30/30 = 1$ chair → Jana makes tables, Ivo makes chairs. Autarky: Ivo 30 chairs + 10 tables, Jana 15 chairs + 15 tables, totals 45 chairs and 25 tables. Full specialisation: Ivo 60 chairs, Jana 30 tables. Chairs rise from 45 to 60, i.e. by 15 — and tables rise from 25 to 30 as well, so both goods increase with no extra work or technology.

questions.q: Continuing with Ivo (opportunity cost of a table: 3 chairs) and Jana (1 chair), at which price would both gain from trading tables for chairs?
options: 0.5 chairs per table
1 chair per table
2 chairs per table
4 chairs per table
questions.explain: The price must lie strictly between the two opportunity costs: $1 < q < 3$ chairs per table. Only 2 qualifies. At $q = 1$ Jana is exactly indifferent and captures none of the gain; at $q = 0.5$ she would rather make chairs herself; at $q = 4$ Ivo would rather make his own tables (they only cost him 3 chairs). Every price inside the interval yields the same total gain — the price decides only how the gain is split, which is a bargaining question the model does not answer.

questions.q: Three technologies each produce one batch of output: V = (3 workers, 10 tonnes of coal), W = (6, 5), Z = (12, 2). The wage is 5 per worker and coal costs 4 per tonne. What is the minimum cost of a batch?
questions.explain: V $= 5(3)+4(10) = 15+40 = 55$; W $= 5(6)+4(5) = 30+20 = \mathbf{50}$; Z $= 5(12)+4(2) = 60+8 = 68$. The cheapest is W at 50. None of the three is dominated (each uses less of one input and more of the other), so all three had to be evaluated — and note that Z uses the least coal while V uses the fewest workers, yet neither is cheapest. Always compute $wL+pR$.

questions.q: The wage is 9 and coal costs 3 per tonne. With workers on the horizontal axis and coal on the vertical axis, the isocost line for a cost of 54 is:
questions.explain: From $54 = 9L + 3R$ we get $R = 54/3 - (9/3)L = \mathbf{18 - 3L}$. The vertical intercept is $c/p = 18$ tonnes, the horizontal intercept is $c/w = 54/9 = 6$ workers, and the slope is $-w/p = -3$: firing one worker saves 9, which buys three tonnes of coal. Options 2 and 4 swap the intercept $c/p$ for $c/w$; options 3 and 4 invert the price ratio.

questions.q: Which of the following statements are true?
options: A producer who has an absolute advantage in both goods can still gain by specialising and trading.
Doubling both the wage and the price of coal leaves the cost-minimising technology unchanged.
Sunk costs should be added to the opportunity cost of an action.
An equilibrium is by definition an outcome that no one would want to change if they could redesign the situation.
Innovation rent falls as more firms adopt the new technology.
Monetary incentives can reduce the behaviour they are meant to encourage.
questions.explain: (1) True — this is the core of comparative advantage; Greta beats Carlos at both goods and both still gain. (2) True — the isocost slope is $-w/p$, so a proportional rise in both prices raises cost but leaves the ratio, and therefore the choice, untouched. (5) True — as rivals adopt, the price falls towards the new cost and the rent is competed away; that is what makes the diffusion S-curve flatten. (6) True — the Swedish blood-donation experiment and the Haifa daycare fine both show monetary incentives crowding out intrinsic and social motivation. (3) is false: sunk costs are unrecoverable and identical under all options, so they are excluded entirely. (4) is false: equilibrium means self-perpetuating given everyone else's behaviour — a prisoners' dilemma equilibrium is one both players would happily replace.

questions.q: A firm can produce 100 units with technology A = (2 workers, 10 tonnes of coal), B = (5, 4) or C = (12, 1). Currently the wage is $w=4$ and coal costs $p=4$. (a) Find the cost-minimising technology and its cost, and state the isocost slope. (b) A carbon tax raises the coal price to $p=10$. Recompute the choice and explain the change in terms of the isocost diagram. (c) At the original prices, an engineer offers technology D = (4 workers, 3 tonnes). Compute the innovation rent per 100 units and the annual rent if the firm makes 50 000 units per year. (d) Explain what happens to that rent over the following years and why.
questions.solution:
(a) At $w=4$, $p=4$. A $=4(2)+4(10)=8+40=48$; B $=4(5)+4(4)=20+16=\mathbf{36}$; C $=4(12)+4(1)=48+4=52$. The cost-minimising technology is B at a cost of 36. The isocost slope is $-w/p = -1$: the two inputs cost the same, so one worker trades against one tonne of coal, and the balanced technology wins. (No technology is dominated here — each uses less of one input and more of the other — so all three had to be evaluated.)

(b) Carbon tax, $p=10$. A $=8+100=108$; B $=20+40=60$; C $=48+10=\mathbf{58}$. The firm switches to C, at a cost of 58. The isocost slope flattens from $-1$ to $-w/p = -0.4$, because a worker's wage now buys only 0.4 tonnes of coal. Flatter lines reach furthest towards the lower right of the diagram, which is exactly where the coal-saving, labour-intensive technologies sit — so the lowest attainable isocost now touches C rather than B. Note the technology set itself has not moved: prices rotate the lines, they never shift the points. Coal use per 100 units falls from 4 tonnes to 1, and employment rises from 5 workers to 12. On top of this substitution effect there is a scale effect: minimum cost has risen from 36 to 58, so the firm will produce less, cutting coal use further.

(c) Innovation rent from D. At $w=4$, $p=4$: D $=4(4)+4(3)=16+12=28$, against the previous minimum of 36 with B. D saves $36-28 = \mathbf{8}$ per 100 units. (D also uses fewer workers and less coal than C, so it dominates C outright.) Annual output of 50 000 units is $50\,000/100 = 500$ batches, so the annual innovation rent is $8 \times 500 = \mathbf{4\,000}$ while rivals stay on B.

(d) What happens to the rent. The rent is both a reward and a signal. Rival firms observe the innovator's above-normal profit and copy the technology; as they do, competition pushes the price of the product down towards the new, lower cost, and the rent per unit shrinks. Once adoption is complete the rent is zero and the innovator earns only a normal return. The process is asymmetric and therefore self-reinforcing: as the price falls below the old cost of 36, firms that have not adopted face a negative rent — losses on every unit — so standing still stops being a safe option and becomes an exit sentence. That combination of positive rent pulling adopters in and negative rent pushing laggards out produces the steep middle section of the S-shaped diffusion curve, which then flattens as the remaining rent disappears.

questions.q: Two countries each have 8 000 labour hours. Nord needs 4 hours per tonne of wheat and 16 hours per machine. Sud needs 10 hours per tonne of wheat and 20 hours per machine. (a) Determine absolute and comparative advantage. (b) Compute total output when each country splits its hours evenly. (c) Reallocate production so that the world still gets 450 machines and compute the gain. (d) Give the range of terms of trade, and show a price that splits the gain equally. (e) Name one reason the model's policy conclusion should be treated with caution.
questions.solution:
(a) Absolute advantage. Nord needs fewer hours for both goods (4 < 10 and 16 < 20), so it has an absolute advantage in both. This determines nothing.

Comparative advantage. Opportunity cost of one machine, in tonnes of wheat: Nord $16/4 = 4$; Sud $20/10 = 2$. Sud's cost is lower → Sud specialises in machines. Opportunity cost of one tonne of wheat, in machines: Nord $4/16 = 0.25$; Sud $10/20 = 0.5$ → Nord specialises in wheat. Check: within each country the two costs are reciprocals (4 and 0.25; 2 and 0.5) ✔.

(b) Autarky, 4 000 hours each way. Nord: $4000/4 = 1\,000$ tonnes of wheat and $4000/16 = 250$ machines. Sud: $4000/10 = 400$ tonnes and $4000/20 = 200$ machines. World totals: 1 400 tonnes of wheat and 450 machines.

(c) Reallocation keeping machines at 450. Machines should be made by the low-cost producer first, so Sud uses all 8 000 hours on machines: $8000/20 = 400$ machines. The remaining 50 machines must come from Nord, using $50 \times 16 = 800$ hours; Nord's other $8000-800 = 7\,200$ hours give $7200/4 = 1\,800$ tonnes of wheat. World totals: 1 800 tonnes of wheat and 450 machines — the same machines and 400 extra tonnes of wheat, from nothing but reallocation. (Note this is partial specialisation for Nord: complete specialisation by both would give 2 000 tonnes but only 400 machines, so machines would have to fall.)

(d) Terms of trade. One machine must exchange for between 2 and 4 tonnes of wheat — Sud will not sell below its own cost of 2, Nord will not buy above its own cost of 4. Take the midpoint, 3 tonnes per machine. Nord produces 1 800 tonnes and 50 machines, wants to consume 250 machines, so it imports 200 machines and pays $200 \times 3 = 600$ tonnes: it consumes 1 200 tonnes + 250 machines against an autarky bundle of 1 000 tonnes + 250 machines, a gain of +200 tonnes. Sud produces 400 machines, exports 200 and receives 600 tonnes: it consumes 600 tonnes + 200 machines against 400 tonnes + 200 machines, also +200 tonnes. The two gains sum to the 400 tonnes created in (c) ✔. At a price of 2 the whole gain would go to Nord, at 4 the whole gain to Sud; the price divides the surplus, specialisation creates it.

(e) Caution. Any one of the following: (i) the aggregate gain is not automatically shared — inside Nord, machine builders lose their jobs while the gains are spread thinly over consumers, so a majority of those directly affected can be worse off without compensation and retraining; (ii) the model compares two static equilibria and ignores adjustment costs, unemployment and regional decline during the transition; (iii) constant opportunity costs are an assumption — with rising costs specialisation is incomplete and the gains smaller; (iv) comparative advantage is not fixed: specialising in low-technology goods today can prevent the learning that would create tomorrow's advantage; (v) the terms of trade depend on bargaining power, so a small country facing a large buyer may capture almost none of the surplus.

lessons.html:
Every choice you make is a trade-off, and economics needs a way to write down what you are willing to trade for what. This lesson gives you that tool: utility and indifference curves. By the end you will be able to draw somebody's preferences on a graph, read their willingness to trade off the slope, and tell from the picture whether a person is a workaholic or a beach lover.

🎯Lesson objectives
  • Explain what a utility function does — and what it does not claim.
  • Define an indifference curve and justify all four of its standard properties.
  • Compute the marginal rate of substitution (MRS) and say what it means in one plain English sentence.
  • Explain diminishing MRS and link it to the convex shape of the curves.
  • Sketch indifference maps for two people with different tastes and compare them.

1 · The trade-off we will use all semester

Meet Tereza, a first-year student at VŠE with a part-time job at a café in Žižkov. She has 16 waking hours a day and can split them between two things she cares about:

  • Free time $t$ — hours per day she does not work: sleep-ins, gym, Netflix, friends.
  • Consumption $c$ — Czech crowns per day she can spend, which comes from the hours she does work.

Both are goods: more of either is better. But she cannot have more of both, because an hour spent earning money is an hour not spent at the gym. This is the scarcity problem from Lesson 1, now with two named axes. Everything in Block 3 — and later the whole theory of the firm, of borrowing and of climate policy — is built on exactly this picture.

📐Definition — preferences and utility

A person's preferences are a ranking of all possible bundles $(t,c)$: for any two bundles she can say which she prefers, or that she is indifferent. A utility function $u(t,c)$ is any formula that reproduces that ranking: bundle A is preferred to bundle B if and only if $u(A)>u(B)$.

Read that definition twice. Utility is a representation of a ranking, not a measurement of happiness in some universal unit. If Tereza's utility is $u=t\cdot c$, then the bundle $(8,\,1600)$ gives $u=12\,800$ and $(4,\,1600)$ gives $u=6400$. The only thing this says is the first bundle is better. It does not say it is "twice as good", and it certainly does not let you compare Tereza's 12 800 with somebody else's 12 800.

📌Why the numbers themselves do not matter

If $u=t\cdot c$ represents Tereza's preferences, so does $v=\sqrt{t\cdot c}$ or $w=\ln t+\ln c$ — any strictly increasing transformation keeps the ranking, and therefore keeps every indifference curve in exactly the same place. This is called ordinal utility. It is why economists draw curves rather than quote utility numbers.

2 · Indifference curves

📐Definition — indifference curve

An indifference curve joins all the bundles $(t,c)$ that give the same level of utility — bundles among which the person is indifferent. Algebraically it is the set of solutions to $u(t,c)=\bar u$ for a fixed number $\bar u$. A whole family of such curves is an indifference map.

With $u=t\cdot c$ and $\bar u=3200$, the indifference curve is $t\cdot c=3200$, i.e. $c=3200/t$. Tereza is equally happy with 4 hours of free time and 800 CZK, with 8 hours and 400 CZK, or with 16 hours and 200 CZK. Different lives, same utility.

ΣFour properties of well-behaved indifference curves
  1. They slope downward. Both $t$ and $c$ are goods. If you take an hour of free time away, the only way to keep utility unchanged is to give more consumption back. A flat or upward-sloping segment would mean more of both leaves you equally happy — a contradiction with "more is better".
  2. Curves further from the origin represent higher utility. Take any bundle and add a bit of both goods: you must be better off, and the new bundle lies up and to the right. So the whole map is ordered like contour lines on a hiking map.
  3. They never cross. Suppose curves $\bar u=10$ and $\bar u=20$ met at a point $X$. Then $X$ would have utility 10 and utility 20 at the same time — impossible, since $u$ assigns one number to each bundle. (Equivalently: indifference is transitive, and crossing curves would break transitivity.)
  4. They are convex to the origin — they bow inwards. They are steep on the left (little free time) and flat on the right (lots of free time). Section 4 explains why.
⚠Common error — "the curve gets flatter, so utility falls"

No. Along one indifference curve utility is constant by definition, however the slope changes. The slope tells you about willingness to trade, not about the level of wellbeing. Utility only changes when you move to a different curve.

3 · The marginal rate of substitution

📐Definition — MRS

The marginal rate of substitution of consumption for free time at a bundle is the absolute value of the slope of the indifference curve through that bundle:

$$\text{MRS}=\left|\frac{dc}{dt}\right|_{u=\bar u}.$$

In words: how many crowns of consumption you are willing to give up for one extra hour of free time, while staying exactly as well off as before.

The MRS is a statement about tastes only. It is measured in CZK per hour, so it can be compared directly with a wage — which is exactly what we will do in Lesson 8.

For $u=t\cdot c$ the curve is $c=\bar u/t$, so $dc/dt=-\bar u/t^{2}=-c/t$ and

$$\text{MRS}=\frac{c}{t}.$$

At the bundle $A=(8,400)$ that is $400/8=50$: Tereza would sacrifice 50 CZK for a ninth hour of free time and feel no different. At $(4,800)$ the MRS is $800/4=200$ — she is much more desperate for free time there, because she has very little of it and plenty of money.

💡How to remember which way round MRS goes

Read the slope as "rise over run" on the axes as drawn: MRS = (crowns given up) ÷ (hours gained) = CZK per hour. If your number comes out in "hours per crown", you have flipped it. And check the units against a wage — if a wage of 200 CZK/h and your MRS are not in the same units, something is wrong.

4 · Diminishing MRS and why curves bow inwards

📐Definition — diminishing MRS

Preferences show a diminishing marginal rate of substitution if, as you move down and to the right along an indifference curve (more free time, less consumption), the MRS falls. Diminishing MRS is exactly the same thing as the curve being convex to the origin.

The intuition is that people like balance. If Tereza works almost all day she is rich but exhausted: one more hour off is worth a lot of crowns to her. If she already lounges around 14 hours a day and is broke, one more hour off is worth almost nothing, but 50 CZK would be very welcome. So her willingness to pay for free time falls as she gets more of it.

Check it with the formula. Along $u=3200$: at $(4,800)$ the MRS is 200; at $(8,400)$ it is 50; at $(16,200)$ it is 12.5. Steadily falling — the curve flattens out as we move right, which is precisely what "convex to the origin" looks like.

📌The two extreme shapes

Straight-line indifference curves mean a constant MRS: the two goods are perfect substitutes and the person is happy at any mix. L-shaped curves mean the goods are perfect complements (left shoe / right shoe) — extra units of one alone are worthless. Real preferences over free time and consumption sit between these, which is exactly the convex case.

5 · Different people, different maps

Preferences differ, and the shape of the map is how we record that. Compare two students at the same bundle $(8\text{ h},400\text{ CZK})$:

Adam — loves free time

He is a competitive climber, lives with his parents and barely spends anything. At $(8,400)$ he would give up 150 CZK for one more free hour. His MRS is high, so his indifference curves are steep.

Bára — loves consumption

She is saving for an Erasmus semester in Lisbon. At the same bundle she would give up only 15 CZK for a free hour. Her MRS is low and her curves are flat.

⚠Common error — comparing utility numbers across people

"Adam's utility at that bundle is 3200 and Bára's is 800, so Adam is happier." Meaningless. Utility numbers are labels for one person's ranking; the scale is arbitrary. What you can compare across people is the MRS, because it is measured in real units (CZK per hour) and describes an actual willingness to trade.

📊Where this shows up in data analysis

MRS is the theoretical twin of a marginal willingness to pay, and estimating it is a whole industry. Discrete-choice models (conditional logit) fitted to survey or transaction data return coefficients whose ratio is exactly an MRS: divide the coefficient on "commuting time" by the coefficient on "rent" and you get a household's willingness to pay for a shorter commute, in CZK per minute. Hedonic regressions of Prague flat prices on distance to a metro station do the same job. Whenever you see "value of a statistical life" or "willingness to pay for cleaner air", somebody has estimated an MRS.

Worked examples

Example 1Plotting one indifference curve

Tereza's utility is $u(t,c)=t\cdot c$, $t$ in hours per day, $c$ in CZK per day. Find four bundles on the indifference curve through $(5,\,960)$ and state its equation.

1

Find the utility level. $\bar u=5\cdot 960=4800$.

2

Write the curve. $t\cdot c=4800 \Rightarrow c=\dfrac{4800}{t}$.

3

Tabulate. $t=4\Rightarrow c=1200$; $t=6\Rightarrow c=800$; $t=8\Rightarrow c=600$; $t=12\Rightarrow c=400$.

4

Sanity check. As $t$ rises, $c$ falls — the curve slopes down, as it must for two goods.

Result: $c=4800/t$; e.g. $(4,1200)$, $(6,800)$, $(8,600)$, $(12,400)$ all give the same utility as $(5,960)$.
Example 2Reading a diminishing MRS out of a table

A student says these five bundles are all equally good to her. Compute the MRS between consecutive bundles and check whether the MRS diminishes.

BundleABCDE
free time $t$ (h)4681012
consumption $c$ (CZK)16001000700560500
1

What we compute. Between two neighbouring bundles, MRS $\approx \left|\Delta c/\Delta t\right|$ — crowns given up per hour gained.

2

A→B: $|1000-1600|/2=600/2=\mathbf{300}$ CZK per hour.

3

B→C: $300/2=\mathbf{150}$. C→D: $140/2=\mathbf{70}$. D→E: $60/2=\mathbf{30}$.

4

Interpret. 300 → 150 → 70 → 30: the more free time she already has, the fewer crowns an extra hour is worth to her. That is a diminishing MRS, so her curve is convex to the origin.

Result: MRS = 300, 150, 70, 30 CZK/h — strictly diminishing, so the preferences are well behaved (convex).
Example 3Which bundle is preferred — and by how much is a trap

With $u=t\cdot c$, rank the bundles $P=(6,600)$, $Q=(9,400)$ and $R=(4,1000)$. Is $R$ "better by 400 units"?

1

Evaluate. $u(P)=6\cdot600=3600$, $u(Q)=9\cdot400=3600$, $u(R)=4\cdot1000=4000$.

2

Rank. $P$ and $Q$ have the same utility, so they lie on the same indifference curve; $R$ lies on a higher curve, so $R\succ P\sim Q$.

3

The trap. "Better by 400" is meaningless. Represent the same preferences by $v=\sqrt{t c}$: then $v(P)=v(Q)=60$ and $v(R)\approx 63.2$, a gap of 3.2. The ranking is unchanged; the "size" of the gap is not a fact about the world.

Result: $R\succ P\sim Q$. The order is meaningful, the differences are not.
Example 4Reading tastes off the utility function

Adam has $u_A=t^{0.75}c^{0.25}$ and Bára has $u_B=t^{0.25}c^{0.75}$. For a Cobb–Douglas utility $u=t^{a}c^{1-a}$ the MRS equals $\dfrac{a}{1-a}\cdot\dfrac{c}{t}$. Compute both MRS at $(8,400)$ and interpret.

1

Adam. $a=0.75$, so $\dfrac{a}{1-a}=3$ and MRS$_A=3\cdot\dfrac{400}{8}=3\cdot 50=150$ CZK/h.

2

Bára. $a=0.25$, so $\dfrac{a}{1-a}=\dfrac13$ and MRS$_B=\dfrac13\cdot 50\approx 16.7$ CZK/h.

3

Interpret. At the very same bundle Adam would pay 150 CZK for an extra free hour, Bára under 17 CZK. Adam's curve through that point is nine times steeper than Bára's.

4

Look ahead. Facing a wage of 200 CZK/h, both would find the wage above their MRS at this bundle — both would be tempted to work more. That comparison of MRS with the wage is the whole of Lesson 8.

Result: MRS$_A=150$ CZK/h, MRS$_B\approx16.7$ CZK/h — Adam's map is steep, Bára's is flat.

Practice

Problem 1

With $u=t\cdot c$, find three more bundles on the indifference curve through $(10,\,360)$, and state the equation of the curve.

Solution

Procedure: compute the utility level, then invert. $\bar u=10\cdot360=3600$, so the curve is $c=3600/t$.

$t=4\Rightarrow c=900$; $t=6\Rightarrow c=600$; $t=12\Rightarrow c=300$.

Result: $c=3600/t$; e.g. $(4,900)$, $(6,600)$, $(12,300)$.

Problem 2

Still with $u=t\cdot c$ (so MRS $=c/t$): compute the MRS at $(4,900)$ and at $(12,300)$, both on the curve $\bar u=3600$. Explain in one sentence, without formulas, why the second number is smaller.

Solution

At $(4,900)$: MRS $=900/4=225$ CZK per hour. At $(12,300)$: MRS $=300/12=25$ CZK per hour.

Explanation: at the first bundle she is time-poor and cash-rich, so an extra hour off is worth a lot of crowns; at the second she already has plenty of free time and little money, so she values the crowns much more than yet another hour.

Result: 225 CZK/h and 25 CZK/h — a diminishing MRS.

Problem 3

Prove that two indifference curves of the same person cannot cross. Use the "more is better" assumption and transitivity.

Solution

Suppose curve $I_1$ and curve $I_2$ cross at bundle $X$. Take a bundle $Y$ on $I_1$ only and a bundle $Z$ on $I_2$ only, chosen so that $Z$ has more of both goods than $Y$.

Because $Y$ and $X$ are on the same curve, $Y\sim X$. Because $X$ and $Z$ are on the same curve, $X\sim Z$. Transitivity then gives $Y\sim Z$.

But $Z$ has more of both goods than $Y$, so by "more is better" $Z\succ Y$. Contradiction. Hence the curves cannot cross.

Result: crossing curves would force a bundle to have two different utility levels at once — impossible.

Problem 4

These four bundles lie on one indifference curve: $(3,\,1800)$, $(5,\,1200)$, $(9,\,700)$, $(13,\,540)$. Compute the MRS on each of the three segments and say whether the preferences are convex.

Solution

Segment 1: $\Delta c=1200-1800=-600$, $\Delta t=2$, MRS $=600/2=300$ CZK/h.

Segment 2: $\Delta c=700-1200=-500$, $\Delta t=4$, MRS $=500/4=125$ CZK/h.

Segment 3: $\Delta c=540-700=-160$, $\Delta t=4$, MRS $=160/4=40$ CZK/h.

300 > 125 > 40, so the MRS diminishes as free time rises.

Result: yes, the preferences are convex — the curve bows in towards the origin.

Problem 5

Two friends are both at the bundle $(6\text{ h},\,1200\text{ CZK})$. Jana's MRS there is 300 CZK/h; Petr's is 60 CZK/h. (a) Whose indifference curve through that bundle is steeper? (b) A neighbour offers either of them 150 CZK to babysit for one hour. Who accepts?

Solution

(a) The MRS is the absolute slope, so Jana's curve (MRS 300) is steeper — she values free time more.

(b) Giving up an hour of free time costs Jana the equivalent of 300 CZK; 150 CZK does not compensate her, so she refuses. For Petr the hour is worth only 60 CZK, so 150 CZK makes him strictly better off — he accepts.

Result: (a) Jana's; (b) only Petr accepts. Rule of thumb: accept if the payment exceeds your MRS.

Problem 6

A student claims: "My indifference curve for free time and consumption is the straight line $c=2000-100t$." What does this imply about his MRS, and what kind of preferences is he describing? Is such a curve consistent with "more is better"?

Solution

Slope $dc/dt=-100$ everywhere, so MRS $=100$ CZK/h at every bundle — it does not diminish.

He is describing free time and consumption as perfect substitutes at a fixed rate: one hour always trades for exactly 100 CZK, no matter how much of each he already has.

It is perfectly consistent with "more is better" — the curve still slopes down and higher lines are better. It only violates the extra assumption of a diminishing MRS (strict convexity). It is a legitimate but unusual preference; most people like balance.

Result: constant MRS = 100 CZK/h; perfect substitutes; consistent with monotonicity, not with strict convexity.

Problem 7

With $u=t^{0.5}c^{0.5}$ (so MRS $=c/t$), a student is at $(4,\,1000)$. She is offered a deal: 3 extra hours of free time in exchange for 600 CZK. Should she take it? Compute her utility before and after.

Solution

Before: $u=\sqrt{4\cdot 1000}=\sqrt{4000}\approx 63.2$. After the deal the bundle is $(7,400)$: $u=\sqrt{7\cdot 400}=\sqrt{2800}\approx 52.9$.

So she should refuse. Why? The deal charges her $600/3=200$ CZK per hour, but her MRS at the starting bundle is only $1000/4=250$ — that looks acceptable at first. The problem is that the MRS falls as she gains hours: by $(7,400)$ it is down to $400/7\approx 57$. Averaged over the whole 3-hour jump she is willing to pay far less than 200 CZK per hour.

Result: refuse — utility falls from about 63.2 to about 52.9. Comparing the initial MRS with a price only works for small changes.

Problem 8

Sketch (in words is fine) the indifference map of a person for whom free time is a bad: a workaholic who is miserable when idle, but still likes consumption. What happens to the slope of the curves, and where does utility increase?

Solution

If free time is a bad, then giving him more of it reduces utility, so to stay indifferent he must be compensated with more consumption. Along one curve, more $t$ goes with more $c$: the curves slope upward.

Utility rises as you move up and to the left: more consumption, less free time. So the "better" direction is north-west, not north-east.

Result: upward-sloping indifference curves; utility increases towards the top-left. The downward slope in the standard picture is a consequence of both variables being goods, not a law of nature.

Summary

Preferences are a ranking; a utility function is just a convenient way of writing that ranking down, and only its order carries information. Drawing the ranking as contour lines gives the indifference map: downward-sloping, never crossing, higher is better, convex to the origin. The slope of a curve at a point — the MRS — is the single most useful number on the whole picture, because it is measured in crowns per hour and can therefore be compared with a wage. In Lesson 8 we add what Tereza can actually afford, and the optimum will be the point where her MRS meets the wage.

📌Key takeaways
  • Utility is ordinal. Only "higher / lower / equal" is meaningful; the numbers and their differences are not.
  • An indifference curve joins equally-good bundles: $u(t,c)=\bar u$.
  • Four properties: slopes down (both are goods), higher curves are better, curves never cross (transitivity), convex to the origin (diminishing MRS).
  • MRS = absolute slope = crowns you would give up for one more hour of free time, in CZK per hour.
  • Diminishing MRS = you value whichever good is scarce for you; steep on the left, flat on the right.
  • Steep map = loves free time; flat map = loves consumption. The MRS at a given bundle is the honest way to compare two people.

quiz.q: Tereza's utility is $u(t,c)=t\cdot c$ and she is currently at the bundle $(6\text{ h},\,500\text{ CZK})$. Which of the following bundles lies on the same indifference curve?
quiz.explain: The current utility level is $6\cdot 500=3000$, so the indifference curve is $t\cdot c=3000$. Check each: $10\cdot 300=3000$ ✓; $5\cdot 700=3500$ (a higher curve, strictly preferred); $12\cdot 200=2400$ (a lower curve); $4\cdot 800=3200$ (also higher). Only the first bundle leaves her exactly as well off.

quiz.q: With $u=t\cdot c$ the marginal rate of substitution equals $c/t$. What is the MRS at the bundle $(5\text{ h},\,900\text{ CZK})$, in CZK per hour?
quiz.explain: MRS $=c/t=900/5=180$ CZK per hour. Meaning: at that bundle she would hand over 180 CZK for one extra hour of free time and feel exactly the same. Note the units — crowns per hour — which is what lets us compare the MRS directly with a wage in the next lesson.

quiz.q: Why can two indifference curves of the same person never cross?
options: Because both curves slope downward
Because at the crossing point the bundle would have to give two different utility levels at once
Because the MRS must diminish along every curve
Because the curves would then have the same slope everywhere
quiz.explain: A utility function assigns exactly one number to each bundle. If curves for $\bar u=10$ and $\bar u=20$ met at bundle $X$, then $u(X)$ would be both 10 and 20 — a contradiction. Equivalently, transitivity plus 'more is better' is violated: the crossing would force you to be indifferent between two bundles when one clearly has more of both goods. Downward slope and diminishing MRS are separate properties and neither of them rules out crossing on its own.

quiz.q: A student says the bundles $(6\text{ h},\,1400\text{ CZK})$ and $(9\text{ h},\,800\text{ CZK})$ are equally good for her. What is her average MRS between these two bundles, in CZK per hour?
quiz.explain: MRS $=\left|\Delta c/\Delta t\right|=\left|(800-1400)/(9-6)\right|=600/3=200$ CZK per hour. She gives up 600 CZK for 3 extra hours, i.e. 200 CZK per hour on average over that stretch. Careful: this is an average over a 3-hour move. Because the MRS diminishes, the true MRS is above 200 at the start of the move and below 200 at the end.

quiz.q: Adam and Bára are at the same bundle. Adam's indifference curve through it is much steeper than Bára's. What follows?
options: Adam has higher utility than Bára
Adam values an extra hour of free time more highly, in crowns, than Bára does
Adam's preferences are not convex
Adam consumes more than Bára
quiz.explain: A steeper curve means a larger absolute slope, i.e. a larger MRS, i.e. more crowns willingly given up for one more hour of free time. That is a genuine, comparable statement about tastes. It says nothing about who is 'happier' — utility numbers are ordinal labels that cannot be compared across people — and nothing about convexity or about how much each of them actually consumes (they are at the same bundle).

quiz.q: Which of the following statements about well-behaved preferences over free time and consumption are correct?
options: Along a single indifference curve utility is constant, even though the slope changes
Utility functions $u=t\cdot c$ and $v=\ln t+\ln c$ produce exactly the same indifference curves
A diminishing MRS is the same thing as indifference curves being convex to the origin
If bundle A gives utility 400 and bundle B gives 200, then A is exactly twice as good as B
quiz.explain: The first is the definition of an indifference curve — the flattening slope tells you about willingness to trade, not about the level of wellbeing. The second holds because $v=\ln(t\cdot c)$ is a strictly increasing transformation of $u$, and such transformations preserve the ranking and therefore every curve. The third is simply two names for the same geometric fact. The fourth is the classic ordinality error: only the order of utility numbers is meaningful, never their ratios or differences.

quiz.q: A person's indifference curves between free time and consumption are straight downward-sloping lines. What does this say about him?
options: He treats free time and consumption as perfect complements
His MRS is constant, so he treats the two goods as perfect substitutes at a fixed rate
His preferences violate 'more is better'
He is indifferent between all bundles
quiz.explain: A straight line has a constant slope, so the MRS is the same at every bundle: one hour always trades against the same number of crowns, whatever mix he already has. That is the definition of perfect substitutes. Perfect complements would give L-shaped curves. 'More is better' is not violated — the lines still slope down and higher lines are still better; what is lost is the extra assumption of a diminishing MRS.

quiz.q: Explain, without using any formula, what a diminishing marginal rate of substitution means for a student choosing between free time and consumption, and why it makes indifference curves convex to the origin. Illustrate with a concrete bundle at each end of one curve.
quiz.solution:
What the MRS is. The MRS at a bundle is the number of crowns of consumption a student would willingly give up in exchange for one more hour of free time, while staying exactly as well off as before. It is measured in CZK per hour and it is the absolute slope of the indifference curve at that bundle.

What 'diminishing' means. As we move along one and the same indifference curve towards more free time and less consumption, that number gets smaller. The student values whichever good she currently has little of.

Concrete illustration. Take one curve. At its left-hand end she has 4 hours of free time and 900 CZK a day: she is time-poor and cash-rich, exhausted from working, so an extra hour off is worth a great deal — say 225 CZK. At the right-hand end of the same curve she has 12 hours free and only 300 CZK: she is bored and broke, so a thirteenth idle hour is worth almost nothing — say 25 CZK. Same utility level at both ends, very different willingness to trade.

Why this is convexity. The MRS is the steepness of the curve. A high MRS on the left means the curve starts steep; a low MRS on the right means it ends flat. A curve that is steep at the left and flat at the right bows in towards the origin — that is exactly what 'convex to the origin' means. Economically, convexity is a formal statement that people prefer balanced bundles to extreme ones: an average of two equally good extreme bundles is at least as good as either extreme.

lessons.html:
Lesson 7 told you what Tereza wants. This lesson adds what she can actually get, and then puts the two together. The result — choose the point where your marginal rate of substitution equals the marginal rate of transformation — is the single most reusable piece of machinery in the whole course: the same diagram will later explain how a firm sets prices, how you split income between today and tomorrow, and how a farmer and a landowner divide a harvest.

🎯Lesson objectives
  • Write down the feasible frontier from a wage and a time endowment, and draw the feasible set.
  • Interpret the slope of the frontier as the marginal rate of transformation (MRT) and as the opportunity cost of free time.
  • Explain and apply the optimality condition MRS = MRT, and argue why any other feasible point is worse.
  • Solve a constrained-choice problem numerically, both from a table and from a utility function.
  • Predict how the optimum moves when the frontier rotates or shifts.

1 · What is feasible

Tereza has 16 waking hours a day (call this the time endowment $T=16$; the other 8 are sleep, which we treat as fixed). If she takes $t$ hours of free time, she works $h=T-t=16-t$ hours. Her café pays $w$ crowns an hour, she has no other income and no savings, so she can spend

$$c=w\,(T-t)=w\,(16-t).$$
📐Definition — feasible frontier and feasible set

The feasible frontier is the set of bundles $(t,c)$ that use up the constraint exactly — here the straight line $c=w(T-t)$. The feasible set is everything on or below the frontier (and with $t\le T$): all bundles she could actually have. Bundles above the frontier are infeasible.

This is a technical and biological constraint, not a preference. The 16 hours come from human physiology and the day; the wage comes from the labour market. Neither has anything to do with what Tereza likes.

With $w=150$ CZK/h the frontier runs from $(0,\,2400)$ — work all 16 waking hours, earn 2400 CZK, no life — to $(16,\,0)$ — pure leisure, nothing to eat. Everything in the triangle between them is feasible.

2 · The slope of the frontier: MRT

Rewrite the frontier as $c=wT-wt$. It is a straight line with intercept $wT$ and slope

$$\frac{dc}{dt}=-w.$$
📐Definition — marginal rate of transformation

The marginal rate of transformation (MRT) is the absolute value of the slope of the feasible frontier: the amount of consumption you must give up to obtain one extra hour of free time. Here

$$\text{MRT}=w.$$

It is exactly the opportunity cost of an hour of free time, measured in CZK per hour.

At $w=150$, one hour off costs 150 CZK of forgone consumption. That is not a metaphor: it is the wage she does not earn. Notice that both MRS and MRT are in CZK per hour, so they are directly comparable — which is the whole trick.

⚠Common error — mixing up MRS and MRT

They look symmetric and they are measured in the same units, but they come from completely different places.

  • MRS = slope of an indifference curve = what you are willing to give up. It comes from preferences. It changes as you slide along the curve.
  • MRT = slope of the feasible frontier = what you must give up. It comes from technology, prices and the wage. Here it is constant, because the frontier is a straight line.

Memory hook: S for Subjective (taste), T for Technical (the world). A change in taste moves the MRS; a pay rise moves the MRT.

3 · The optimum: MRS = MRT

Tereza wants the highest indifference curve that still touches the feasible set. Because the curves are convex and the frontier is a straight line, that curve touches the frontier at exactly one point — it is tangent there. At a tangency the two slopes are equal:

ΣThe constrained-choice rule

At the optimal bundle $(t^\ast,c^\ast)$, provided it is not a corner,

$$\boxed{\ \text{MRS}=\text{MRT}=w\ }$$

and the bundle lies on the frontier: $c^\ast=w(T-t^\ast)$. Two equations, two unknowns.

The argument for why no other feasible point can be better is worth internalising, because you will be asked for it:

  • If MRS > MRT (indifference curve steeper than the frontier): an extra hour of free time is worth more to you than the wage it costs. Take it. Move right along the frontier — utility rises.
  • If MRS < MRT (curve flatter than the frontier): the hour you are enjoying is worth less to you than the wage you could earn. Sell it. Move left along the frontier — utility rises.
  • Only when MRS = MRT is there no direction left that improves things. Additionally, any point strictly inside the feasible set is beaten by a point on the frontier directly above it (more consumption, same free time), so the optimum must lie on the frontier.

4 · Solving it with numbers

Throughout this lesson Tereza's preferences are represented by

$$u(t,c)=c+900\sqrt{t},\qquad\text{so}\qquad \text{MRS}=\frac{450}{\sqrt{t}}.$$
