You are not expected to derive that MRS in this course — you will be given it, or given a table. What you must be able to do is use it. The recipe is always the same three steps:

  1. Write the frontier: $c=w(T-t)$, so MRT $=w$.
  2. Set MRS $=w$ and solve for $t^\ast$.
  3. Put $t^\ast$ back into the frontier to get $c^\ast$, and report hours worked $h^\ast=T-t^\ast$.
💡Always sanity-check the answer

Is $0\le t^\ast\le T$? Is $c^\ast\ge 0$? Does $c^\ast$ really equal $w(T-t^\ast)$? And does the story make sense — a higher wage should not produce a starving worker. Two minutes of checking saves whole exam questions.

5 · When the frontier moves

Two very different things can happen to the frontier, and the exam loves to test whether you can tell them apart.

A higher wage — the frontier rotates

The point $(T,0)$ is fixed (no work, no income, whatever the wage), but the intercept $wT$ rises. The frontier gets steeper: MRT rises. Both the price of free time and total achievable income change at once — which is why Lesson 9 has to split the effect in two.

Unearned income — the frontier shifts up

A grant, a scholarship or a parental transfer of $M$ crowns a day gives $c=M+w(T-t)$. The slope is unchanged at $-w$, so MRT is unchanged; the whole line moves up by $M$. The price of free time is the same, you are simply richer.

⚠Common error — "a higher wage always means working more"

The picture above shows one possible answer, not the general one. Rotating the frontier makes free time more expensive (push towards working more) and makes Tereza richer (push towards buying more free time). Which push wins depends on preferences. In Lesson 9 you will see a perfectly sensible utility function for which the optimum stays at $t^\ast=8$ no matter what the wage is, and data showing that over 150 years wages went up while hours worked went sharply down.

📌Corner solutions

The tangency rule assumes the optimum is inside the frontier's range. If the wage is so low that MRS $>$ MRT at every feasible point, the best you can do is the corner $t^\ast=T$ — do not work at all. Here that happens when $w<450/\sqrt{16}=112.5$ CZK/h. This is precisely the logic behind a reservation wage: below it, nobody takes the job.

📊Where this shows up in data analysis

"Maximise an objective subject to a constraint, and the answer is a tangency" is the skeleton of an enormous amount of applied work. Portfolio choice puts expected return against risk and finds the tangency of an indifference curve with the efficient frontier. Machine learning with an $\ell_1$ or $\ell_2$ penalty (LASSO, ridge) is literally "minimise loss subject to a budget on the coefficients", and the picture in every textbook is a loss contour touching a constraint set. When you later run `optim()` in R or `scipy.optimize` in Python, the first-order condition it is hunting for is a MRS = MRT condition in disguise.

Worked examples

Example 1Finding the optimum from a table

A student has $T=16$ waking hours and a wage of $w=250$ CZK/h. Her MRS at various points on the frontier has been measured and is shown below. Find her optimum.

free time $t$ (h)4681012
consumption $c=250(16-t)$30002500200015001000
MRS (CZK/h)700480330250190
1

Find the MRT. The frontier is $c=250(16-t)$, a straight line of slope $-250$, so MRT $=250$ CZK/h at every point.

2

Compare at $t=8$. MRS $=330>250=$ MRT. An extra hour off is worth 330 CZK to her but only costs 250 CZK of forgone wages — she should take it and move right.

3

Compare at $t=12$. MRS $=190<250=$ MRT. The twelfth hour of idleness is worth only 190 CZK to her, but selling it earns 250 CZK — she should work more and move left.

4

Find the crossing. At $t=10$, MRS $=250=$ MRT. No further improvement is available in either direction.

Result: $t^\ast=10$ hours of free time, $h^\ast=6$ hours of work, $c^\ast=250\cdot 6=1500$ CZK per day.
Example 2Solving it algebraically, and checking that nothing else beats it

Tereza has $u(t,c)=c+900\sqrt{t}$ (so MRS $=450/\sqrt{t}$), $T=16$ and $w=150$ CZK/h. Find the optimum and verify that two other feasible bundles are worse.

1

Frontier. $c=150(16-t)=2400-150t$, so MRT $=150$.

2

Tangency. $\dfrac{450}{\sqrt{t}}=150 \Rightarrow \sqrt{t}=\dfrac{450}{150}=3 \Rightarrow t^\ast=9$ hours.

3

Back to the frontier. $c^\ast=150(16-9)=150\cdot 7=1050$ CZK; hours worked $h^\ast=7$.

4

Utility there. $u^\ast=1050+900\sqrt{9}=1050+2700=3750$.

5

Check two rivals on the frontier. At $t=4$: $c=150\cdot 12=1800$, $u=1800+900\cdot 2=3600<3750$. At $t=12$: $c=150\cdot 4=600$, $u=600+900\sqrt{12}\approx 600+3118=3718<3750$. Both worse, as the tangency argument predicts.

Result: $t^\ast=9$ h free time, $h^\ast=7$ h of work, $c^\ast=1050$ CZK/day, $u^\ast=3750$.
Example 3A pay rise: the frontier rotates

Same student, same preferences (MRS $=450/\sqrt{t}$, $T=16$). The café raises her wage to $w=225$ CZK/h. What happens to her choice?

1

New frontier. $c=225(16-t)=3600-225t$. The intercept rises from 2400 to 3600; the point $(16,0)$ is unchanged, so the line has rotated and is steeper. New MRT $=225$.

2

New tangency. $\dfrac{450}{\sqrt{t}}=225\Rightarrow \sqrt{t}=2\Rightarrow t^\ast=4$ hours.

3

New bundle. $c^\ast=225(16-4)=225\cdot 12=2700$ CZK; $h^\ast=12$ hours of work. Utility $u^\ast=2700+900\cdot 2=4500$, up from 3750.

4

Interpret. Free time got more expensive (150 → 225 CZK an hour) and for these particular preferences she responds by buying much less of it: hours worked jump from 7 to 12. She is better off, but her life is busier.

Result: $t^\ast$ falls 9 → 4 h, $h^\ast$ rises 7 → 12 h, $c^\ast$ rises 1050 → 2700 CZK, utility 3750 → 4500.
Example 4Preferences for which the wage does not matter at all

Her flatmate Marek has $u(t,c)=t\cdot c$, so MRS $=c/t$. With $T=16$, find his optimum at $w=200$ and again at $w=300$ CZK/h.

1

Set up. Frontier $c=w(16-t)$, MRT $=w$. Tangency: $\dfrac{c}{t}=w$, i.e. $c=wt$.

2

Combine. $wt=w(16-t)$. Divide both sides by $w$ (it is positive): $t=16-t$, hence $t^\ast=8$ — the wage cancels out.

3

At $w=200$: $t^\ast=8$, $h^\ast=8$, $c^\ast=200\cdot 8=1600$. Check MRS $=1600/8=200=w$ ✓.

4

At $w=300$: $t^\ast=8$, $h^\ast=8$, $c^\ast=300\cdot 8=2400$. Check MRS $=2400/8=300=w$ ✓.

5

Interpret. Marek works exactly 8 hours whatever he is paid; the whole pay rise goes into consumption. Compare with Tereza in Example 3, who worked five hours more. Same wage change, opposite-looking behaviour — the difference is entirely in the preferences. This is the puzzle Lesson 9 resolves.

Result: $t^\ast=8$ at both wages; $c^\ast$ rises from 1600 to 2400 CZK/day.

Practice

Problem 1

A student has $T=16$ waking hours and earns $w=180$ CZK/h with no other income. (a) Write the equation of the feasible frontier. (b) How much can she consume if she takes 10 hours of free time? (c) What is the MRT, and what does it mean in words?

Solution

(a) Hours worked are $16-t$, so $c=180(16-t)=2880-180t$.

(b) $c=180(16-10)=180\cdot 6=1080$ CZK per day.

(c) The slope is $-180$, so MRT $=180$ CZK per hour. In words: one extra hour of free time costs her 180 CZK of forgone consumption — that is the opportunity cost of leisure, and it comes entirely from the wage, not from her tastes.

Result: $c=2880-180t$; 1080 CZK; MRT $=180$ CZK/h.

Problem 2

Tereza's MRS is $450/\sqrt{t}$, $T=16$. Her wage rises to $w=180$ CZK/h. Find $t^\ast$, $h^\ast$, $c^\ast$ and her utility if $u=c+900\sqrt{t}$.

Solution

Frontier: $c=180(16-t)$, MRT $=180$.

Tangency: $450/\sqrt{t}=180\Rightarrow\sqrt{t}=2.5\Rightarrow t^\ast=6.25$ hours.

Hours worked: $h^\ast=16-6.25=9.75$. Consumption: $c^\ast=180\cdot 9.75=1755$ CZK.

Utility: $u=1755+900\cdot 2.5=1755+2250=4005$.

Check: $0\le 6.25\le 16$ ✓, $c^\ast>0$ ✓, and it sits between the $w=150$ answer ($t=9$) and the $w=225$ answer ($t=4$), as it should.

Result: $t^\ast=6.25$ h, $h^\ast=9.75$ h, $c^\ast=1755$ CZK, $u=4005$.

Problem 3

Two students face the same wage $w=200$ CZK/h and the same $T=16$. Ondřej's MRS is $450/\sqrt{t}$; Klára's is $600/\sqrt{t}$. Who works more, and why does that make sense?

Solution

Ondřej: $450/\sqrt{t}=200\Rightarrow\sqrt{t}=2.25\Rightarrow t^\ast=5.0625$ h, so $h^\ast\approx 10.94$ h.

Klára: $600/\sqrt{t}=200\Rightarrow\sqrt{t}=3\Rightarrow t^\ast=9$ h, so $h^\ast=7$ h.

Klára works less. At any given bundle her MRS is higher — she is willing to pay more crowns for an hour off — so her indifference curves are steeper and the tangency with the same frontier occurs further to the right.

Result: Ondřej works about 10.9 h, Klára 7 h. Steeper preferences (higher MRS) → more free time at the same wage.

Problem 4

A student with $u=t\cdot c$ (MRS $=c/t$) has $T=14$ usable hours and $w=250$ CZK/h. Find the optimum. Then her university cuts lecture obligations and $T$ rises to 16. What happens?

Solution

Tangency: $c/t=w\Rightarrow c=wt$. Frontier: $c=w(T-t)$. So $wt=w(T-t)\Rightarrow t^\ast=T/2$.

With $T=14$: $t^\ast=7$ h, $h^\ast=7$ h, $c^\ast=250\cdot 7=1750$ CZK.

With $T=16$: $t^\ast=8$ h, $h^\ast=8$ h, $c^\ast=250\cdot 8=2000$ CZK.

Interpretation: an extra 2 hours in the day get split evenly — one more hour of leisure and one more hour of work. Note this is a shift of the endowment, not of the wage: the slope $-250$ is unchanged, but the whole frontier moves outward.

Result: $(7,1750)\to(8,2000)$; free time and work each rise by one hour.

Problem 5

Tereza (MRS $=450/\sqrt{t}$, $u=c+900\sqrt{t}$, $T=16$, $w=150$) is offered a scholarship of $M=500$ CZK per day, paid whether she works or not. (a) Write the new frontier. (b) Find the new optimum. (c) Explain the result.

Solution

(a) $c=500+150(16-t)=2900-150t$. The slope is still $-150$, so the line has shifted up by 500 without changing its steepness.

(b) MRT is unchanged at 150, so the tangency condition $450/\sqrt{t}=150$ still gives $t^\ast=9$ h. Then $c^\ast=500+150\cdot 7=1550$ CZK and $u=1550+2700=4250$.

(c) These preferences are quasi-linear: the MRS depends on $t$ only, never on $c$. Extra income therefore goes entirely into consumption and leaves hours worked untouched — there is no income effect on free time. Under different preferences (e.g. $u=t\cdot c$) the scholarship would have bought extra leisure too.

Result: $c=2900-150t$; $t^\ast=9$ h unchanged, $h^\ast=7$ h unchanged, $c^\ast=1550$ CZK, utility 3750 → 4250.

Problem 6

A student claims his optimum is $t=6$, $c=1400$ with $T=16$ and $w=200$ CZK/h, and that his MRS there is 320. Find two separate mistakes in his answer.

Solution

Mistake 1 — the bundle is not on the frontier. At $t=6$ the frontier gives $c=200(16-6)=2000$, not 1400. The bundle $(6,1400)$ is strictly inside the feasible set: he is throwing away 600 CZK of consumption he could have had for free. The optimum can never be inside the set, because the point directly above it has more consumption and the same free time.

Mistake 2 — the tangency condition fails. His MRS is 320 while MRT $=w=200$. Since MRS > MRT, an extra hour of free time is worth 320 CZK to him but costs only 200 CZK — he should take more free time, moving right along the frontier until the two are equal.

Result: the point is neither on the frontier nor a tangency; the true optimum lies on $c=200(16-t)$ at a larger $t$ than 6.

Problem 7

At what wage would Tereza (MRS $=450/\sqrt{t}$, $T=16$) choose not to work at all? Explain the economics of the number you get.

Solution

She works nothing when the tangency condition would demand $t>16$, i.e. when her MRS exceeds the wage even at the maximum possible free time.

At $t=16$: MRS $=450/\sqrt{16}=450/4=112.5$ CZK per hour.

So for any $w<112.5$ CZK/h we have MRS > MRT everywhere in the feasible range, and the best she can do is the corner $t^\ast=16$, $h^\ast=0$.

Economically 112.5 CZK/h is her reservation wage: the lowest hourly rate at which working at all is worth it. Reservation wages are the reason a minimum wage or an unemployment benefit changes who takes a job, not just what they are paid.

Result: $w<112.5$ CZK/h → corner solution, no work. The reservation wage is 112.5 CZK/h.

Problem 8

Explain, in a way you could write in an exam, why the optimum must satisfy MRS = MRT, and why the argument needs the indifference curves to be convex.

Solution

Step 1 — the optimum is on the frontier. Any bundle strictly inside the feasible set is beaten by the bundle directly above it, which has the same free time and more consumption. Since more is better, the optimum lies on the frontier.

Step 2 — no improving move must remain. At a frontier point with MRS > MRT, one more hour of free time is worth more to you (MRS) than it costs (MRT), so moving right raises utility. At a point with MRS < MRT, the hour you are consuming is worth less to you than the wage it forgoes, so moving left raises utility. Only where MRS = MRT does neither direction help.

Step 3 — why convexity matters. Convex curves mean the MRS falls steadily as $t$ rises. That makes the tangency point unique and guarantees it is a maximum rather than a minimum: MRS starts above MRT on the left, crosses it once, and stays below on the right. Without convexity the curve could touch the frontier at several points, or touch it from the wrong side, and the tangency would identify the worst feasible bundle instead of the best.

Result: MRS = MRT plus a point on the frontier characterises the optimum; convexity makes that point unique and a maximum.

Summary

The feasible frontier says what the world allows: $c=w(T-t)$, a straight line whose absolute slope, the MRT, equals the wage and therefore equals the opportunity cost of an hour of free time. The indifference map says what you want. The best you can do is the bundle where the two slopes coincide — MRS = MRT — because anywhere else there is a trade you would happily make. Put a table in front of you and you find that point by asking, at each row, "is an extra hour worth more or less to me than the wage?". Put a formula in front of you and you set MRS $=w$ and solve. The remaining question — what happens when $w$ changes — is the subject of Lesson 9, and the honest answer turns out to be "it depends".

📌Key takeaways
  • Feasible frontier: $c=w(T-t)$; the feasible set is everything on or below it.
  • MRT = $w$ = absolute slope of the frontier = opportunity cost of one hour of free time.
  • MRS is subjective (taste), MRT is technical (wage and technology). Never swap them.
  • Optimum: on the frontier and MRS = MRT. If MRS > MRT take more free time; if MRS < MRT work more.
  • Recipe: write the frontier → set MRS $=w$ → solve for $t^\ast$ → substitute back for $c^\ast$ → check $0\le t^\ast\le T$.
  • Higher wage = rotation (steeper, same $(T,0)$ point); unearned income = parallel shift up. The two have very different effects.
  • A wage rise need not raise hours worked — it depends on preferences.

quiz.q: A student has $T=16$ waking hours and a wage of 240 CZK per hour, with no other income. What is the marginal rate of transformation, and what does it mean?
options: 16, because that is the number of hours available
240 CZK per hour — the consumption she must give up to obtain one more hour of free time
3840 CZK, because that is the most she could earn in a day
It cannot be determined without knowing her preferences
quiz.explain: The frontier is $c=240(16-t)$, a straight line with slope $-240$. The MRT is the absolute slope, i.e. 240 CZK per hour: every extra hour of free time costs exactly one hour of wages. 3840 CZK is the vertical intercept (income if she never rests), not the slope. And crucially the MRT comes from the wage alone — preferences play no part in it; that is the MRS.

quiz.q: A student's marginal rate of substitution is $\text{MRS}=600/\sqrt{t}$ (in CZK per hour). She has $T=16$ waking hours and a wage of 200 CZK per hour. How much does she consume per day at her optimum, in CZK?
quiz.explain: Set MRS = MRT = $w$: $600/\sqrt{t}=200\Rightarrow\sqrt{t}=3\Rightarrow t^\ast=9$ hours of free time. Hours worked are $16-9=7$, so $c^\ast=200\cdot 7=1400$ CZK per day. Check: the bundle is on the frontier and $0\le 9\le 16$. A frequent slip is stopping at $t^\ast=9$ and reporting 9, or forgetting to convert free time into hours worked before multiplying by the wage.

quiz.q: At her current bundle on the feasible frontier a worker's MRS is 400 CZK/h while her wage is 250 CZK/h. What should she do?
options: Work more hours — the wage exceeds what free time is worth to her
Take more free time — an extra hour is worth more to her than it costs
Stay where she is; she is already at the optimum
Move to a point inside the feasible set
quiz.explain: MRS > MRT means an extra hour of free time is worth 400 CZK to her but costs only the 250 CZK of wages she gives up. Taking it makes her strictly better off, so she should move right along the frontier — and as she does, her diminishing MRS falls until it meets 250. She is not at an optimum, and moving inside the feasible set is never sensible: the point directly above gives more consumption for the same free time.

quiz.q: With $T=16$ waking hours and a wage of 180 CZK per hour, how much can a student consume per day if she takes 10 hours of free time? Answer in CZK.
quiz.explain: Hours worked are $16-10=6$, so $c=180\cdot 6=1080$ CZK. Equivalently, plug into the frontier $c=180(16-t)=2880-180t$, giving $2880-1800=1080$. The classic error is $180\cdot 10=1800$ — multiplying the wage by free time instead of by hours worked.

quiz.q: Which of the following correctly describe what happens to the feasible frontier $c=w(T-t)$?
options: A higher wage rotates the frontier about the point $(T,0)$ and makes it steeper
A daily scholarship paid regardless of work shifts the frontier up without changing its slope
A higher wage raises the MRT
An increase in the wage always reduces the optimal amount of free time
quiz.explain: With no work you earn nothing whatever the wage, so $(T,0)$ is fixed and a wage rise pivots the line about it, raising the intercept $wT$ — the frontier gets steeper and the MRT, which equals $w$, rises with it. Unearned income $M$ gives $c=M+w(T-t)$: same slope $-w$, whole line up by $M$. The last statement is false: rotating the frontier makes free time dearer but also makes the person richer, and for some preferences (e.g. $u=t\cdot c$) the optimal free time does not change at all.

quiz.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes the MRS from the MRT?
options: The MRS comes from the wage; the MRT comes from preferences
The MRS is the slope of the feasible frontier; the MRT is the slope of an indifference curve
The MRS is what you are willing to give up (preferences); the MRT is what you must give up (the wage and technology)
They are two names for the same quantity, which is why they are equal at the optimum
quiz.explain: MRS = absolute slope of an indifference curve = subjective willingness to trade, and it changes as you move along the curve. MRT = absolute slope of the feasible frontier = the objective rate the world offers you, here simply the wage. They are conceptually different objects that happen to be measured in the same units (CZK per hour) — which is exactly why setting them equal is meaningful. If they were the same quantity, the equality would be an empty statement rather than a condition that picks out one bundle.

quiz.q: A worker's MRS is $450/\sqrt{t}$ and she has $T=16$ hours. For which wages will she choose not to work at all?
options: For any wage below 112.5 CZK/h
For any wage below 450 CZK/h
For any wage above 450 CZK/h
She always works some positive number of hours
quiz.explain: She refuses to work when her MRS exceeds the wage even at the maximum possible free time $t=16$. There MRS $=450/\sqrt{16}=450/4=112.5$ CZK/h. For $w<112.5$ the MRS beats the MRT everywhere in the feasible range, so the best point is the corner $t^\ast=16$, $h^\ast=0$ — and 112.5 CZK/h is her reservation wage. For $w>112.5$ an interior tangency exists and she works.

quiz.q: A student has $T=16$ waking hours, a wage of 300 CZK/h and MRS $=900/\sqrt{t}$. (a) Find her optimal free time, hours worked and consumption. (b) Explain carefully why a feasible bundle with $t=4$ would leave her worse off, referring to MRS and MRT.
quiz.solution:
(a) Solving the problem. The feasible frontier is $c=300(16-t)=4800-300t$, a straight line whose absolute slope is the MRT $=300$ CZK per hour.

Tangency condition MRS = MRT: $\dfrac{900}{\sqrt{t}}=300\Rightarrow\sqrt{t}=3\Rightarrow t^\ast=9$ hours of free time.

Hours worked: $h^\ast=16-9=7$. Consumption: $c^\ast=300\cdot 7=2100$ CZK per day. The bundle satisfies $0\le t^\ast\le 16$ and lies on the frontier, so it is a valid interior optimum.

(b) Why $t=4$ is worse. At $t=4$ the frontier gives $c=300\cdot 12=3600$ CZK, so the bundle is feasible. But her MRS there is $900/\sqrt{4}=900/2=450$ CZK per hour, while the MRT is only 300.

MRS > MRT means the fifth hour of free time is worth 450 CZK to her, yet taking it costs only the 300 CZK of wages she forgoes. She can therefore give up 300 CZK of consumption, gain an hour she values at 450, and end up on a strictly higher indifference curve. The same argument applies again and again as she moves right, and it only runs out at $t=9$, where her (diminishing) MRS has fallen to exactly 300.

Geometrically: at $t=4$ her indifference curve is steeper than the frontier, so it cuts through the frontier rather than touching it — and whenever a curve cuts the frontier there are feasible points on both sides of it, some of which lie on higher curves. Only at the tangency does the whole feasible set lie on or below the indifference curve.

lessons.html:
Since 1870 real wages in rich countries have risen roughly tenfold — and annual hours worked have fallen by about half. Yet the model in Lesson 8 sometimes predicts that a pay rise makes you work more. This lesson shows that both things are perfectly consistent, by splitting the effect of a wage change into a substitution effect and an income effect, and it ends with the data on who actually works how much, and why.

🎯Lesson objectives
  • Define the substitution and income effects of a wage change and state the sign of each on free time.
  • Perform the graphical decomposition correctly, including the auxiliary (hypothetical) budget line.
  • Explain why the net effect on hours worked is ambiguous, and compute all three cases numerically.
  • Derive and interpret a backward-bending labour supply curve.
  • Use the cross-country and historical data on working hours, and name the non-wage factors behind the differences.

1 · Why a pay rise pulls in two directions

When Tereza's wage rises from 200 to 300 CZK an hour, two genuinely different things happen at the same time.

Free time got more expensive

The opportunity cost of an hour off — the MRT — rose from 200 to 300 CZK. Relative prices changed, so she substitutes away from the thing that got dearer: less free time, more work.

She got richer

At any given number of hours she can now buy more. Free time is a normal good (when people get richer they take more of it), so being richer pushes towards more free time, less work.

These two forces point in opposite directions. The observed change in hours is their sum, and which one wins is an empirical question, not a theoretical one.

📐Definition — the two effects

The substitution effect is the change in the chosen bundle caused by the change in the relative price of free time, holding utility constant. On free time it is always negative when the wage rises.

The income effect is the change caused by the change in purchasing power, holding relative prices constant. On free time it is positive when the wage rises, provided free time is a normal good.

2 · The decomposition, step by step

The trick is to invent a bundle that nobody actually chooses: the bundle the person would have chosen if free time had become more expensive but she had been made no better off. The construction has four steps and one line that students draw wrong more often than any other object in this course.

ΣHow to build the diagram
  1. Draw the old frontier and mark the old optimum A, on indifference curve $u_1$.
  2. Draw the new frontier (steeper, same point $(T,0)$) and mark the new optimum C, on indifference curve $u_2$ with $u_2>u_1$.
  3. Draw the auxiliary line: it has the new slope $-w_2$ but is shifted down until it is tangent to the old indifference curve $u_1$. Call that tangency point B.
  4. Read off: A → B is the substitution effect (price changed, utility held at $u_1$); B → C is the income effect (price held at the new one, utility allowed to rise).
⚠Common error — drawing the auxiliary line wrong

Three mistakes, all fatal:

  • Wrong slope. The auxiliary line must have the new slope. If you draw it parallel to the old frontier you have not changed the relative price at all, and there is no substitution effect left to measure.
  • Wrong curve. It must be tangent to the old indifference curve $u_1$ — the whole point is to hold utility constant, not income.
  • Wrong direction. After a wage rise the auxiliary line lies below the new frontier: you are taking income away to cancel the gain. After a wage fall it lies above it.

Slogan: new slope, old curve.

3 · Three cases, three answers

The substitution effect always pushes free time down when the wage rises. The income effect always pushes it up (free time being normal). So the net effect can be anything. Here are the same wage rise and the same $T=16$ under three different sets of preferences.

PreferencesSubstitution effect on $t$Income effect on $t$Net effect on hours worked
$u=c+900\sqrt{t}$ (quasi-linear)negativezero — MRS does not depend on $c$hours rise
$u=t\cdot c$ (Cobb–Douglas)negativepositive, exactly equal in sizehours unchanged
$u=(c-800)\cdot t$ (subsistence need)negativepositive and largerhours fall

The third row is the interesting one. If 800 CZK a day must go on rent and food before any of it counts as "consumption", then at low wages you are forced to work long hours just to cover the fixed bill. As the wage rises, the bill is covered sooner and the extra income buys leisure. Historically, this is not a bad description of what happened.

4 · The backward-bending labour supply curve

📐Definition — labour supply curve

The labour supply curve of an individual plots the optimal number of hours worked $h^\ast$ against the wage $w$. It is backward bending if it slopes upward at low wages (substitution effect dominates) and downward at high wages (income effect dominates).

Take the subsistence preferences $u=(c-800)t$, for which the optimum works out as $t^\ast=8-\dfrac{400}{w}$ with $T=16$:

wage $w$ (CZK/h)60100200400800
free time $t^\ast$ (h)1.334677.5
hours worked $h^\ast$ (h)14.67121098.5
consumption $c^\ast$ (CZK)8801200200036006800

At every step the wage rises and hours worked fall: this whole range is the backward-bending part. Notice consumption still rises throughout — she is unambiguously better off, she simply chooses to take part of the gain as time rather than as things.

⚠Common error — "higher wages always mean more hours worked"

This is the single most common wrong answer on this topic, and it is wrong twice over. In theory the income effect can outweigh the substitution effect, so the labour supply curve can slope downwards. In the data that is exactly what has happened: real wages in rich countries are roughly ten times higher than in 1870 while annual hours are around half. A wage rise raises hours only when the substitution effect dominates — say for a short, temporary bonus, where the income effect is tiny because lifetime wealth barely changes.

5 · What the data actually show

Two facts stand out, and the exam expects you to explain both.

Fact 1 — the long fall. Around 1870 a typical worker in the Netherlands or the United States put in well over 3000 hours a year: something like 60 hours a week, almost every week. Today it is roughly 1400–1800. Wages rose enormously over the same period. Over the long run, then, the income effect has clearly dominated.

Fact 2 — countries differ a lot at similar income levels. In 2023 the OECD figures are roughly: Netherlands 1430, Germany 1340, France 1500, Czechia 1750, United States 1800, Korea 1870, Mexico 2200 hours per worker. The Dutch and the Americans are about equally rich, yet Americans work some 25 % more hours. Wages alone cannot explain that.

📌What explains the gaps besides the wage
  • Taxes. A higher marginal tax wedge lowers the net wage and so weakens the substitution effect towards work. Prescott (2004) argued this accounts for much of the US–Europe gap; others find the effect too small to explain all of it.
  • Unions and regulation. Hours are often set collectively, not individually: the French 35-hour week, statutory minimum paid leave of four weeks in the EU (five in Czechia by law for many employers) versus no federal minimum in the US.
  • Part-time work. The Netherlands has by far the highest part-time share in the EU — around 40 % of employees — which mechanically pulls average hours per worker down.
  • Culture and social norms. Leisure is more enjoyable when your friends are also free, so norms about holidays and weekends are self-reinforcing (Alesina, Glaeser & Sacerdote, 2005).
  • Composition. Hours per worker and hours per person are different statistics: a country with low employment among students and the elderly can have high hours per worker and low hours per capita.

6 · The household, not the individual

The model treats one person choosing between paid work and free time, but most time-use decisions are made in households, and a large share of work is unpaid: cooking, childcare, laundry, care of elderly parents. Time-use surveys in Czechia and across the EU consistently find that women do substantially more unpaid work than men — the gap is typically over an hour a day — so measured "hours worked" understates women's total workload.

The same MRS = MRT logic applies, with two twists. First, a household member's relevant "wage" is their own market wage, so if one partner earns much more, specialising them into paid work and the other into unpaid work can look efficient — and that in turn feeds back into who accumulates experience and earns more later. Second, the family's non-labour income (the other partner's earnings, parental leave benefits, child allowances) enters as a pure income effect, which is why generous transfers tend to reduce measured labour supply somewhat even when they leave the wage untouched.

📊Where this shows up in data analysis

Labour supply elasticities are among the most-estimated numbers in applied economics, because every tax reform forecast needs them. The empirical strategy is exactly the theory: find a change that moves the net wage without moving wealth much (a tax-bracket reform, a change in the EITC or in Czech tax credits) and you identify something close to a pure substitution effect; find a change that moves wealth without moving the wage (a lottery win, an inheritance, a lump-sum benefit) and you identify a pure income effect. Studies of lottery winners typically find a modest but clearly negative effect of unearned income on hours — evidence that free time really is a normal good. In R or Python this is a difference-in-differences or IV regression, but the object being estimated is the decomposition you just drew.

Worked examples

Example 1Full numerical decomposition

Tereza has $u=t\cdot c$ (MRS $=c/t$) and $T=16$. Her wage rises from $w_1=200$ to $w_2=300$ CZK/h. Decompose the change in free time.

1

Point A (old optimum). Tangency $c/t=200$ with $c=200(16-t)$ gives $200t=200(16-t)$, so $t_A=8$, $c_A=1600$, $u_1=8\cdot 1600=12\,800$.

2

Point C (new optimum). Same algebra with $w=300$: $t_C=8$, $c_C=300\cdot 8=2400$, $u_2=19\,200$.

3

Point B (new slope, old curve). Require MRS $=300$, i.e. $c=300t$, and utility still $12\,800$: $t\cdot 300t=12\,800\Rightarrow t^{2}=42.67\Rightarrow t_B=6.53$, $c_B=300\cdot 6.53=1960$.

4

Read off the effects. Substitution A→B: $6.53-8=\mathbf{-1.47}$ h of free time. Income B→C: $8-6.53=\mathbf{+1.47}$ h.

5

Where is the auxiliary line? Slope $-300$ through B: intercept $=1960+300\cdot 6.53=3919$ CZK. The real new frontier has intercept $300\cdot 16=4800$, so the construction hypothetically confiscates $4800-3919\approx 881$ CZK a day.

Result: SE $=-1.47$ h, IE $=+1.47$ h, net change in free time $=0$. Hours worked stay at 8; the entire pay rise is consumed.
Example 2When the income effect wins

Marta must spend 800 CZK a day on rent and food, so her preferences are $u=(c-800)\cdot t$ with MRS $=\dfrac{c-800}{t}$. With $T=16$, her wage rises from 100 to 200 CZK/h. Decompose.

1

General solution. Tangency $\dfrac{c-800}{t}=w$ and frontier $c=w(16-t)$ give $w(16-t)-800=wt$, hence $t^\ast=8-\dfrac{400}{w}$.

2

Point A. $w=100$: $t_A=8-4=4$ h, $c_A=100\cdot 12=1200$, $u_1=(1200-800)\cdot 4=1600$.

3

Point C. $w=200$: $t_C=8-2=6$ h, $c_C=200\cdot 10=2000$, $u_2=(2000-800)\cdot 6=7200$.

4

Point B. New slope: $c-800=200t$. Old utility: $(c-800)t=1600\Rightarrow 200t^{2}=1600\Rightarrow t_B=\sqrt{8}=2.83$ h.

5

Effects. SE $=2.83-4=\mathbf{-1.17}$ h; IE $=6-2.83=\mathbf{+3.17}$ h; net $=+2$ h of free time. Hours worked fall from 12 to 10.

Result: SE $-1.17$ h, IE $+3.17$ h, net $+2$ h free time. The income effect dominates: she doubles her wage and works less.
Example 3A pure income effect: winning money

Petr has $u=t\cdot c$, $T=16$, $w=200$ CZK/h. He starts receiving 800 CZK a day from a family trust, regardless of whether he works. What happens to his hours?

1

Before. $t^\ast=8$, $h^\ast=8$, $c^\ast=1600$ (from Example 1).

2

New frontier. $c=800+200(16-t)=4000-200t$. The slope is still $-200$: the MRT is unchanged, so there is no substitution effect at all.

3

New optimum. MRS $=c/t=200\Rightarrow c=200t$. Substitute: $200t=4000-200t\Rightarrow t^\ast=10$ h, $c^\ast=2000$ CZK, $h^\ast=6$ h.

4

Check. On the frontier: $800+200\cdot 6=2000$ ✓. MRS $=2000/10=200=w$ ✓.

5

Interpret. A pure income effect: free time rises by 2 hours, work falls by 2 hours. This is the isolated version of the force that pulls against the substitution effect in a wage rise — and it is what lottery-winner studies try to measure.

Result: $t^\ast$ 8 → 10 h, $h^\ast$ 8 → 6 h, $c^\ast$ 1600 → 2000 CZK. Free time is a normal good.
Example 4Building the labour supply curve

Using Marta's rule $t^\ast=8-\dfrac{400}{w}$ (with $T=16$), tabulate hours worked at $w=60,\,100,\,200,\,400$ and describe the shape of her labour supply curve.

1

$w=60$: $t^\ast=8-6.67=1.33$, $h^\ast=14.67$ h.

2

$w=100$: $t^\ast=4$, $h^\ast=12$ h.   $w=200$: $t^\ast=6$, $h^\ast=10$ h.   $w=400$: $t^\ast=7$, $h^\ast=9$ h.

3

Shape. Plotting $w$ on the vertical axis and $h^\ast$ on the horizontal, the curve leans to the left as we go up: higher wage, fewer hours. Over this whole range the income effect dominates, so the curve is backward bending.

4

Where does it stop? $t^\ast\to 8$ as $w\to\infty$, so hours worked never fall below 8 however rich she gets. And $t^\ast=0$ at $w=50$, which is her reservation wage — below it the model gives no sensible interior answer.

Result: $h^\ast=14.67,\,12,\,10,\,9$ hours at $w=60,\,100,\,200,\,400$ — a backward-bending supply curve approaching 8 hours from above.

Practice

Problem 1

State the sign of the substitution effect and of the income effect on free time when the wage falls, and explain each in one sentence. Assume free time is a normal good.

Solution

Substitution effect: positive (more free time). Free time has become cheaper — the wage you forgo by resting is smaller — so you substitute towards it.

Income effect: negative (less free time). You are poorer, and since free time is a normal good you buy less of it, i.e. you work more to defend your consumption.

Both signs are simply the mirror image of the wage-rise case. The net effect on hours worked is again ambiguous.

Result: SE on $t$ positive, IE on $t$ negative; net ambiguous.

Problem 2

A worker has $u=t\cdot c$ (MRS $=c/t$) and $T=16$. Her wage rises from 150 to 250 CZK/h. Find A, B and C and the two effects.

Solution

A: $c/t=150$ and $c=150(16-t)$ give $t_A=8$, $c_A=150\cdot 8=1200$, $u_1=9600$.

C: same algebra at $w=250$: $t_C=8$, $c_C=2000$, $u_2=16\,000$.

B: new slope means $c=250t$; old utility means $t\cdot c=9600$. So $250t^{2}=9600\Rightarrow t^{2}=38.4\Rightarrow t_B=6.20$ h, $c_B=250\cdot 6.20=1549$ CZK.

Effects: SE $=6.20-8=-1.80$ h; IE $=8-6.20=+1.80$ h; net $=0$.

Result: the two effects cancel exactly, as they always do for $u=t\cdot c$; hours worked stay at 8.

Problem 3

A student draws the decomposition diagram and makes the auxiliary line parallel to the old frontier, tangent to the new indifference curve. Explain precisely what is wrong and what she would end up measuring.

Solution

Two errors, and they compound.

Wrong slope. The auxiliary line exists to change the relative price of free time while holding utility fixed. If it has the old slope, no relative price change has been imposed, so the move A → B contains no substitution effect at all.

Wrong curve. Making it tangent to the new indifference curve holds nothing constant that we care about: utility has already risen, so this move is not a "compensated" change.

What she actually measures is a hypothetical income change at the old price — a pure income effect from $u_1$ to $u_2$ — mislabelled as a substitution effect. Her decomposition will report a substitution effect with the wrong sign or size, even though A and C, and hence the total effect, are correct.

Result: the auxiliary line must have the new slope and be tangent to the old indifference curve. New slope, old curve.

Problem 4

Explain how a person can end up working fewer hours after a pay rise even though free time became more expensive. Then give one real-world piece of evidence that this happens.

Solution

Mechanism. The pay rise does two things. It raises the opportunity cost of an hour off (substitution effect: work more) and it makes the person richer at every level of hours (income effect: since free time is a normal good, work less). If the income effect is the larger of the two, hours worked fall on net. Nothing is contradictory: she can afford more of both consumption and free time than before, and she chooses to take some of the gain as time.

Evidence. Over the last 150 years real wages in rich countries rose by roughly a factor of ten while annual hours worked per worker roughly halved — from over 3000 hours around 1870 to about 1400–1800 today. If the substitution effect always dominated, hours would have risen.

Result: the income effect can dominate; the long-run historical record says it usually has.

Problem 5

In 2023 an average Dutch worker put in about 1430 hours a year and an average American about 1800, although the two countries have similar GDP per capita. Give three explanations that do not rely on differences in the wage, and say how each would show up in the model.

Solution

1 · Taxes. Higher marginal tax and social-contribution wedges in the Netherlands lower the net wage, which is what the worker actually faces. In the model this flattens the feasible frontier, weakening the substitution effect towards work.

2 · Collective bargaining and regulation. Statutory paid leave (at least four weeks in the EU, none federally mandated in the US), negotiated standard weeks and strong part-time rights mean hours are partly chosen collectively. In the model the worker is not free to pick any point on the frontier — the feasible set is restricted.

3 · Social norms and the part-time share. Leisure is more valuable when others are also free, and about 40 % of Dutch employees work part-time. In the model this is a difference in preferences: steeper indifference curves, a higher MRS at any bundle, therefore more free time at the same wage.

(One could add composition effects: hours per worker and hours per person of working age are different statistics.)

Result: taxes (frontier), regulation and bargaining (feasible set), norms and part-time work (preferences).

Problem 6

A government replaces a lump-sum child benefit of 400 CZK a day with a wage subsidy that raises the net wage. Compare the effects of the two policies on hours worked, using the decomposition.

Solution

Lump-sum benefit. The frontier shifts up in parallel: $c=400+w(T-t)$. The slope, and therefore the MRT, is unchanged, so there is no substitution effect. Only the income effect operates, and it is positive on free time: hours worked fall unambiguously.

Wage subsidy. The frontier rotates and becomes steeper. Now both effects operate: the substitution effect pushes hours up, the income effect pushes them down. The net effect is ambiguous, though for low earners — where the income gain is small relative to the price change — the substitution effect typically dominates and hours rise.

This is precisely why in-work subsidies (the US EITC, Czech tax credits for working parents) are preferred to unconditional transfers when the stated goal is to raise employment.

Result: lump sum → hours fall for sure; wage subsidy → ambiguous but usually raises hours, especially at low wages.

Problem 7

Marta's optimum satisfies $t^\ast=8-\dfrac{400}{w}$ with $T=16$. (a) Find her hours worked at $w=80$ and at $w=500$. (b) What is the lowest wage at which she works at all? (c) What is the limit of her hours worked as $w$ grows without bound, and what does it mean?

Solution

(a) $w=80$: $t^\ast=8-5=3$ h, $h^\ast=13$ h.   $w=500$: $t^\ast=8-0.8=7.2$ h, $h^\ast=8.8$ h.

(b) She works only if $t^\ast<16$, which holds for all $w>0$; the binding condition is $t^\ast\ge 0$, i.e. $8\ge 400/w$, i.e. $w\ge 50$ CZK/h. Below 50 CZK/h she cannot even cover the 800 CZK subsistence requirement by working all 16 hours ($50\cdot 16=800$), so the model has no interior solution.

(c) As $w\to\infty$, $400/w\to 0$ and $t^\ast\to 8$, so $h^\ast\to 8$ hours. The subsistence requirement becomes negligible relative to income, and her behaviour converges to the plain Cobb–Douglas case, where hours are independent of the wage.

Result: (a) 13 h and 8.8 h; (b) 50 CZK/h; (c) hours worked fall towards 8 from above — a backward-bending curve with a floor.

Problem 8

A couple both have $T=16$ waking hours. Adéla earns 400 CZK/h, Tomáš 200 CZK/h. The household needs 4 hours of unpaid domestic work a day, which either of them can do equally well. Who should do it if the household simply wants to maximise total consumption, and name two reasons why this "efficient" answer is a poor guide to policy.

Solution

The arithmetic. An hour of domestic work costs Adéla 400 CZK of forgone earnings and Tomáš 200 CZK. Total consumption is maximised if Tomáš does all 4 hours: cost 800 CZK instead of 1600 CZK. Comparative advantage in the household, exactly as in Lesson 5.

Why this is a poor guide.

(1) It ignores how the wages arose. If the lower-paid partner specialises in unpaid work, they accumulate less experience and their wage falls further behind — the "efficient" allocation is self-reinforcing and locks in the initial gap. In the data this is a large part of the observed motherhood wage penalty.

(2) It ignores distribution and preferences within the household. Maximising total consumption says nothing about who consumes it or who bears the burden of the extra work. Bargaining power, not efficiency, determines the split — a theme we return to in Lesson 12.

Result: Tomáš, on comparative-advantage grounds; but the calculation is static, ignores feedback on future wages, and is silent about who actually gains.

Summary

A wage change moves two things at once: the price of an hour of free time and how rich you are. Splitting them is a mechanical procedure — draw the auxiliary line with the new slope tangent to the old indifference curve, and the move from A to that tangency is the substitution effect, the rest is the income effect. The substitution effect always reduces free time when the wage rises; the income effect always increases it. Which one wins is preference-dependent, so the labour supply curve can slope either way, and over the long run in rich countries it has clearly bent backwards. But wages are not the whole story: taxes, unions, part-time institutions, norms and the unpaid work done at home explain much of why a Dutch worker and an American worker with the same income live very differently.

📌Key takeaways
  • Substitution effect: relative price of free time changes, utility held constant. Wage up → free time down.
  • Income effect: purchasing power changes, prices held constant. Wage up → free time up (free time is normal).
  • Auxiliary line: new slope, old curve, drawn below the new frontier after a wage rise.
  • Net effect on hours is ambiguous: quasi-linear → hours rise; $u=t\cdot c$ → hours unchanged; subsistence needs → hours fall.
  • Backward-bending labour supply: upward at low wages, downward once the income effect dominates.
  • Lump-sum income = pure income effect → hours fall for certain. A wage subsidy is ambiguous.
  • Data: hours halved over 150 years while wages rose tenfold; today NL ≈ 1430, CZ ≈ 1750, US ≈ 1800 hours a year. Taxes, institutions and norms explain the residual gaps.

quiz.q: The wage rises. What is the sign of the substitution effect on free time, and why?
options: Positive — the worker is richer and buys more free time
Negative — free time has become more expensive, so the worker substitutes away from it
Zero — the substitution effect only concerns consumption
Ambiguous — it depends on whether free time is a normal good
quiz.explain: The substitution effect isolates the change in the relative price of free time, holding utility constant. A higher wage means an hour off now costs more forgone consumption, so the worker takes less of it: the effect on free time is negative and this sign is guaranteed, never ambiguous. The story about being richer is the income effect, and it is the income effect (not the substitution effect) whose sign depends on free time being a normal good.

quiz.q: A worker has $u=t\cdot c$ (MRS $=c/t$) and $T=16$ waking hours. Her wage rises from 200 to 800 CZK/h. At the auxiliary point B (new slope, old indifference curve), how many hours of free time does she take?
quiz.explain: First find A: $c/t=200$ with $c=200(16-t)$ gives $t_A=8$, $c_A=1600$, so $u_1=12\,800$. Point B must satisfy the new tangency slope, MRS $=800$, i.e. $c=800t$, while staying on the old curve $t\cdot c=12\,800$. Substituting: $800t^{2}=12\,800\Rightarrow t^{2}=16\Rightarrow t_B=4$ hours. The substitution effect is therefore $4-8=-4$ hours of free time; the income effect brings her back to $t_C=8$, so the net effect is zero — as it always is for $u=t\cdot c$.

quiz.q: In the graphical decomposition of a wage rise, the auxiliary (hypothetical) budget line must be:
options: parallel to the old frontier and tangent to the new indifference curve
of the new slope and tangent to the old indifference curve, lying below the new frontier
of the new slope and tangent to the new indifference curve
parallel to the old frontier and passing through the old optimum
quiz.explain: The auxiliary line answers the question: what would she choose if free time had become dearer but she had been made no better off? So it must carry the new relative price (the new slope) and touch the old indifference curve — new slope, old curve. Because it holds utility at the old, lower level while the wage is higher, it lies below the new frontier: conceptually we confiscate exactly enough income to cancel the gain. Drawing it parallel to the old frontier removes the price change entirely, so no substitution effect can be measured.

quiz.q: A worker's labour supply curve is backward bending. What does this mean?
options: She always works fewer hours when the wage rises
At low wages a wage rise increases hours worked; above some wage a further rise reduces them
Her preferences are not convex
Her free time is an inferior good
quiz.explain: Backward bending means the curve first slopes upward (substitution effect dominates at low wages) and then leans back (income effect dominates once income is high enough). It is not a claim that hours always fall — that would be a curve that slopes down everywhere. Convexity of preferences is unrelated: the backward bend comes from the relative sizes of the two effects, not from the shape of a single indifference curve. And if free time were inferior, the income effect would push free time down too, so both effects would point the same way and no backward bend could occur.

quiz.q: A student has $u=t\cdot c$ (MRS $=c/t$), $T=16$ waking hours and a wage of 250 CZK/h. She starts receiving an unconditional transfer of 1000 CZK per day. How many hours per day does she now work?
quiz.explain: The new frontier is $c=1000+250(16-t)=5000-250t$; the slope is still $-250$, so the MRT is unchanged and there is no substitution effect. Tangency: $c/t=250\Rightarrow c=250t$. Substituting, $250t=5000-250t\Rightarrow t^\ast=10$ hours of free time, so hours worked are $16-10=6$ (down from 8 before the transfer), and $c^\ast=2500$ CZK. This is a pure income effect, and it is negative on hours worked because free time is a normal good.

quiz.q: Which of the following statements are correct?
options: Over the last 150 years real wages in rich countries rose sharply while annual hours worked fell by roughly half
The substitution effect and the income effect of a wage rise push hours worked in opposite directions
Differences in working hours between the Netherlands and the United States can be fully explained by differences in hourly wages
An unconditional lump-sum benefit reduces hours worked unambiguously, whereas an in-work wage subsidy has an ambiguous effect
quiz.explain: The first is the central empirical fact of the lesson — over the long run the income effect has dominated. The second is the definition of the ambiguity: substitution pushes hours up, income pushes them down. The fourth follows from the geometry: a lump sum shifts the frontier up without changing its slope, so only an income effect operates, while a subsidy rotates the frontier and sets both effects in motion. The third is false: the two countries have comparable income levels, and the roughly 25 % gap in hours per worker is attributed to taxes, collective bargaining and statutory leave, the very high Dutch part-time share, and social norms.

quiz.q: Which situation would you expect to produce the largest substitution effect relative to the income effect?
options: A permanent doubling of a worker's lifetime earnings
A one-off offer of triple pay for a single extra weekend shift
An inheritance that raises household wealth by two years' salary
A cut in the standard working week from 40 to 35 hours
quiz.explain: A temporary, one-off pay premium sharply raises the price of that particular hour of free time while barely changing lifetime wealth, so the substitution effect dominates almost completely — this is why overtime and surge pricing for shifts work. A permanent doubling of lifetime earnings carries a large income effect alongside the price effect. An inheritance changes wealth without changing any wage at all: it is a pure income effect with no substitution effect. A statutory change in the working week is a restriction on the feasible set, not a price change.

quiz.q: A worker's wage rises from 150 to 300 CZK per hour. Decompose the effect on her hours worked into a substitution effect and an income effect, describing the diagram you would draw, and explain why the net effect on hours is ambiguous. Refer to the historical evidence on working hours.
quiz.solution:
The diagram. Put free time $t$ on the horizontal axis and daily consumption $c$ on the vertical axis. The old feasible frontier is $c=150(T-t)$; the new one is $c=300(T-t)$. Both start from the same point $(T,0)$ — with no work you earn nothing at any wage — so the wage rise rotates the frontier and makes it steeper. Mark the old optimum A, where an indifference curve $u_1$ is tangent to the old frontier, and the new optimum C, tangent to the new frontier on a higher curve $u_2$.

The auxiliary line. Now draw a hypothetical budget line with the new slope $-300$, shifted down until it is tangent to the old indifference curve $u_1$. Call the tangency point B. This line lies below the new frontier: it represents 'free time is now dearer, but you have been made no better off'.

The two effects. The move A → B is the substitution effect. Utility is held at $u_1$ and only the relative price has changed; because free time is now more expensive, B lies to the left of A. Free time falls, so hours worked rise. This sign is guaranteed.

The move B → C is the income effect. The relative price is the same at both points (both lie on lines of slope $-300$) and the only difference is purchasing power. Since free time is a normal good, C lies to the right of B: free time rises and hours worked fall.

Why the net effect is ambiguous. The two effects have opposite signs on hours worked, and their relative sizes depend entirely on the shape of the indifference curves — that is, on preferences, which theory does not pin down. If the person's willingness to pay for free time is very sensitive to income (say because a fixed subsistence bill must be covered first), the income effect is large and hours fall. If it is insensitive (quasi-linear preferences), the income effect vanishes and hours rise. For $u=t\cdot c$ the two effects cancel exactly and hours do not change at all. All three are internally consistent, so the model cannot deliver a single prediction — only the data can.

Evidence. Over roughly the last 150 years real wages in rich countries rose by something like a factor of ten, while annual hours worked per worker fell from over 3000 around 1870 to about 1400–1800 today (Netherlands about 1430, Czechia about 1750, United States about 1800 in 2023). Over that horizon the income effect has plainly dominated. Short-run, temporary wage changes — an overtime premium, a single high-paid shift — carry almost no income effect and typically do raise hours, which is exactly what the decomposition predicts.

test.sub: Block 3 · Scarcity, wellbeing and working hours. Covers Lessons 7–9: preferences, indifference curves and the MRS; the feasible frontier, the MRT and the constrained-choice optimum MRS = MRT; income and substitution effects, the backward-bending labour supply curve, and the evidence on hours worked. Bring a calculator.

questions.q: Which of the following would violate the standard assumptions about a single person's preferences over free time and consumption?
options: Two indifference curves of that person intersecting at one bundle
An indifference curve becoming flatter as free time increases
Indifference curves further from the origin representing higher utility
Two different people's indifference curves intersecting
questions.explain: One person's curves cannot cross: a utility function assigns exactly one number to each bundle, so the crossing point would have two utility levels at once, and transitivity plus 'more is better' would be violated. A curve flattening as free time rises is simply a diminishing MRS — the standard convexity assumption. Higher curves being better is the ordering assumption itself. And curves belonging to different people are drawn on separate maps; where they happen to cross on a shared diagram tells us the two people would trade, not that anything is inconsistent.

questions.q: A student is indifferent between the bundles $(5\text{ h},\,1500\text{ CZK})$ and $(8\text{ h},\,900\text{ CZK})$. What is her average marginal rate of substitution between these two bundles, in CZK per hour?
questions.explain: MRS $=\left|\Delta c/\Delta t\right|=\left|(900-1500)/(8-5)\right|=600/3=200$ CZK per hour: she gives up 600 CZK for 3 extra hours of free time, i.e. 200 CZK per hour on average. Because the MRS diminishes, the true MRS is above 200 at the left-hand bundle and below 200 at the right-hand one — the 200 is a chord slope, not a tangent slope.

questions.q: A worker's wage doubles but her tastes do not change. What happens to her MRS and her MRT at the bundle she was originally consuming?
options: Both double
The MRT doubles; the MRS at that bundle is unchanged
The MRS doubles; the MRT is unchanged
Neither changes; only the chosen bundle moves
questions.explain: The MRT is the absolute slope of the feasible frontier and equals the wage, so it doubles immediately. The MRS is the absolute slope of an indifference curve and depends only on preferences and on which bundle you evaluate it at — at the original bundle it is exactly what it was. The wage rise then makes that bundle non-optimal (now MRS < MRT there), so she moves along the new frontier until her MRS has risen to meet the new MRT. Confusing the two is the classic Block 3 error.

questions.q: A worker has $T=16$ waking hours, a wage of 240 CZK per hour and MRS $=720/\sqrt{t}$ (CZK per hour). How much does she consume per day at her optimum, in CZK?
questions.explain: Set MRS = MRT = $w$: $720/\sqrt{t}=240\Rightarrow\sqrt{t}=3\Rightarrow t^\ast=9$ hours of free time. Hours worked are $16-9=7$, so $c^\ast=240\cdot 7=1680$ CZK. Check the bundle lies on the frontier $c=240(16-t)$ and that $0\le t^\ast\le 16$. The two standard slips are reporting $t^\ast=9$ instead of consumption, and multiplying the wage by free time rather than by hours worked ($240\cdot 9=2160$ is wrong).

questions.q: A worker has $T=16$ hours and faces $c=w(16-t)$. Which statements are correct?
options: Raising the wage rotates the frontier about $(16,0)$ and increases the MRT
An unconditional benefit of 500 CZK a day shifts the frontier up by 500 without changing the MRT
The optimum can never lie strictly inside the feasible set
At the optimum the indifference curve cuts through the feasible frontier
questions.explain: With no work you earn nothing whatever the wage, so the frontier pivots about $(16,0)$; its slope is $-w$, so the MRT rises with the wage. A lump-sum benefit gives $c=500+w(16-t)$: same slope, whole line up by 500 — a pure change in income with no change in the price of free time. The optimum cannot be interior to the set because the point directly above it offers more consumption for the same free time. The last option describes exactly what does not happen at an optimum: at the optimum the curve is tangent to the frontier. If it cut through, there would be feasible points on a higher curve.

questions.q: Bundle A gives a student utility 900 and bundle B gives 300 under the utility function $u=t\cdot c$. Which conclusion is legitimate?
options: A is exactly three times as good as B
A is preferred to B, and this ranking survives replacing $u$ by $\sqrt{u}$
The student gets 600 more units of happiness from A
Another student with utility 500 at some bundle is worse off than this student at A
questions.explain: Utility is ordinal: only the order of the numbers carries information. A is preferred to B, and any strictly increasing transformation — here $\sqrt{u}$, giving 30 and about 17.3 — preserves that order and leaves every indifference curve exactly where it was. Ratios ('three times as good') and differences ('600 more units') are artefacts of the arbitrary scale. And utility numbers are never comparable across people, so nothing can be concluded from one student's 500 versus another's 900.

questions.q: A worker has $u=t\cdot c$ (MRS $=c/t$) and $T=16$ waking hours. Over her career her wage rises from 120 to 480 CZK per hour. At the auxiliary point B used to isolate the substitution effect, how many hours of free time does she take?
questions.explain: Point A: $c/t=120$ with $c=120(16-t)$ gives $t_A=8$, $c_A=120\cdot 8=960$, so $u_1=8\cdot 960=7680$. Point B carries the new slope, MRS $=480$, i.e. $c=480t$, while remaining on the old curve $t\cdot c=7680$. Hence $480t^{2}=7680\Rightarrow t^{2}=16\Rightarrow t_B=4$ hours. The substitution effect is $4-8=-4$ hours of free time; the income effect returns her to $t_C=8$, so the net change is zero and she still works 8 hours — with four times the consumption.

questions.q: Economists observe that a temporary overtime premium raises hours worked, while a permanent tenfold rise in real wages over 150 years coincided with hours roughly halving. What is the standard explanation?
options: Preferences changed completely between the two situations
A temporary premium is almost a pure substitution effect, while a permanent wage rise also carries a large income effect
The historical data are unreliable and should be ignored
Free time is a normal good in the short run and an inferior good in the long run
questions.explain: A one-off premium raises the price of one particular hour of free time while leaving lifetime wealth essentially untouched, so the substitution effect dominates and hours rise. A permanent tenfold wage rise makes people vastly richer, and since free time is a normal good the income effect is large and pushes hours down; historically it has dominated. No change in preferences and no reversal of normality is needed — one model with two effects of different relative sizes explains both facts.

questions.q: A worker has $T=16$ hours and MRS $=600/\sqrt{t}$. Below which wage will she choose not to work at all?
options: 150 CZK/h
200 CZK/h
600 CZK/h
She always works a positive number of hours
questions.explain: She refuses to work when her MRS exceeds the wage even at maximum free time $t=16$: there MRS $=600/\sqrt{16}=600/4=150$ CZK per hour. For $w<150$ we have MRS > MRT throughout the feasible range, so the best point is the corner $t^\ast=16$, $h^\ast=0$. That threshold, 150 CZK/h, is her reservation wage. For $w>150$ an interior tangency exists.

questions.q: Which of the following changes involve a pure income effect on a worker's choice of hours, with no substitution effect at all?
options: An inheritance that pays a fixed sum every month regardless of work
A cut in the income tax rate on earnings
A universal basic income paid to everyone unconditionally
A rise in the hourly wage
questions.explain: A substitution effect requires a change in the relative price of free time, i.e. in the slope of the frontier. A fixed monthly inheritance payment and an unconditional basic income both shift the frontier up in parallel: the wage, and therefore the MRT, is untouched, so only purchasing power changes. Both reduce hours worked unambiguously if free time is normal. A cut in the tax on earnings and a rise in the wage both raise the net wage, rotating the frontier and setting both effects in motion — which is why their effect on hours is ambiguous.

questions.q: Karolína works in a Prague café, has $T=16$ waking hours a day, and her wage rises from 200 to 320 CZK per hour. Decompose the effect on her hours worked into a substitution effect and an income effect. Describe the diagram precisely, including how the auxiliary line must be drawn, state the sign of each effect, and explain why the net effect on hours worked cannot be signed by theory alone. Support your answer with evidence.
questions.solution:
Setting up the diagram. Free time $t$ (0 to 16 hours) on the horizontal axis, daily consumption $c$ in CZK on the vertical axis. The old frontier is $c=200(16-t)$, running from $(0,3200)$ to $(16,0)$; the new frontier is $c=320(16-t)$, from $(0,5120)$ to $(16,0)$. Because no work means no income at any wage, the point $(16,0)$ is common to both: the wage rise rotates the frontier about it and makes it steeper. The MRT rises from 200 to 320 CZK per hour.

The two optima. Mark A, where an indifference curve $u_1$ is tangent to the old frontier (there MRS $=200$), and C, the tangency with the new frontier on a higher curve $u_2$ (there MRS $=320$). The move A → C is the total effect, and it is what we would observe in data.

The auxiliary line. Draw a hypothetical budget line with the new slope $-320$ and shift it down until it is just tangent to the old indifference curve $u_1$. Call this tangency B. Two features are essential: the slope must be the new one (otherwise no relative price change has been imposed) and the tangency must be with the old curve (because we are holding utility, not income, constant). After a wage rise this line necessarily lies below the new frontier — we are notionally taking income away to cancel the welfare gain.

Substitution effect: A → B, negative on free time. Utility is unchanged between A and B; only the relative price has moved. An hour of free time now costs 320 CZK instead of 200, so Karolína substitutes away from it: B lies to the left of A, free time falls and hours worked rise. This sign is guaranteed by the convexity of the indifference curve — a steeper tangent line must touch the same curve further to the left.

Income effect: B → C, positive on free time. B and C lie on lines of the same slope, so the relative price is identical; the only difference is purchasing power. Free time is a normal good — richer people take more of it — so C lies to the right of B: free time rises and hours worked fall.

Why theory cannot sign the net effect. The two effects act on hours worked in opposite directions, and their relative sizes depend entirely on the curvature of the indifference map, which theory does not restrict. Three internally consistent examples with the same wage rise: with quasi-linear preferences such as $u=c+900\sqrt{t}$ the MRS does not depend on consumption, the income effect on free time is exactly zero, and hours rise. With $u=t\cdot c$ the optimum is always $t^\ast=T/2=8$, so the two effects cancel exactly and hours are unchanged. With a subsistence requirement, $u=(c-800)t$, the optimum is $t^\ast=8-400/w$, which rises with the wage, so the income effect dominates and hours fall. Only data can tell us which case a given worker is in.

Evidence. Over roughly 150 years real wages in rich countries rose by about a factor of ten while annual hours per worker fell from over 3000 around 1870 to about 1400–1800 today (Netherlands roughly 1430, Czechia roughly 1750, United States roughly 1800 in 2023). Over long horizons the income effect has clearly dominated. By contrast, short-lived wage changes — an overtime premium or a single high-paid shift — carry almost no income effect, and these reliably raise hours, exactly as the decomposition predicts.

questions.q: A student has $T=16$ waking hours, no unearned income, a wage of 300 CZK per hour, and MRS $=900/\sqrt{t}$ CZK per hour. (a) Find her optimal free time, hours worked and consumption. (b) Show that the feasible bundle with $t=1$ is worse, using MRS and MRT explicitly. (c) Explain what role the convexity of her indifference curves plays in the argument. (d) Her employer instead offers a flat bonus of 900 CZK a day on top of the old wage. Without full calculation, say what happens to the MRT and in which direction her hours move.
questions.solution:
(a) The optimum. Frontier: $c=300(16-t)=4800-300t$, so MRT $=300$ CZK per hour at every point. Tangency condition MRS = MRT: $\dfrac{900}{\sqrt{t}}=300\Rightarrow\sqrt{t}=3\Rightarrow t^\ast=9$ hours of free time. Hours worked $h^\ast=16-9=7$; consumption $c^\ast=300\cdot 7=2100$ CZK per day. Checks: $0\le 9\le 16$, $c^\ast>0$, and the bundle lies on the frontier.

(b) Why $t=1$ is worse. At $t=1$ the frontier gives $c=300\cdot 15=4500$ CZK, so the bundle is feasible — she works 15 hours. But her MRS there is $900/\sqrt{1}=900$ CZK per hour, against an MRT of only 300.

MRS > MRT means the second hour of free time is worth 900 CZK to her, while taking it costs only the 300 CZK of wages she forgoes. She can give up 300 CZK of consumption, gain something she values at 900, and move to a strictly higher indifference curve. The same improving trade is available again and again as she moves right, and it only runs out at $t=9$, where her MRS has fallen to exactly 300. Geometrically, at $t=1$ her indifference curve is much steeper than the frontier, so it cuts through it rather than touching it — and whenever a curve cuts the frontier there are feasible points above that curve.

(c) The role of convexity. Convexity means the MRS falls monotonically as free time rises: here $900/\sqrt{t}$ is 900 at $t=1$, 300 at $t=9$ and 225 at $t=16$. Three things follow. First, MRS crosses MRT exactly once, so the tangency point is unique. Second, MRS is above MRT to the left of it and below it to the right, so utility rises as we approach $t^\ast$ from either side — the tangency is a maximum, not a minimum. Third, it justifies the whole marginal argument in part (b): each successive hour of free time is worth less than the last, which is why the sequence of improving trades must eventually stop. Without convexity a tangency could identify the worst feasible bundle, or there could be several tangencies with different utility levels.

(d) A flat bonus. A bonus of 900 CZK a day paid regardless of hours gives the frontier $c=900+300(16-t)$. The slope is still $-300$, so the MRT is unchanged at 300 and there is no substitution effect: the price of an hour of free time has not moved. Only an income effect operates. For general preferences, free time being a normal good means the income effect raises free time and therefore reduces hours worked — with $u=t\cdot c$, for instance, hours would clearly fall.

Here, though, her MRS $=900/\sqrt{t}$ depends on $t$ alone and not on $c$ — the preferences are quasi-linear. The tangency condition is still $900/\sqrt{t}=300$, so $t^\ast=9$ and hours stay at exactly 7; the whole bonus goes into consumption, which rises to $900+2100=3000$ CZK. The income effect on free time is zero in this special case. Either way the contrast with part (a) is the point: a rotation of the frontier changes the price of free time and income together, a parallel shift changes only income.

lessons.html:
Until now every model in this course had a single decision-maker facing a constraint: Angela chooses hours, a firm chooses a technology. In this lesson the constraint becomes another person. You will learn to read a payoff matrix, find best responses, spot dominant strategies and locate the Nash equilibrium — the four tools that CORE uses in every single strategic model from here to the end of the course.

🎯Learning objectives
  • Recognise a situation of strategic interaction and write it down as a payoff matrix.
  • Read a 2×2 matrix correctly: who chooses rows, who chooses columns, whose payoff is whose.
  • Find a player's best response to each strategy of the other player.
  • Identify a dominant strategy and a dominant strategy equilibrium — and know why not every game has one.
  • Find all Nash equilibria in pure strategies by underlining or circling best responses.
  • Work through the prisoners' dilemma, the invisible hand game, and coordination games, and say precisely why the prisoners' dilemma outcome is Pareto inefficient.

1 · Strategic interaction: when your payoff depends on other people

A social interaction is any situation in which what you get depends not only on what you do, but also on what somebody else does. Choosing whether to cycle or drive to school, whether to pay for the tram ticket, whether a country cuts emissions — in all of them your outcome is jointly produced by many people's decisions.

Economists model these situations as games. A game is a complete description of three things: who plays (the players), what each of them can do (the strategies), and what each of them gets for every combination of choices (the payoffs). Nothing else. If you can write those three things down, you have a model.

📐Definition — game, strategy, payoff

A game consists of a set of players, a set of strategies available to each player, and a payoff for each player for every possible combination of strategies.

A strategy is a complete action that a player can take. A payoff is the benefit the player receives, measured in whatever unit the model uses: money, utility, kilograms of grain, or (with a minus sign) years in prison.

Two more assumptions run through everything below. First, players are self-interested in the baseline model: each cares only about their own payoff. Second, the payoffs are common knowledge — both players know the whole matrix and know that the other one knows it. Lesson 11 will relax the first assumption; the CORE experiments show it is often wrong.

2 · The payoff matrix and how to read it

With two players and two strategies each, the whole game fits into a 2×2 table. The row player chooses which row; the column player chooses which column. Their two choices together pick out one cell, and that cell contains two numbers: the row player's payoff first, the column player's payoff second.

Here is the CORE pest-control story with concrete numbers. Anil and Bala farm neighbouring plots near Znojmo. Each can control pests with IPC (integrated pest control: labour-intensive, keeps the predator insects alive) or with Pesticide (cheap and effective on your own field, but it drifts and kills the neighbour's predator insects too). Payoffs are the season's profit in thousands of CZK.

Anil ↓   Bala →Bala: IPCBala: Pesticide
Anil: IPC4 , 41 , 5
Anil: Pesticide5 , 12 , 2

Read the cell (Pesticide, IPC) = "5 , 1": Anil sprays, Bala uses IPC, so Anil earns 5 thousand and Bala earns 1 thousand. Bala is hurt because Anil's spray drifted onto his field while Bala did the expensive labour.

⚠Common mistake

Reading the payoffs in the wrong order. The convention in this course is (row player, column player). CORE's own figures sometimes put the row player's payoff in the bottom-left corner of the cell and the column player's in the top-right, which is the same information laid out differently. Before you do anything else with a matrix, write down explicitly which number belongs to whom. Half of all exam errors in this topic start here.

3 · Simultaneous and sequential games

In a simultaneous game the players choose without knowing what the other has chosen. It does not have to be literally at the same second — what matters is that when you decide, you do not yet know the other's decision. Sealed-bid auctions, penalty kicks and "do I spray this week?" are simultaneous.

In a sequential game one player moves first and the second sees the move before choosing. This changes the analysis completely: the second mover's strategy is a rule ("if he entered, I fight; if he stayed out, I do nothing"), and you solve the game backwards from the last decision. Sequential games are drawn as a tree, not a matrix.

Everything else in this lesson is about simultaneous games, because that is what the CORE final test asks for.

4 · Best response and dominant strategy

📐Definition — best response

A player's best response is the strategy that gives that player the highest payoff, given the strategy chosen by the other player.

A best response is always a response to something. "Anil's best response is Pesticide" is an incomplete sentence; "Anil's best response to Bala playing IPC is Pesticide" is a statement you can check. To find it, hold the other player's choice fixed — i.e. fix a column when you analyse the row player — and compare that player's own numbers.

📐Definition — dominant strategy

A strategy is dominant for a player if it is the best response to every strategy the other player might choose. If every player has a dominant strategy and all of them play it, the result is a dominant strategy equilibrium.

A dominant strategy is a gift: you do not need to predict, guess or trust the other player. Whatever they do, you do the same thing. Most games are not that kind: usually your best move genuinely depends on theirs.

5 · Nash equilibrium

ΣDefinition — Nash equilibrium

A Nash equilibrium is a combination of strategies — one for each player — such that every player's strategy is a best response to the strategies of the others. Equivalently: no player can raise their own payoff by unilaterally changing strategy, holding everyone else's choice fixed.

The mechanical method, and the one you should use in the exam, is underlining (or circling) best responses:

  1. Take column 1. Underline the row player's higher payoff in that column. Repeat for column 2.
  2. Take row 1. Underline the column player's higher payoff in that row. Repeat for row 2.
  3. Any cell in which both numbers are underlined is a Nash equilibrium.
⚠Classic misconception 1 — "Nash equilibrium = the best outcome"

It is not. A Nash equilibrium is only a stable outcome: nobody regrets their own choice given what the other did. It says nothing about total payoffs. In the matrix above the Nash equilibrium gives 2 + 2 = 4, while (IPC, IPC) gives 4 + 4 = 8. The equilibrium is the worst of the two symmetric outcomes and it is still the equilibrium.

⚠Classic misconception 2 — confusing dominant strategy with Nash equilibrium

They are different concepts and one implies the other only in one direction. Every dominant strategy equilibrium is a Nash equilibrium (if a strategy is best against everything, it is certainly best against what the other player actually chose). The reverse is false: the coordination game in Worked example 3 has two Nash equilibria and no dominant strategy for anyone. "There is no dominant strategy, therefore there is no Nash equilibrium" is simply wrong.

6 · The prisoners' dilemma

The pest-control game is a prisoners' dilemma: a game in which each player has a dominant strategy, and the resulting equilibrium is worse for everyone than an outcome they could have reached together. The name comes from the original story: two suspects are questioned in separate rooms and each is offered a deal for confessing.

Suspect A ↓   Suspect B →B: Stay silentB: Confess
A: Stay silent−1 , −1−10 , 0
A: Confess0 , −10−5 , −5

Payoffs are years in prison with a minus sign, because more prison is worse. Confessing is dominant for A (0 > −1 and −5 > −10) and by symmetry for B. So both confess and get five years each, while both staying silent would have given one year each.

📐Definition — Pareto improvement, Pareto efficiency

Allocation X is a Pareto improvement over Y if at least one player is better off in X and nobody is worse off. An allocation is Pareto efficient if no Pareto improvement over it exists.

(IPC, IPC) with (4, 4) is a Pareto improvement over (Pesticide, Pesticide) with (2, 2): both players gain. Therefore the Nash equilibrium of a prisoners' dilemma is Pareto inefficient — and this is the single most examined sentence in the whole block. The reason is an external effect: when you spray, part of the cost falls on your neighbour, so your private calculation ignores it.

📊Where this shows up in data work

Whenever a dataset contains an outcome jointly produced by several decision-makers — emissions by country, antibiotic prescriptions by GP practice, price setting by competing e-shops, contributions to an open-source project — a naive regression treating each unit as independent is mis-specified. The game-theoretic structure tells you what to expect in the data: clustering at the "everyone defects" outcome, a jump when an enforcement rule changes, and a difference between one-shot and repeated relationships. In Lesson 11 you will see experimental data (contributions over rounds) generated exactly to test these predictions.

7 · The invisible hand game and coordination problems

Not every game with dominant strategies ends badly. In CORE's invisible hand game, Anil's plot is better suited to cassava and Bala's to rice, and if both grow the same crop the local price collapses.
