Result: the profit-maximising point always has $\varepsilon \gt 1$. If you compute an optimum with $\varepsilon \lt 1$, you have made an arithmetic mistake.

Problem 6

Classify each as a technological or a non-technological (cost) advantage of size: (a) a supermarket chain negotiating a 12 % discount on Coca-Cola; (b) a container ship twice as long carrying more than twice the containers; (c) spreading a 200 million CZK advertising campaign over more units; (d) a factory large enough to employ a full-time maintenance engineer; (e) a large firm borrowing at 4 % while a small one pays 9 %.

Solution

Procedure: ask whether the advantage comes from physics/engineering/specialisation (technological) or from the terms on which the firm buys or spreads costs (cost advantage).

(a) Cost advantage — buying power, nothing about the production process changed.

(b) Technological — the classic geometric scaling effect (volume grows faster than surface).

(c) Cost advantage — spreading an indivisible expenditure over more units.

(d) Technological — specialisation and division of labour, only possible above a size threshold.

(e) Cost advantage — better terms in the credit market (and see Lesson 16: collateral and the principal–agent problem in lending explain why).

Result: technological: (b), (d); cost advantages: (a), (c), (e).

Problem 7

Vltava Bikes' landlord raises the monthly lease by 60 000 CZK. What happens to $MC$, $AC$, $Q^*$, $P^*$ and profit? What if instead the price of batteries rises so that variable cost per bike goes up by 500 CZK?

Solution

Case 1 — higher fixed cost. $F$ rises from 90 000 to 150 000. $MC = 10\,000+50Q$ is unchanged (constants differentiate to zero). $AC$ shifts up. Since $MR = MC$ does not move, $Q^* = 72$ and $P^* = 20\,800$ are unchanged. Profit falls by exactly 60 000, from 558 000 to 498 000 CZK. The firm still operates because profit is positive.

Case 2 — higher variable cost. Now $C = 90\,000+10\,500Q+25Q^2$, so $MC = 10\,500+50Q$. Set $MR=MC$: $28\,000-200Q = 10\,500+50Q \Rightarrow 17\,500 = 250Q \Rightarrow Q^*=70$, $P^* = 28\,000-7\,000 = 21\,000$ CZK.

New $AC(70) = \frac{90\,000}{70}+10\,500+1\,750 = 1\,285.7+10\,500+1\,750 = 13\,535.7$. Profit $= (21\,000-13\,535.7)(70) = 7\,464.3\times 70 = 522\,500$ CZK.

Result: a fixed-cost shock changes only profit; a marginal-cost shock changes price and quantity too. Note the pass-through: MC rose by 500 CZK but the price rose by only 200 CZK — the firm absorbs the rest, because demand is downward-sloping.

Problem 8

A regulator forces Vltava Bikes to price at marginal cost. Show that the firm then makes a loss, compute it, and explain the dilemma this creates for regulating natural monopolies.

Solution

Procedure: at $P = MC$ the quantity is 120 and the price 16 000 CZK (Example 4). Compare price with average cost.

$AC(120) = \frac{90\,000}{120}+10\,000+25(120) = 750+10\,000+3\,000 = 13\,750$ CZK.

Here $P = 16\,000 \gt AC = 13\,750$, so this particular firm actually still profits: $\pi = 2\,250\times 120 = 270\,000$ CZK. Marginal-cost pricing is viable because MC is rising steeply enough.

Now consider a true natural monopoly, where MC is roughly constant and the fixed cost is huge (a water network: MC of an extra cubic metre near zero, billions invested in pipes). Then $MC \lt AC$ at every output, so pricing at MC guarantees a loss equal to the fixed cost. The regulator must choose: average-cost pricing (no loss, but $P \gt MC$ so some deadweight loss remains), a two-part tariff (a fixed standing charge plus MC per unit — efficient at the margin), or a subsidy funded by taxes that create distortions elsewhere.

Result: for Vltava Bikes MC pricing yields a 270 000 CZK profit; for a genuine natural monopoly it yields a loss equal to the fixed cost, which is the central dilemma of utility regulation.

Summary

A firm with any market power at all sets its price by balancing two things it can see: how fast demand falls away as it raises the price, and what an extra unit costs to make. The balance point is the tangency of the highest isoprofit curve with demand, and it always leaves a triangle of unrealised gains behind it.

📌What to take away
  • $C = F + VC$; $AC = C/Q$; $MC = dC/dQ$. Fixed cost never enters MC.
  • MC cuts AC at the minimum of AC. Falling AC = economies of scale (technological advantages of size, or cost advantages such as bulk discounts and spreading fixed costs).
  • The demand curve read vertically is the marginal willingness to pay.
  • $\varepsilon = -\dfrac{dQ}{dP}\dfrac{P}{Q}$. Elastic ($\gt 1$): a price rise cuts revenue. Slope $\ne$ elasticity.
  • Profit is maximised where the isoprofit curve is tangent to demand, equivalently $MR = MC$. For $P=a-bQ$, $MR = a-2bQ$.
  • Markup rule: $\dfrac{P-MC}{P}=\dfrac{1}{\varepsilon}$. More elastic demand → smaller markup → price closer to MC.
  • $P \gt MC$ leaves mutually beneficial trades unmade: the deadweight loss triangle. A transfer from consumers to the firm is not deadweight loss.
  • Competition policy attacks the triangle; natural monopolies are regulated rather than broken up.

quiz.q: A firm's landlord raises the annual rent by 500 000 CZK. Nothing else changes. What happens to the firm's profit-maximising output?
options: It falls, because costs are higher.
It rises, because the firm must sell more to cover the rent.
It does not change, because rent is a fixed cost and does not affect marginal cost.
It falls to zero — the firm shuts down.
quiz.explain: The optimum is where MR = MC, and a constant differentiates to zero, so MC is unaffected by any fixed cost. Price and quantity stay put; only profit falls, by exactly 500 000 CZK. A fixed cost can only decide whether the firm operates, never how much it produces.

quiz.q: A firm faces demand $P = 28\,000 - 100Q$ and has $MC = 10\,000 + 50Q$. What is the profit-maximising quantity $Q^*$?
quiz.explain: For linear demand $P=a-bQ$, $MR = a-2bQ = 28\,000-200Q$. Setting $MR = MC$: $28\,000-200Q = 10\,000+50Q \Rightarrow 18\,000 = 250Q \Rightarrow Q^*=72$ (and $P^* = 20\,800$). A very common error is to set demand itself equal to MC — that gives 120, which is the efficient quantity, not the profit-maximising one.

quiz.q: At a price of 20 000 CZK a firm sells 80 units; at 22 000 CZK it sells 68. Compute the price elasticity of demand using the initial values as the base (give a positive number).
quiz.explain: $\%\Delta P = 2\,000/20\,000 = +10\,\%$ and $\%\Delta Q = -12/80 = -15\,\%$, so $\varepsilon = 15/10 = 1.5$. Because $\varepsilon \gt 1$ demand is elastic, and revenue must fall: indeed $1\,600\,000 \to 1\,496\,000$ CZK.

quiz.q: A firm's price elasticity of demand at its optimum is 4. What proportion of its price is markup over marginal cost?
quiz.explain: The markup rule says $(P-MC)/P = 1/\varepsilon = 1/4 = 0.25$, i.e. 25 % of the price. The more elastic the demand, the thinner the markup; as $\varepsilon\to\infty$ the markup goes to zero and $P \to MC$, which is the perfectly competitive outcome.

quiz.q: Which statement about deadweight loss from a price above marginal cost is correct?
options: It equals the firm's profit.
It is the consumer surplus that the firm captures by charging a high price.
It is the surplus on units that would be worth more to buyers than they cost to produce, but which are never made.
It disappears if the firm donates its profit to charity.
quiz.explain: Surplus that moves from consumers to the firm is a transfer — it still exists, just in a different pocket. Deadweight loss is only the surplus that is never created: every unit between the firm's quantity and the efficient quantity has willingness to pay above MC, yet is not produced. That is why redistributing the profit does not undo the loss.

quiz.q: Which of the following make the demand a firm faces more elastic?
options: Many close substitutes are available.
The good takes a large share of the buyer's budget.
Buyers have a long time to adjust their behaviour.
The good is addictive.
The firm is the only supplier in a remote region with no alternatives.
quiz.explain: Substitutes are the main driver (A) — this is why demand for petrol in general is inelastic but demand at one particular station is very elastic. A larger budget share makes buyers pay attention and react (B). Elasticity is always higher in the long run, because buyers can switch technology, habits or suppliers (C). Addiction (D) and the absence of alternatives (E) both make demand less elastic, which is exactly why such firms can sustain large markups.

quiz.q: A firm has $C(Q) = 90\,000 + 10\,000Q + 25Q^2$ (CZK per month) and faces $P = 28\,000 - 100Q$. (a) Find the profit-maximising price, quantity and profit. (b) Find the efficient quantity and the deadweight loss. (c) Explain in words why the firm does not produce the efficient quantity even though both it and the buyer would gain from the extra sale.
quiz.solution:
(a) The firm's optimum.

$MC = 10\,000+50Q$; $MR = 28\,000-200Q$.

$MR = MC:\ 28\,000-200Q = 10\,000+50Q \Rightarrow 250Q = 18\,000 \Rightarrow Q^* = 72$.

$P^* = 28\,000-100(72) = 20\,800$ CZK.

$AC(72) = \frac{90\,000}{72}+10\,000+25(72) = 1\,250+10\,000+1\,800 = 13\,050$ CZK.

$\pi = (20\,800-13\,050)\times 72 = 7\,750 \times 72 = \mathbf{558\,000}$ CZK per month.

(b) Efficiency and deadweight loss.

Efficiency requires price (= marginal willingness to pay) to equal marginal cost: $28\,000-100Q = 10\,000+50Q \Rightarrow 150Q = 18\,000 \Rightarrow Q_{eff} = 120$, at $P = 16\,000$ CZK.

The deadweight loss is the triangle between the demand curve and MC from 72 to 120. Its height at $Q=72$ is $20\,800 - MC(72) = 20\,800-13\,600 = 7\,200$ CZK and it closes to zero at 120:

$DWL = \tfrac12 \times (120-72)\times 7\,200 = \tfrac12\times 48\times 7\,200 = \mathbf{172\,800}$ CZK per month.

(c) Why the firm stops at 72.

The 73rd bike is worth about 20 700 CZK to the next buyer and costs 13 650 CZK to make — a gain of roughly 7 000 CZK waiting to be realised. But the firm sells at a single price to everybody. To sell that extra unit it must cut the price on all 72 units it was already selling, and the loss of 100 CZK on each of those 72 units (7 200 CZK) more than wipes out the margin on the extra one. So marginal revenue is far below the price, and the firm rationally stops.

The inefficiency is therefore not greed or stupidity: it is the direct consequence of market power plus uniform pricing. A firm that could perfectly price-discriminate would produce the efficient 120 units — and capture the entire surplus. Competition policy attacks the problem from the other side, by making demand more elastic so that the markup, and with it the triangle, shrinks.

lessons.html:
Take away the single firm's market power and put thousands of buyers and thousands of sellers in a room. Nobody can set a price any more — the price is set by the market, and everybody takes it. This lesson builds the supply and demand model from the ground up, drills the distinction between a shift of a curve and a movement along it (which is where most exam points are lost), and then uses the model on taxes and on why cartels fall apart.

🎯Lesson objectives
  • Build the market demand curve from willingness to pay and the market supply curve from reservation prices.
  • Find equilibrium price and quantity algebraically and graphically.
  • Say correctly, every time, whether an event causes a shift or a movement along a curve.
  • Work out the effect of a demand shock and a supply shock on $P^*$ and $Q^*$.
  • Compute consumer, producer and total surplus in competitive equilibrium and explain why $P = MC$ is efficient.
  • Compute tax incidence and the deadweight loss of a tax, and link the split to elasticities.
  • Explain, in game-theory terms, why more competitors make a cartel collapse.

Running example: the market for a 1 kg loaf of rye bread in a Czech region. Demand and supply, with $P$ in CZK per loaf and $Q$ in thousands of loaves per week: $$Q^D = 900 - 30P, \qquad Q^S = 20P - 100 .$$

1 · Price-taking and where the curves come from

📐Definition — competitive market and price-taking

A market is competitive when there are many buyers and many sellers of a nearly identical good, and each participant is small relative to the whole. Then each is a price-taker: the demand curve facing an individual seller is horizontal at the market price, even though the market demand curve slopes down.

Charge one crown more and you sell nothing; charge one crown less and you throw money away. So you take the price as given and only choose the quantity.

Demand. Each buyer has a maximum willingness to pay. Order buyers from highest WTP to lowest and you get a descending staircase; with thousands of buyers it smooths into the market demand curve. Inverting $Q^D = 900-30P$ gives the inverse demand curve $P = 30 - Q/30$: the buyer of the 300-thousandth loaf is willing to pay 20 CZK, and the very keenest buyer would pay up to 30 CZK (the choke price).

Supply. Each seller has a reservation price — the lowest price at which selling beats not selling, which is her marginal cost. Order sellers from lowest reservation price to highest and you get an ascending staircase: the market supply curve. Inverting $Q^S = 20P-100$ gives $P = 5 + Q/20$: the cheapest bakery would sell at 5 CZK, the 300-thousandth loaf costs 20 CZK to make.

ΣRule — a price-taking firm produces where P = MC

The firm's marginal revenue is the price (selling one more unit changes revenue by exactly $P$, with no need to cut the price on other units). Since profit is maximised where $MR = MC$, a price-taker produces where $P = MC$.

This is why the market supply curve is the horizontal sum of the firms' marginal cost curves, and why competitive equilibrium is efficient: price equals marginal cost, so no mutually beneficial trade is left unmade. The markup is zero because $\varepsilon$ for the individual firm is infinite.

2 · Equilibrium

📐Definition — competitive equilibrium

An equilibrium is a price at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied, so that nobody has an incentive to change their behaviour. It is self-correcting: above $P^*$ there is excess supply, unsold bread and price cuts; below $P^*$ there are queues, shortages and price rises.

Set $Q^D = Q^S$: $900-30P = 20P-100 \Rightarrow 1\,000 = 50P \Rightarrow P^* = 20$ CZK and $Q^* = 300$ thousand loaves per week.

Surplus. $CS = \tfrac12 (300)(30-20) = 1\,500$ and $PS = \tfrac12(300)(20-5) = 2\,250$, both in thousands of CZK per week. Total surplus is 3 750 — and no other quantity does better. Below 300 there are buyers valuing bread above its marginal cost who go without; above 300 loaves are baked that cost more than anyone will pay for them.

3 · Shift versus movement — read this twice

ΣThe rule that decides it

A change in the price of the good itself causes a MOVEMENT ALONG the curve. Anything else causes a SHIFT of the curve.

Reason: price is on the axis. Everything else is held fixed when the curve is drawn, so changing it redraws the curve.

EventWhich curveShift or movement?Direction
Bread gets more expensivedemandmovement alongup and to the left
Household incomes risedemandshiftright (if bread is a normal good)
Rice, a substitute, gets dearerdemandshiftright
Butter, a complement, gets dearerdemandshiftleft
A media scare about glutendemandshiftleft
Bread gets more expensivesupplymovement alongup and to the right
Wheat harvest failssupplyshiftleft
Energy prices fallsupplyshiftright
A tax of 5 CZK per loaf on bakeriessupplyshiftleft (up by 5 CZK at every quantity)
New bakeries enter the marketsupplyshiftright
⚠The single most common exam mistake

"The price of bread went up, so demand fell." Wrong wording, wrong economics. Demand did not fall — quantity demanded fell, and it fell because we moved along an unchanged demand curve. Saying "demand fell" claims the whole curve moved, which would need a different cause (income, tastes, the price of a substitute).

Discipline yourself: "demand" = the whole curve; "quantity demanded" = one point on it. Same for supply.

💡The two-step routine that never fails

1. Ask which curve moved — and check the cause is not the price of the good itself. 2. Move that curve, find the new intersection, then describe the other curve's change as a movement along. Never move both curves unless the question gives you two separate shocks.

4 · Demand shocks and supply shocks

Demand shock. Incomes rise and bread demand increases by 150 thousand loaves at every price: $Q^D = 1\,050-30P$. Then $1\,050-30P = 20P-100 \Rightarrow P^* = 23$ CZK, $Q^* = 360$. Both price and quantity rise; sellers moved along their unchanged supply curve.

Supply shock. Energy costs jump and supply falls by 100 at every price: $Q^S = 20P-200$. Then $900-30P = 20P-200 \Rightarrow P^* = 22$ CZK, $Q^* = 240$. Price up, quantity down; buyers moved along their unchanged demand curve.

📌How to tell shocks apart in real data

Price and quantity move in the same direction after a demand shock and in opposite directions after a supply shock. So if you see energy prices up and consumption down, that is a supply shock; if you see house prices up and transactions up, that is a demand shock. This is the whole intuition behind identifying supply and demand separately in econometrics.

5 · Short run and long run

In the short run the number of firms and the capital stock are fixed, so supply is relatively inelastic and a demand shock shows up mostly in the price. In the long run firms can enter or exit and adjust capacity, so supply is much more elastic and the same shock shows up mostly in the quantity, with the price returning towards average cost.

Long-run competitive equilibrium has a striking property: entry continues until economic profit is zero, i.e. $P = \min AC$. "Zero economic profit" does not mean the owners earn nothing — it means they earn exactly the return they could get elsewhere, their opportunity cost.

6 · Taxes: who actually pays?

ΣRule — tax incidence

Who legally pays a tax has no effect on who economically bears it. The burden splits according to elasticities: $$\text{buyers' share} = \frac{\varepsilon_S}{\varepsilon_S+\varepsilon_D},\qquad \text{sellers' share} = \frac{\varepsilon_D}{\varepsilon_S+\varepsilon_D}.$$ The more inelastic side bears more of the tax — it has fewer ways to escape.

That is why excise duty on cigarettes and alcohol falls almost entirely on smokers and drinkers, and why a tax on a good with many substitutes is absorbed largely by producers. The worked example below does the arithmetic.

⚠Common mistake

Two traps with taxes. First, students report the whole fall in surplus as deadweight loss. It is not: most of it is tax revenue, a transfer that still exists and can be spent. Only the triangle over the trades that never happened is destroyed. Second, when a per-unit tax shifts the supply curve, it shifts it vertically upwards by the amount of the tax — not horizontally by that amount. Draw the shift by moving each point straight up, then read off the new intersection.

7 · More competition breaks a cartel

Two bakeries can quietly agree to keep the price high. Set out the payoffs (profit in thousands of CZK per week):

Bakery B: high priceBakery B: low price
Bakery A: high priceA: 40, B: 40A: 15, B: 55
Bakery A: low priceA: 55, B: 15A: 25, B: 25

Check best responses. If B plays high, A gets 55 by playing low versus 40 by playing high → play low. If B plays low, A gets 25 versus 15 → play low. Low is a dominant strategy for both, so the Nash equilibrium is (low, low) with 25 each — worse for both than (high, high) with 40 each. The cartel is a prisoners' dilemma.

With two players a cartel can sometimes survive, because the game is repeated and each can punish the other by cutting prices for a while — the threat makes cooperation a Nash equilibrium of the repeated game. Add more firms and it collapses: the gain from undercutting is larger (you steal from more rivals), detecting who cheated is harder, punishment is diluted across many firms, and one defector is enough to break the agreement. This is exactly why competition authorities focus on concentrated markets, and why the EU and Czech leniency programmes — full immunity for the first cartel member who confesses — are so destructive to cartels: they turn the prisoners' dilemma from a metaphor into the actual legal situation.

📊Where this shows up in data work

Estimating a demand curve from market data is the identification problem in a nutshell: every observed $(P,Q)$ pair is an intersection, so a scatter of equilibria traces out neither curve. If only supply shifts, the points map out the demand curve; if only demand shifts, they map out supply; if both shift, you get a cloud. The fix is an instrumental variable that moves one curve and not the other — weather for agricultural supply, a fuel-price shock for transport supply. Working out which curve your instrument moves is the whole job.

Worked examples

Example 1Equilibrium and surplus

With $Q^D = 900-30P$ and $Q^S = 20P-100$, find $P^*$, $Q^*$, consumer surplus, producer surplus and total surplus.

1

Set quantities equal: $900-30P = 20P-100 \Rightarrow 1\,000 = 50P \Rightarrow P^* = 20$ CZK.

2

Quantity: $Q^* = 900-600 = 300$; check on supply: $20(20)-100 = 300$ ✔.

3

Inverse curves for the triangles: $P = 30 - Q/30$ (choke price 30) and $P = 5+Q/20$ (lowest reservation price 5).

4

Areas: $CS = \tfrac12(300)(30-20)=1\,500$; $PS = \tfrac12(300)(20-5)=2\,250$.

Result: $P^*=20$ CZK, $Q^*=300$ thousand loaves, $CS = 1\,500$, $PS = 2\,250$, total surplus $3\,750$ (thousands of CZK per week). Producers capture more here because supply is less elastic than demand at this point.
Example 2A demand shock, done properly

Real incomes rise, and at every price households now want 150 thousand more loaves. Find the new equilibrium and describe what happened to each curve.

1

Which curve moves? The cause is income, not the price of bread → demand shifts right: $Q^D = 1\,050-30P$. Supply is untouched.

2

New equilibrium: $1\,050-30P = 20P-100 \Rightarrow 1\,150 = 50P \Rightarrow P^* = 23$ CZK.

3

Quantity: $Q^* = 20(23)-100 = 360$; check on demand: $1\,050-690 = 360$ ✔.

4

Say it correctly: demand shifted; supply did not shift — there was a movement along the supply curve from (300, 20) to (360, 23), because the price of bread itself changed.

Result: $P^*$ rises 20 → 23 CZK, $Q^*$ rises 300 → 360. Price and quantity moved in the same direction, the signature of a demand shock.
Example 3A tax of 5 CZK per loaf on bakeries

The government levies 5 CZK of tax per loaf, collected from bakeries. Find the new price paid by buyers, the price received by sellers, the split of the burden, tax revenue and the deadweight loss.

1

Shift supply. Sellers now keep $P-5$, so they supply $Q^S = 20(P-5)-100 = 20P-200$. The supply curve shifts up by exactly 5 CZK at every quantity.

2

New equilibrium: $900-30P = 20P-200 \Rightarrow 1\,100 = 50P \Rightarrow P_{buyer} = 22$ CZK, $Q = 240$ thousand loaves.

3

Seller's price: $22-5 = 17$ CZK. Buyers pay 2 CZK more than before, sellers receive 3 CZK less. Split: buyers 40 %, sellers 60 %.

4

Check with elasticities at the original point $(P=20, Q=300)$: $\varepsilon_D = 30\cdot\frac{20}{300}=2.0$ and $\varepsilon_S = 20\cdot\frac{20}{300}=1.333$. Buyers' share $=\frac{\varepsilon_S}{\varepsilon_S+\varepsilon_D}=\frac{1.333}{3.333}=0.40$ ✔ — exactly the 2 CZK out of 5.

5

Revenue: $5 \times 240 = 1\,200$ thousand CZK per week.

6

Deadweight loss: the triangle over the 60 thousand loaves no longer traded: $DWL = \tfrac12 \times 5 \times (300-240) = 150$ thousand CZK per week.

Result: buyers pay 22, sellers get 17; burden split 40 : 60; revenue 1 200; DWL 150 (thousands of CZK per week). If the tax had been collected from buyers instead, every one of these numbers would be identical — legal incidence is irrelevant.
Example 4The cartel game

Using the payoff table in section 7, find the Nash equilibrium and explain what changes when eight bakeries operate instead of two.

1

A's best responses: against B-high, A gets 55 (low) versus 40 (high) → low. Against B-low, A gets 25 (low) versus 15 (high) → low. Low is dominant.

2

By symmetry low is dominant for B too.

3

Nash equilibrium: (low, low), payoffs (25, 25) — Pareto-dominated by (high, high) with (40, 40). A textbook prisoners' dilemma.

4

With eight firms: the undercutter steals customers from seven rivals instead of one, so the temptation payoff is much larger; each rival's loss is diluted, so nobody notices quickly; agreeing on and monitoring a common price becomes far harder; and only one defector out of eight is needed to break the cartel.

Result: the equilibrium is (low, low). More competitors make cooperation harder to sustain, which is why the competitive outcome — price down at marginal cost — emerges in markets with many sellers, and why competition authorities police concentrated ones.

Practice problems

Problem 1

A market has $Q^D = 500-10P$ and $Q^S = 4P-40$. Find the equilibrium price and quantity, and the consumer and producer surplus.

Solution

Procedure: equate quantities, then invert for the triangles.

$500-10P = 4P-40 \Rightarrow 540 = 14P \Rightarrow P^* = 38.57$ CZK; $Q^* = 500-385.7 = 114.3$.

Inverse demand: $P = 50 - Q/10$ → choke price 50. Inverse supply: $P = 10 + Q/4$ → lowest reservation price 10.

$CS = \frac12(114.3)(50-38.57) = \frac12(114.3)(11.43) = 653.1$.   $PS = \frac12(114.3)(38.57-10) = \frac12(114.3)(28.57) = 1\,632.6$.

Result: $P^* \approx 38.57$, $Q^*\approx 114.3$, $CS \approx 653$, $PS \approx 1\,633$, total $\approx 2\,286$.

Problem 2

For each event, state which curve moves, in which direction, and what happens to $P^*$ and $Q^*$ in the market for train tickets: (a) petrol becomes much more expensive; (b) the rail operator's electricity bill doubles; (c) a new high-speed line opens; (d) ticket prices are cut by the operator; (e) working from home becomes permanent for a third of office workers.

Solution

(a) Petrol is a substitute for rail. Demand shifts right; $P^*\uparrow$, $Q^*\uparrow$ (movement along supply).

(b) An input cost. Supply shifts left; $P^*\uparrow$, $Q^*\downarrow$ (movement along demand).

(c) Capacity increases. Supply shifts right; $P^*\downarrow$, $Q^*\uparrow$.

(d) The price of the good itself changed — this is not a shift at all. It is a movement along the demand curve (quantity demanded rises) and along the supply curve. Strictly, if the operator sets the price below equilibrium, the result is excess demand: full trains and no seats.

(e) Tastes/needs change. Demand shifts left; $P^*\downarrow$, $Q^*\downarrow$.

Result: shifts in (a), (b), (c), (e); a pure movement along in (d). Notice that (a) and (e) both change demand, while (b), (c) change supply — being able to say which is which is worth a lot of exam points.

Problem 3

In the bread market ($Q^D = 900-30P$, $Q^S = 20P-100$) a bad harvest cuts supply to $Q^S = 20P-250$. Find the new equilibrium and the change in consumer surplus.

Solution

Procedure: supply shifts left; solve again.

$900-30P = 20P-250 \Rightarrow 1\,150 = 50P \Rightarrow P^* = 23$ CZK; $Q^* = 20(23)-250 = 210$.

Old CS $= \frac12(300)(30-20) = 1\,500$. New CS $= \frac12(210)(30-23) = \frac12(210)(7) = 735$.

Change: $735 - 1\,500 = -765$ thousand CZK per week.

Result: $P^*$ rises to 23 CZK, $Q^*$ falls to 210, consumer surplus falls by 765. Buyers moved along their unchanged demand curve — demand did not fall.

Problem 4

A tax of 3 CZK per unit is imposed on buyers in a market with $Q^D = 400-20P$ and $Q^S = 30P-100$. Find the price sellers receive, the price buyers pay, and the incidence split. Then confirm that the answer would be the same if the tax were collected from sellers.

Solution

Procedure: a tax on buyers means they pay $P_s + 3$ in total, so demand as a function of the seller's price is $Q^D = 400-20(P_s+3) = 340-20P_s$.

$340-20P_s = 30P_s-100 \Rightarrow 440 = 50P_s \Rightarrow P_s = 8.80$ CZK; buyers pay $11.80$; $Q = 30(8.8)-100 = 164$.

No-tax equilibrium: $400-20P = 30P-100 \Rightarrow 500 = 50P \Rightarrow P = 10$, $Q = 200$. So buyers pay 1.80 more and sellers get 1.20 less: 60 : 40.

Check with elasticities: $\varepsilon_D = 20\cdot\frac{10}{200} = 1.0$, $\varepsilon_S = 30\cdot\frac{10}{200}=1.5$. Buyers' share $= \frac{1.5}{2.5} = 0.6$ ✔.

Tax on sellers instead: $Q^S = 30(P_b-3)-100 = 30P_b-190$. Then $400-20P_b = 30P_b-190 \Rightarrow 590 = 50P_b \Rightarrow P_b = 11.80$, sellers get 8.80, $Q = 164$ — identical.

Result: buyers 1.80, sellers 1.20, $Q$ falls to 164. Legal incidence is irrelevant; only elasticities matter. Here demand is the more inelastic side, so buyers bear more.

Problem 5

Explain why a competitive firm produces where $P = MC$, and why this makes the competitive equilibrium efficient. Then explain why the firm in Lesson 14 did not do this.

Solution

Why P = MC. A price-taker can sell as much as it likes at the market price without depressing it, so its marginal revenue equals the price. Profit maximisation requires $MR = MC$; substituting, $P = MC$. Graphically the firm's own demand curve is horizontal.

Why efficient. In equilibrium the price simultaneously equals the marginal willingness to pay of the last buyer and the marginal cost of the last seller. So there is no unit that is worth more to some buyer than it costs some seller to produce — every mutually beneficial trade has been made, and total surplus is maximised. This is the sense in which competitive equilibrium is Pareto efficient.

Why not in Lesson 14. There the firm faced the whole downward-sloping market demand curve. Selling one more unit forced it to cut the price on all the units it was already selling, so $MR \lt P$. Setting $MR = MC$ therefore left $P \gt MC$, and the units between the firm's quantity and the efficient quantity were never produced: deadweight loss.

Result: the difference is entirely about whether the firm faces a horizontal or a downward-sloping demand curve — i.e. whether it has market power.

Problem 6

Two petrol stations at a motorway exit can each set a high or a low price. Both high: 30 each. Both low: 12 each. One low, one high: 45 for the low one, 5 for the high one. (a) Find the Nash equilibrium. (b) Is it Pareto efficient for the two firms? (c) Name two things that could sustain the high-price outcome in practice, and one legal instrument designed to destroy it.

Solution

(a) Against high, low pays 45 versus 30 → low. Against low, low pays 12 versus 5 → low. Low is dominant for both; the Nash equilibrium is (low, low) with 12 each.

(b) No — (high, high) gives 30 each, which both prefer, so (low, low) is Pareto-dominated from the firms' point of view. (Note: it is better for drivers, and total surplus including consumers is higher at low prices. "Pareto efficient" always requires you to say for whom.)

(c) Sustaining factors: repetition with credible punishment (a price war after any defection), easy observability of the rival's price (the price is on a big sign at the roadside, which is why petrol is unusually cartel-prone), few firms, high barriers to entry, and social norms or explicit communication.

Legal instrument: the leniency programme — the first cartel member to confess to the competition authority (ÚOHS in Czechia, DG COMP in the EU) gets full immunity from fines. This converts the cartel into a real prisoners' dilemma where defecting is safe and staying silent is dangerous.

Result: (low, low) is the equilibrium; it is Pareto-dominated for the firms but better for consumers; repetition and observability sustain collusion, leniency destroys it.

Problem 7

The government sets a maximum price of 15 CZK per loaf in the bread market ($Q^D = 900-30P$, $Q^S = 20P-100$). Compute the shortage and the deadweight loss, and comment on who gains.

Solution

Procedure: a price ceiling below the equilibrium of 20 CZK binds.

At $P=15$: $Q^D = 900-450 = 450$; $Q^S = 300-100 = 200$. Shortage $= 450-200 = 250$ thousand loaves per week.

Only 200 are traded. The 200th loaf has willingness to pay $30 - 200/30 = 23.33$ CZK and marginal cost $5+200/20 = 15$ CZK. At the efficient quantity 300 the gap is zero.

$DWL = \frac12(300-200)(23.33-15) = \frac12(100)(8.33) = 416.7$ thousand CZK per week.

Who gains: the buyers who actually get bread pay only 15 instead of 20 — they gain 5 CZK each. But 100 thousand loaves that would have been baked are not, and rationing is now by queueing, luck or connections rather than by willingness to pay, which destroys further value. Producer surplus falls sharply.

Result: shortage 250, DWL ≈ 417. Price controls transfer surplus to lucky buyers and destroy some of it; they are the classic worked example of the difference between a transfer and a deadweight loss.

Problem 8

You have five years of monthly data on the price and quantity of butter and you regress $\ln Q$ on $\ln P$. You get a coefficient of $+0.3$. Explain why this does not mean demand slopes upwards, and what you would need to estimate the demand elasticity properly.

Solution

Procedure: recognise the simultaneity problem.

Every observed $(P,Q)$ pair is an equilibrium — an intersection of supply and demand. If the dominant source of variation over those five years was demand shifting (income, tastes, health scares), the intersections trace out the supply curve, which slopes upwards. Your $+0.3$ is an estimate of a supply elasticity, or a mixture of the two, not of demand.

What you need: an instrumental variable that shifts supply but is uncorrelated with demand — a shock to feed prices, weather affecting milk yields, an energy-price shock, or an exchange-rate movement affecting imported inputs. Two-stage least squares with that instrument recovers the demand curve. An alternative is a genuine randomised price experiment across stores.

Result: the regression is biased by simultaneity; identification requires a supply shifter that is excluded from the demand equation.

Summary

Supply and demand is the most-used diagram in economics and the most-misused. If you keep one thing from this lesson, keep the shift-versus-movement rule, and the habit of saying "quantity demanded" when you mean a point and "demand" when you mean the curve.

📌What to take away
  • In a competitive market everyone is a price-taker; the individual firm faces a horizontal demand curve and produces where $P = MC$.
  • Demand is built from willingness to pay, supply from reservation prices (marginal costs). Equilibrium is where the two quantities are equal, and it is self-correcting.
  • A change in the price of the good itself = movement along the curve. Anything else = shift of the curve. Never move both curves for one shock.
  • Demand shock: $P$ and $Q$ move the same way. Supply shock: they move opposite ways.
  • Competitive equilibrium maximises total surplus, because $P$ equals both marginal willingness to pay and marginal cost.
  • Tax incidence does not depend on who legally pays. Buyers' share $= \varepsilon_S/(\varepsilon_S+\varepsilon_D)$; the more inelastic side bears more. A tax also creates a DWL triangle over the trades it prevents.
  • A cartel is a prisoners' dilemma: undercutting is a dominant strategy. More firms make collusion harder to sustain — which is what competition does.

quiz.q: The price of butter rises sharply and households buy less butter. Which description is correct?
options: Demand for butter fell — the demand curve shifted left.
Quantity demanded fell — a movement along an unchanged demand curve.
Both the demand and the supply curve shifted left.
Supply of butter fell — the supply curve shifted left.
quiz.explain: Price is on the axis, so a change in the price of the good itself can never shift the curve — it moves you along it. 'Demand fell' would claim that at every price households want less, which needs a different cause (income, tastes, the price of a substitute). This wording distinction is the single most frequently penalised error in the course.

quiz.q: A market has $Q^D = 900 - 30P$ and $Q^S = 20P - 100$. What is the equilibrium price?
quiz.explain: Set the quantities equal: $900-30P = 20P-100 \Rightarrow 1\,000 = 50P \Rightarrow P^* = 20$. Then $Q^* = 900-600 = 300$, and the supply side confirms it: $20(20)-100 = 300$. Always check the quantity in both equations — it catches sign errors immediately.

quiz.q: In the market $Q^D = 900-30P$, $Q^S = 20P-100$ (equilibrium $P=20$, $Q=300$), the government imposes a tax of 5 CZK per unit on sellers. By how many CZK does the price paid by buyers rise?
quiz.explain: Supply becomes $Q^S = 20(P-5)-100 = 20P-200$. Then $900-30P = 20P-200 \Rightarrow P_{buyer} = 22$, so buyers pay 2 CZK more and sellers receive 17, i.e. 3 CZK less. Check with elasticities at the old point: $\varepsilon_D = 2.0$, $\varepsilon_S = 1.333$, buyers' share $=\varepsilon_S/(\varepsilon_S+\varepsilon_D) = 0.4$, and $0.4\times 5 = 2$ ✔.

quiz.q: In a market you observe that price rose and quantity traded fell. What most likely happened?
options: Demand shifted right.
Demand shifted left.
Supply shifted left.
Supply shifted right.
quiz.explain: After a demand shock, price and quantity move in the same direction (both up, or both down). After a supply shock they move in opposite directions. Price up plus quantity down is the signature of supply shifting left — an input-cost shock, a bad harvest, a new tax. This simple sign rule is the basis of identifying supply and demand shocks in real data.

quiz.q: Why does a firm in a perfectly competitive market produce where price equals marginal cost, while the firm in Lesson 14 chose a price above marginal cost?
options: Because competitive firms have lower costs.
Because a price-taker's marginal revenue equals the price, whereas a firm facing a downward-sloping demand curve has MR below the price.
Because competition law forbids charging more than marginal cost.
Because competitive firms do not maximise profit.
quiz.explain: Both firms maximise profit and both set $MR = MC$. The difference is the demand curve each faces. A price-taker sells extra units without depressing the price, so $MR = P$ and therefore $P = MC$. A firm with market power must cut the price on all units to sell one more, so $MR \lt P$ and the optimum leaves $P \gt MC$ — and a deadweight loss.

quiz.q: In the market for train tickets, which of the following shift the demand curve?
options: Petrol becomes much more expensive.
The rail operator cuts ticket prices.
A third of office workers switch permanently to working from home.
The operator's electricity bill doubles.
Real household incomes rise by 6 %.
quiz.explain: Demand shifts when something other than the ticket price changes what people want at each price: a dearer substitute (A), a change in needs or tastes (C), a change in income (E). Cutting ticket prices (B) is a change in the price of the good itself, so it is a movement along demand, not a shift. A higher electricity bill (D) is an input cost and shifts supply, not demand.

quiz.q: A market has $Q^D = 400 - 20P$ and $Q^S = 30P - 100$. (a) Find the equilibrium and total surplus. (b) A tax of 3 CZK per unit is imposed on buyers. Find the new quantity, the price buyers pay, the price sellers receive, tax revenue and the deadweight loss. (c) Explain why it makes no difference whether the tax is legally collected from buyers or from sellers, and which side bears more of it here and why.
quiz.solution:
(a) Equilibrium and surplus.

$400-20P = 30P-100 \Rightarrow 500 = 50P \Rightarrow P^* = 10$, $Q^* = 400-200 = 200$ (supply check: $300-100 = 200$ ✔).

Inverse demand $P = 20 - Q/20$ (choke price 20); inverse supply $P = 10/3 + Q/30$, so the lowest reservation price is $3.33$.

$CS = \tfrac12(200)(20-10) = 1\,000$;   $PS = \tfrac12(200)(10-3.33) = 666.7$;   total surplus $= 1\,666.7$.

(b) A tax of 3 on buyers.

Buyers now pay $P_s + 3$ in total, so demand expressed in the seller's price is $Q^D = 400-20(P_s+3) = 340-20P_s$.

$340-20P_s = 30P_s-100 \Rightarrow 440 = 50P_s \Rightarrow P_s = 8.80$ CZK. Buyers pay $11.80$ CZK. $Q = 30(8.8)-100 = 164$.

Tax revenue $= 3 \times 164 = 492$.

$DWL = \tfrac12 \times \text{tax} \times \Delta Q = \tfrac12 \times 3 \times (200-164) = \tfrac12\times 3\times 36 = \mathbf{54}$.

(c) Legal versus economic incidence.

If the tax is collected from sellers instead, supply becomes $Q^S = 30(P_b-3)-100 = 30P_b-190$, and $400-20P_b = 30P_b-190 \Rightarrow P_b = 11.80$, $P_s = 8.80$, $Q = 164$ — every number is identical. The reason is that the tax simply inserts a fixed wedge of 3 CZK between what buyers pay and what sellers keep; the market then finds the quantity at which the vertical gap between the demand and supply curves equals that wedge. Which side hands the money to the tax office never enters that condition.

Who bears more. Buyers pay 1.80 more than before, sellers receive 1.20 less: a 60 : 40 split. Elasticities at the original equilibrium are $\varepsilon_D = 20\cdot\frac{10}{200} = 1.0$ and $\varepsilon_S = 30\cdot\frac{10}{200} = 1.5$; the buyers' share is $\varepsilon_S/(\varepsilon_S+\varepsilon_D) = 1.5/2.5 = 0.6$ ✔. Demand is the more inelastic side here, and the more inelastic side always bears more, because it has fewer ways to escape the tax by changing behaviour. In the limit, a perfectly inelastic demand would mean buyers bear the whole tax and the quantity — and therefore the deadweight loss — would not change at all.

lessons.html:
Two topics that look unrelated but share one idea. First, credit: moving consumption across time, why the interest rate is its price, and why lending is a principal–agent problem that shuts poor people out. Then market failure: why a market that works beautifully in Lesson 15 gets the quantity badly wrong when costs spill over onto third parties. The shared idea is that the market only gets it right when everyone affected by a decision is a party to it — and in credit and in pollution, they are not.

🎯Lesson objectives
  • Draw the intertemporal feasible frontier and find the optimum where $MRS = 1+r$.
  • Separate pure impatience from diminishing marginal returns to consumption.
  • Explain lending as a principal–agent problem and the role of collateral and equity.
  • Explain credit rationing, why the poor pay more or are excluded, and the effect on wealth inequality.
  • Distinguish private and social marginal cost, find the market and the efficient quantity, and compute the deadweight loss from an externality.
  • Apply Coase bargaining, Pigouvian taxes, regulation and quotas, and say when each works.

1 · Moving consumption through time

You have 5 000 CZK now and expect 5 400 CZK in a year — a summer job that pays later. Whether you spend 5 000 now is entirely up to you: with a credit market you can borrow against the future or lend today's money into it.

📐Definition — the interest rate as a price

The interest rate $r$ is the price of moving consumption from the future to the present. Giving up 1 CZK today buys $1+r$ CZK next year; borrowing 1 CZK today costs $1+r$ CZK next year.

So $1+r$ is the relative price of consumption now in terms of consumption later — exactly the role a relative price plays in any budget constraint you drew in Block 3.

With $r = 8\,\%$, the feasible frontier runs from "consume everything now" to "consume everything later":

  • Maximum now: $5\,000 + \dfrac{5\,400}{1.08} = 5\,000+5\,000 = 10\,000$ CZK.
  • Maximum later: $5\,000 \times 1.08 + 5\,400 = 5\,400+5\,400 = 10\,800$ CZK.

The frontier is the straight line joining them, with slope $-(1+r) = -1.08$, and it passes through your endowment $(5\,000,\ 5\,400)$.

2 · Why people want to smooth — and why they still discount

📐Definition — the two reasons you prefer the present
  • Diminishing marginal returns to consumption: an extra 1 000 CZK is worth more when you have little than when you have a lot. If your income is lumpy, you want to smooth it — move money from the fat year to the lean one. This preference disappears if consumption is already equal in both periods.
  • Pure impatience (discounting): even with equal consumption in both periods, most people would still rather have the cake now. Two ingredients: myopia (the future feels less vivid) and prudence (you might not be around, or the promise might not be kept).

Together they determine the marginal rate of substitution: how much future consumption you would give up for one more unit today. $MRS = 1+\rho$ when consumption is equal, where $\rho$ is the discount rate — the pure-impatience part.

ΣRule — the intertemporal optimum

Choose the point on the feasible frontier where $$MRS = 1+r.$$ If at your endowment $MRS \gt 1+r$ you value present consumption more than the market charges for it → borrow. If $MRS \lt 1+r$ → lend. If they are equal, stay put.

⚠Common mistake

"Impatient people borrow, patient people lend." Only half true. The decision depends on both impatience and the shape of the endowment. A very patient student with zero income now and a big salary next year will still borrow — because of diminishing marginal returns, not impatience. Always compare $MRS$ at the endowment with $1+r$.

3 · Lending is a principal–agent problem

Lesson 13's structure comes back, with new names. The lender is the principal, the borrower is the agent, and the hidden thing is what the borrower does with the money: how hard she works on the project, how much risk she takes, and whether she repays if she can.

📐Definition — the enforcement problem in credit

A loan contract can specify the amount and the repayment. It cannot enforce effort, prudence or honest reporting. So the lender faces:

  • Moral hazard (hidden action): with someone else's money at stake, the borrower has an incentive to take excessive risk — the upside is hers, the downside is partly the lender's.
  • Adverse selection (hidden attributes): raising the interest rate to cover the risk drives away the safe borrowers first, leaving a riskier pool — so a higher rate can lower expected profit.
ΣRule — collateral, equity and credit rationing

The lender's answer is to make the borrower share the downside:

  • Equity: the borrower puts her own money into the project, so failure costs her too.
  • Collateral: an asset (a flat, a machine) the lender can seize on default.

Both require wealth the borrower already has. Someone with no wealth cannot provide either, so lenders either charge a very high rate or refuse to lend at all — credit rationing. Note the crucial point: rationing is not a temporary failure of the market to clear. Raising the interest rate would make the pool of borrowers worse, so the lender rationally refuses to lend even to someone offering to pay more. This is exactly the structure of involuntary unemployment in Lesson 13.

Look at Czech interest rates and you can see the ladder of enforceability directly: a mortgage (secured on the flat) around 5 %, a consumer loan (unsecured but credit-scored) around 10 %, a credit card revolving balance above 20 %, and a small non-bank loan to a borrower with a bad record 40 % or more. The differences are far too large to be explained by the cost of funds; they are the price of the principal–agent problem.

📊Where this shows up in data work

Credit scoring is one of the biggest applied-data industries in the world, and it is a direct attempt to shrink the information asymmetry: replace collateral with prediction. Two things make it hard and interesting. First, selection — you only observe repayment for applicants you accepted, so the training data is truncated (the "reject inference" problem). Second, fairness: a model that predicts well may still be using variables correlated with protected characteristics, which is why the EU AI Act classifies creditworthiness scoring as high-risk and requires documented bias testing.

4 · Credit constraints and wealth inequality

The consequences are large. A person without wealth cannot borrow to invest in education, a machine, or a business — even when the project would return far more than the interest rate. Projects with a high return go unfunded, so the outcome is inefficient, not merely unequal. And because those excluded stay poor, they still have no collateral next year: exclusion is self-perpetuating and inequality persists across generations.

This is why microfinance, state loan guarantees, subsidised student loans and public education all exist. Each is an attempt to work around the collateral requirement: group lending replaces collateral with peer monitoring, guarantees replace the borrower's wealth with the state's, and publicly funded education removes the need to borrow at all.

5 · Externalities

📐Definition — externality

An externality is a cost or benefit of a decision that falls on someone who is not party to it, and which is not reflected in a price.

  • Negative: pollution, congestion, antibiotic resistance, noise, CO₂.
  • Positive: vaccination, R&D and knowledge spillovers, restoring the façade of your building, beekeeping next to an orchard.
ΣRule — private versus social marginal cost

$$MSC = MPC + \text{marginal external cost}.$$ The market equates price with private marginal cost, but efficiency requires price to equal social marginal cost. With a negative externality $MSC \gt MPC$, so the market produces too much. With a positive externality the market produces too little.

Our example: a large pig farm whose slurry pollutes a river used by a downstream fish farm. Let $Q$ be thousands of tonnes of pork per year and $P$ thousands of CZK per tonne. $$\text{Demand: } P = 80 - 0.5Q, \qquad MPC = 20+0.5Q, \qquad \text{external cost} = 10 \text{ per tonne.}$$ So $MSC = 30+0.5Q$.

Market equilibrium: $80-0.5Q = 20+0.5Q \Rightarrow Q = 60$, $P = 50$. Efficient allocation: $80-0.5Q = 30+0.5Q \Rightarrow Q = 50$, $P = 55$. The market makes 10 thousand tonnes too much.

The deadweight loss is the triangle between $MSC$ and demand over the excess 10 thousand tonnes. Its height at $Q=60$ is $MSC - P = 60-50 = 10$ and it closes to zero at $Q=50$: $$DWL = \tfrac12 \times 10 \times 10 = 50 \text{ million CZK per year.}$$

⚠Common mistake

"The efficient level of pollution is zero." No. Efficiency means producing up to the point where the marginal social benefit equals the marginal social cost. Cutting output from 50 to 0 would destroy more value than the pollution it avoids. Only if the marginal damage exceeds the marginal benefit at every quantity is zero the right answer — which is essentially the argument for banning some substances outright (asbestos, CFCs, leaded petrol).

6 · Three ways to fix it

Coase bargaining

Assign clear property rights and let the parties negotiate. Whoever holds the right, if bargaining is costless the efficient quantity results — the rights only decide who pays whom. Works when there are few parties, rights are well defined and enforceable, information is good and transaction costs are low. Fails for CO₂: eight billion parties, no enforceable global rights, enormous transaction costs.

Pigouvian tax

Tax each unit by exactly the marginal external cost. That raises the producer's private cost to the social cost, so profit-maximising behaviour delivers the efficient quantity automatically. Needs the regulator to know the size of the damage — the hard part. Examples: carbon pricing, the EU ETS (a quantity instrument that produces a price), congestion charges, excise on fuel.

Regulation and quotas

Ban the activity, cap emissions, mandate a technology, set standards. Crude — it does not equalise marginal abatement costs across firms unless permits are tradable — but it works when damage is catastrophic, monitoring emissions is impossible, or a price signal would be politically unacceptable. Most environmental policy in practice is a mixture.

Norms and other levers

Social norms, reputation, moral suasion and firm-level reporting requirements shift behaviour without prices — think of the collapse in plastic-bag use after a small charge and a change in what counts as normal. Recall Lesson 11: reciprocity and inequality aversion are real and exploitable.

Worked examples

Example 1The feasible frontier and the choice to borrow

You have 5 000 CZK now and 5 400 CZK next year; $r = 8\,\%$. (a) Find the endpoints of the feasible frontier. (b) You choose to consume 6 000 now. How much do you consume later? (c) At the endowment your $MRS$ is 1.25. Should you borrow or lend?

1

(a) Maximum now: discount the future income and add it: $5\,000+\dfrac{5\,400}{1.08}=5\,000+5\,000=10\,000$ CZK.

2

Maximum later: compound today's income and add: $5\,000(1.08)+5\,400 = 5\,400+5\,400=10\,800$ CZK. The frontier joins $(10\,000, 0)$ and $(0, 10\,800)$ with slope $-1.08$.

3

(b) Consuming 6 000 now means borrowing 1 000. Repayment $= 1\,000\times 1.08 = 1\,080$, so later consumption $= 5\,400-1\,080 = 4\,320$ CZK.

Check on the frontier: $6\,000(1.08)+4\,320 = 6\,480+4\,320 = 10\,800$ ✔.

4

(c) $MRS = 1.25 \gt 1+r = 1.08$. You value 1 CZK today at 1.25 CZK of future consumption, but the market only charges you 1.08. Borrow.

Result: frontier from (10 000, 0) to (0, 10 800); consuming 6 000 now leaves 4 320 later; since $MRS \gt 1+r$ at the endowment, borrowing raises utility.
Example 2Collateral, equity and the interest rate

Two people want to open the same bakery. It costs 1 000 000 CZK and returns 1 250 000 CZK if run diligently, 900 000 CZK if not. Anna has 400 000 CZK of her own; Bára has nothing. The bank's cost of funds is 4 %. Explain what happens.

1

Anna borrows 600 000. She has 400 000 of equity at stake. If the project fails she loses her own 400 000 first, so her incentives are aligned with the bank's — she will run it diligently. The bank lends near its cost of funds, say 6 %: repayment $636\,000$, leaving Anna $1\,250\,000-636\,000 = 614\,000$.

2

Bára would borrow 1 000 000. She has nothing at stake. If it goes well she keeps the surplus; if it fails the bank absorbs the loss. Her incentive to be diligent is weak — this is moral hazard.

3

The bank's options. Charge a higher rate to cover the risk — but that reduces Bára's payoff from success and makes diligence less attractive still, and it drives away safe borrowers (adverse selection). Or demand collateral — which Bára does not have.

4

Outcome: the bank rations: it refuses to lend to Bára at any interest rate, or lends a smaller amount at a much higher one.

Result: the identical project is funded for Anna and not for Bára. This is inefficient — a project with a 25 % return goes unfunded — and it is why wealth begets wealth. Note that Bára is credit-rationed, not simply "charged more": she cannot buy her way in by offering a higher rate.
Example 3The externality: market, efficient and deadweight loss

With demand $P = 80-0.5Q$, $MPC = 20+0.5Q$ and a marginal external cost of 10, find the market and efficient quantities and the deadweight loss.

1

Market outcome: the pig farms ignore the fish farms, so they equate price with private cost: $80-0.5Q=20+0.5Q \Rightarrow Q = 60$, $P = 50$.

2

Social marginal cost: $MSC = MPC + 10 = 30+0.5Q$.

3

Efficient outcome: $80-0.5Q = 30+0.5Q \Rightarrow Q = 50$, and the marginal willingness to pay there is $P = 55$.

4

Deadweight loss: over the excess 10 thousand tonnes, $MSC$ exceeds the value to buyers. The gap is zero at $Q=50$ and $60-50 = 10$ at $Q=60$: $DWL = \tfrac12(10)(10) = 50$.

5

Sanity check the direction: negative externality → $MSC$ above $MPC$ → market quantity too high. ✔

Result: market $Q = 60$ at $P = 50$; efficient $Q = 50$ at $P = 55$; deadweight loss 50 million CZK per year.
Example 4Coase bargaining versus a Pigouvian tax

Continue the pig-farm example. (a) Show there is a bargain the fish farms and the pig farms could strike. (b) Design the Pigouvian tax and check it works.

1

(a) Value of cutting output from 60 to 50 for the fish farms: the external damage avoided is $10 \times 10 = 100$ million CZK.

2

Cost to the pig farms and their customers: the surplus lost on those 10 thousand tonnes is $\int_{50}^{60}\big[(80-0.5Q)-(20+0.5Q)\big]dQ = \int_{50}^{60}(60-Q)\,dQ = 50$ million CZK.

3

Room for a deal: the fish farms would pay up to 100; the pig side needs at least 50. Any payment between 50 and 100 million CZK makes both sides better off, and the net gain of 50 million is exactly the deadweight loss. Who ends up paying whom depends on who holds the property right — the efficiency result does not.

4

(b) Pigouvian tax: set $t = 10$, the marginal external cost. Private cost becomes $20+0.5Q+10 = 30+0.5Q = MSC$.

5

Check: $80-0.5Q = 30+0.5Q \Rightarrow Q = 50$ ✔, exactly the efficient quantity. Tax revenue $= 10 \times 50 = 500$ million CZK per year.

Result: Coase bargaining works here (two well-identified parties, clear damage) with a payment between 50 and 100 million; a Pigouvian tax of 10 per tonne achieves the same quantity and raises 500 million in revenue. For CO₂, the number of parties makes Coase impossible and the tax (or a tradable-permit scheme) is the only workable instrument.

Practice problems

Problem 1

Tomáš has 12 000 CZK now and expects 22 000 CZK next year. The interest rate is 10 %. (a) Find the endpoints of his feasible frontier. (b) If he wants to consume 20 000 CZK now, how much can he consume later? (c) If instead he lends 4 000, what is his consumption next year?

Solution

(a) Maximum now $= 12\,000 + \frac{22\,000}{1.1} = 12\,000+20\,000 = 32\,000$ CZK. Maximum later $= 12\,000(1.1)+22\,000 = 13\,200+22\,000 = 35\,200$ CZK. Slope $-1.1$.

(b) He borrows $20\,000-12\,000 = 8\,000$; repayment $8\,800$; later consumption $= 22\,000-8\,800 = 13\,200$ CZK. Check: $20\,000(1.1)+13\,200 = 22\,000+13\,200 = 35\,200$ ✔.

(c) Lending 4 000 leaves 8 000 now and $22\,000+4\,400 = 26\,400$ CZK later.

Result: frontier (32 000, 0) to (0, 35 200); 13 200 later if he consumes 20 000 now; 26 400 later if he lends 4 000.

Problem 2

Two students have the same preferences and the same pure discount rate $\rho = 5\,\%$. Student A has 30 000 CZK this year and 30 000 next year. Student B has 5 000 this year and 55 000 next year. The interest rate is 5 %. Who borrows? Explain which of the two motives is doing the work.

Solution

Procedure: compare $MRS$ at the endowment with $1+r = 1.05$.

Student A: consumption is already equal in the two periods, so diminishing marginal returns contribute nothing to the MRS, which is therefore just $1+\rho = 1.05$. That equals $1+r$, so A neither borrows nor lends.

Student B: consumption today (5 000) is far below tomorrow's (55 000), so the marginal value of a crown today is much higher — the MRS at the endowment is well above 1.05 even before impatience is added. B borrows.

Result: B borrows, A does not. The motive is diminishing marginal returns to consumption (consumption smoothing), not impatience — the two students are equally impatient. This is the model's answer to why students borrow and why it is rational.

Problem 3

Explain why a bank might refuse to lend to a borrower even when that borrower offers to pay a higher interest rate. Name both information problems by their technical names.

Solution

Procedure: show that raising the rate worsens the pool and the incentives.

Adverse selection (hidden attributes): the borrowers most willing to accept a very high rate are those least likely to repay — safe borrowers with good projects drop out first. The average quality of applicants falls as the rate rises, so beyond some point the bank's expected return goes down, not up.

Moral hazard (hidden action): a higher required repayment reduces the borrower's payoff in the good state, which pushes her towards riskier projects with a small chance of a big payoff. The bank bears the downside, so the loan becomes more dangerous at exactly the moment the bank is charging more for it.

Because the interest rate cannot clear the market, the bank rations credit: it caps the amount lent and refuses some applicants outright. Collateral and equity are the way out, because they make the borrower bear the downside — but they require pre-existing wealth.

Result: credit rationing is an equilibrium, exactly like involuntary unemployment in Lesson 13: in both cases the price cannot be used to clear the market because the price itself changes the other side's behaviour.

Problem 4

A market has demand $P = 120 - 2Q$ and private marginal cost $MPC = 30 + Q$. Production causes an external cost of 15 per unit. Find the market quantity, the efficient quantity and the deadweight loss.

Solution

Procedure: market where demand $= MPC$, efficient where demand $= MSC = MPC + 15$.

Market: $120-2Q = 30+Q \Rightarrow 90 = 3Q \Rightarrow Q_m = 30$, $P = 60$.

Efficient: $MSC = 45+Q$; $120-2Q = 45+Q \Rightarrow 75 = 3Q \Rightarrow Q_e = 25$, $P = 70$.

DWL: the gap between $MSC$ and demand is zero at $Q=25$ and at $Q = 30$ equals $MSC(30) - P(30) = 75 - 60 = 15$.

$DWL = \frac12(30-25)(15) = \frac12(5)(15) = 37.5$.

Result: $Q_m = 30$, $Q_e = 25$, DWL $= 37.5$. A Pigouvian tax of 15 per unit would move the market to 25 and raise revenue of $15\times 25 = 375$.

Problem 5

A pharmaceutical company's basic research produces knowledge that competitors also use — a positive externality worth 20 per unit of research. The firm's private marginal benefit is $MPB = 100 - 4R$ and the marginal cost of research is $MC = 20 + 2R$. Find the private and socially optimal levels of research and the size of the ideal subsidy.

Solution

Procedure: a positive externality means social marginal benefit exceeds private: $MSB = MPB + 20 = 120-4R$.

Private choice: $100-4R = 20+2R \Rightarrow 80 = 6R \Rightarrow R_p = 13.33$.

Social optimum: $120-4R = 20+2R \Rightarrow 100 = 6R \Rightarrow R_s = 16.67$.

The market does too little research — the mirror image of the pollution case.

The ideal instrument is a Pigouvian subsidy of 20 per unit of research, which raises the firm's private benefit to the social benefit and induces $R = 16.67$.

DWL of the market outcome $= \frac12(16.67-13.33)(20) = \frac12(3.33)(20) = 33.3$.

Result: $R_p = 13.33 \lt R_s = 16.67$; a subsidy of 20 per unit closes the gap. This is the standard economic case for public research funding, R&D tax credits and patents — patents work differently, by internalising the benefit rather than subsidising the cost.

Problem 6

Say whether Coase bargaining is likely to solve each problem, and why: (a) a noisy bar below a block of flats; (b) global CO₂ emissions; (c) a factory polluting a river used by one downstream brewery; (d) antibiotic resistance from over-prescription.

Solution

Criteria: few parties, clearly defined and enforceable property rights, low transaction costs, good information about the damage.

(a) Possibly. Few parties and a clear right (noise limits in Czech law). But the residents must coordinate among themselves — a free-rider problem — and the damage is subjective. Bargaining often works in practice, via a compromise on closing times.

(b) No. Billions of emitters and victims, no enforceable global property right, gigantic transaction costs, and the victims include people not yet born who cannot bargain. This is why climate policy uses taxes, permits and treaties rather than negotiation between the parties.

(c) Yes — the textbook case. Two identifiable parties, measurable damage, an enforceable right. Whether the factory has the right to pollute or the brewery the right to clean water changes who pays, but not the efficient quantity.

(d) No. Enormous numbers of dispersed parties, the damage is delayed and probabilistic, and it is impossible to attribute a particular resistant infection to a particular prescription. Regulation (prescription-only rules, stewardship programmes) and public funding of new antibiotics are the instruments used.

Result: Coase works in (c), maybe (a), and not in (b) or (d). The general lesson: bargaining is a solution for small-numbers externalities with enforceable rights, not a general substitute for policy.

Problem 7

In the pig-farm example ($MPC = 20+0.5Q$, external cost 10, demand $P = 80-0.5Q$) the government instead imposes a quota of 50 thousand tonnes. Compare the outcome with the Pigouvian tax of 10 in terms of quantity, price, who gets the money, and what the regulator needs to know.

Solution

Quantity: identical. Both instruments deliver $Q = 50$, the efficient level.

Price: also 55 in both cases — buyers pay the marginal willingness to pay at $Q=50$ either way.

Who gets the money: under the tax, the 500 million CZK (10 × 50) goes to the government. Under a quota handed out free, that same amount stays with the pig farms as scarcity rent — they sell 50 thousand tonnes at 55 while their private marginal cost at 50 is only 45. If the quota rights were auctioned, the revenue would go to the state and the two instruments become equivalent (this is exactly the free-allocation-versus-auctioning debate in the EU ETS).

Information required: the tax requires the regulator to know the marginal external cost (10). The quota requires it to know the efficient quantity (50), which needs knowledge of demand and costs as well. With uncertainty about costs, a price instrument and a quantity instrument are no longer equivalent — a quota fixes the quantity and lets the cost vary; a tax fixes the cost and lets the quantity vary.

Result: same $Q$ and $P$; different distribution of the rent and different informational demands. This is why real schemes often combine them (tradable permits with a price floor).

Problem 8

Explain the common structure shared by involuntary unemployment (Lesson 13) and credit rationing (this lesson). Identify the principal, the agent, the hidden variable and the substitute for the missing enforceable contract in each.

Solution

Common structure: in both cases a contract cannot be written on the thing that matters, so the price cannot be used to clear the market — because changing the price changes the other side's behaviour in a way that hurts the party setting it.

Labour marketCredit market
Principalemployerlender
Agentworkerborrower
Hidden variableefforteffort / risk-taking / willingness to repay
Substitute for the contractemployment rent + threat of dismissalcollateral, equity, threat of no future credit
Equilibrium consequenceinvoluntary unemploymentcredit rationing
Why the price can't cleara lower wage lowers efforta higher rate worsens the borrower pool and incentives

Result: both are principal–agent problems with hidden action, both are solved by making the agent bear a loss (a rent to be forfeited, or wealth to be seized), and in both the market ends up with rationing on one side. The distributional consequence is the same too: those without wealth or without a job are excluded, and the exclusion perpetuates itself.

Summary

The credit market lets you move consumption through time, but only if a lender can trust you — and trust is bought with wealth you may not have. The market for a polluting good works perfectly on its own terms and still gets the quantity wrong, because one of the parties bearing the cost was never in the room. Both are failures of the same kind: something that matters is not in any contract and not in any price.

📌What to take away
  • The feasible frontier runs from $(y_1 + y_2/(1+r),\ 0)$ to $(0,\ y_1(1+r)+y_2)$ with slope $-(1+r)$; the optimum is where $MRS = 1+r$.
  • Two reasons to prefer the present: diminishing marginal returns to consumption (smoothing) and pure impatience (myopia + prudence). Compare MRS at the endowment with $1+r$ to decide who borrows.
  • Lending is a principal–agent problem with moral hazard and adverse selection. Collateral and equity substitute for the missing contract, and both require pre-existing wealth.
  • Credit rationing is an equilibrium: raising the rate worsens the pool, so lenders refuse rather than charge more. This excludes the poor, blocks profitable projects and entrenches wealth inequality.
  • Externality: a cost or benefit falling on a non-party. $MSC = MPC + $ marginal external cost; negative externality → market produces too much, positive → too little.
  • DWL is the triangle between $MSC$ and demand over the excess quantity. Efficient pollution is not zero.
  • Fixes: Coase bargaining (few parties, clear rights, low transaction costs), a Pigouvian tax/subsidy equal to the marginal external cost, or regulation and quotas. Tax and quota give the same quantity but hand the rent to different people.

quiz.q: You have 5 000 CZK now and expect 5 400 CZK in a year. The interest rate is 8 %. What is the maximum you could consume now (in CZK)?
quiz.explain: Borrow against the future income and add it to today's: $5\,000 + \frac{5\,400}{1.08} = 5\,000 + 5\,000 = 10\,000$ CZK. Note you must discount future income (divide by $1+r$), not compound it. The other endpoint, maximum consumption later, is $5\,000(1.08)+5\,400 = 10\,800$ CZK, and the frontier joining them has slope $-1.08$.

quiz.q: At her endowment, Klára's marginal rate of substitution between consumption now and later is 1.30. The interest rate is 6 %. What should she do?
options: Lend, because she is patient.
Borrow, because she values present consumption more highly than the market charges for it.
Stay at the endowment — the MRS and the interest rate are not comparable.
Borrow only if she is also impatient in the pure sense.
quiz.explain: The rule is: compare $MRS$ at the endowment with $1+r$. Here $1.30 \gt 1.06$, so she is willing to give up 1.30 CZK of future consumption for one crown today, while the market only demands 1.06 — borrowing makes her better off. She keeps borrowing until the MRS falls to 1.06. Note the reason may be pure impatience or simply a low endowment today (diminishing marginal returns to consumption).

quiz.q: Why does a lender often refuse to lend to a wealthless borrower rather than simply charging a higher interest rate?
options: Because charging different rates to different customers is illegal.
Because a higher rate attracts riskier applicants and pushes borrowers towards riskier projects, so the lender's expected return can fall.
Because banks are required by law to hold collateral against every loan.
Because wealthless borrowers always have worse business ideas.
quiz.explain: Raising the rate worsens the borrower pool (adverse selection) and weakens the incentive to be prudent (moral hazard), so beyond some point expected profit falls with the rate. The price therefore cannot clear the market and the lender rations. Collateral and equity solve the problem — but both require wealth the borrower does not have, which is exactly why exclusion perpetuates itself.

quiz.q: A market has demand $P = 80 - 0.5Q$ and private marginal cost $MPC = 20 + 0.5Q$. Production imposes an external cost of 10 per unit. What is the efficient quantity?
quiz.explain: Efficiency requires demand = social marginal cost, where $MSC = MPC + 10 = 30+0.5Q$. So $80-0.5Q = 30+0.5Q \Rightarrow 50 = Q$. The market, which uses $MPC$, produces 60 — ten units too many. The deadweight loss is the triangle $\frac12 \times 10 \times 10 = 50$.

quiz.q: In the same market, the government replaces a Pigouvian tax of 10 per unit with a freely handed-out quota of 50 units. What changes?
options: The quantity produced falls further.
Nothing at all — the two policies are identical in every respect.
Quantity and price are the same, but the revenue that the tax would have collected stays with the producers as scarcity rent.
The deadweight loss reappears, because quotas are always inefficient.
quiz.explain: Both instruments deliver the efficient $Q = 50$ at $P = 55$, so the efficiency outcome is identical. The difference is distributional: the tax transfers 10 × 50 = 500 to the state, while a free quota lets producers keep it as rent. Auctioning the quota rights would make the two equivalent — this is precisely the free-allocation-versus-auctioning debate in the EU Emissions Trading System.

quiz.q: Coase bargaining is a plausible solution to an externality when which of the following hold?
options: There are only a few clearly identifiable parties.
Property rights are well defined and enforceable.
Transaction costs of negotiating are low.
The externality is global and affects billions of people.
The damage is impossible to attribute to any particular producer.
quiz.explain: Coase's insight is that with clear rights and costless bargaining, the parties will negotiate their way to the efficient quantity regardless of who holds the right — the allocation of rights determines only who pays whom. The conditions are few parties (A), enforceable rights (B) and low transaction costs (C). A factory and one downstream brewery satisfy all three. Global CO₂ (D) and antibiotic resistance (E) violate them completely, which is why those need taxes, permits or regulation instead.

quiz.q: Explain the structural similarity between involuntary unemployment (Lesson 13) and credit rationing. For each market identify the principal, the agent, the hidden variable and the device that substitutes for the missing enforceable contract — and explain in each case why the price cannot be used to clear the market. Finish with one consequence for inequality.
quiz.solution:
The common structure. Both are principal–agent problems with hidden action. In each, the party providing the resource (a job, money) cannot write an enforceable contract on the thing it actually cares about, so it substitutes an incentive device for the contract — and the side effect of that device is that the market does not clear.

Labour marketCredit market
Principalemployerlender
Agentworkerborrower
Hidden variableefforteffort, risk-taking, willingness to repay
Substitute deviceemployment rent + threat of dismissalcollateral and equity + threat of losing future credit
Rationed sideworkers — involuntary unemploymentborrowers — credit rationing

Why the price cannot clear the labour market. An unemployed worker offering to work for less is not credible: at a lower wage the employment rent shrinks, so her best response is lower effort. The firm therefore refuses the offer, and the wage stays above the market-clearing level. The unemployment that results is not a disequilibrium waiting to be arbitraged away — it is the disciplining device that makes the wage worth paying.

Why the price cannot clear the credit market. A borrower offering a higher interest rate is also not making the lender better off. A higher rate selects the riskiest applicants (adverse selection) and reduces the borrower's payoff in the good state, pushing her towards riskier projects (moral hazard). The lender's expected return can therefore fall as the rate rises, so it caps the loan or refuses outright rather than raising the price.

Consequence for inequality. In both markets access depends on something you must already have. In credit, collateral and equity require pre-existing wealth: a person with no assets cannot fund even a project with a 25 % return, so a profitable investment goes unmade — the outcome is inefficient as well as unequal. And because she stays poor, she still has no collateral next year, so exclusion reproduces itself across time and across generations. The same logic applies to the labour market, where long unemployment spells erode skills and employability. This is the economic case for student loan guarantees, microfinance, publicly funded education and active labour market policy: each is an attempt to substitute for the wealth or the record that the private contract requires.

test.sub: Summative test for Block 5 — Firms, Markets and Market Failure: the firm and its employees (L13), the firm and its customers (L14), supply and demand (L15), and credit, wealth and market failure (L16). One step harder than the lesson quizzes: several questions combine two lessons, and the open questions are at final-exam level.

questions.q: Which of the following is not an example of the same principal–agent structure as the employer–worker relationship?
options: A bank lending to an entrepreneur whose effort it cannot monitor.
Shareholders who cannot observe how hard the CEO works.
A shopper choosing between two loaves of bread of visibly different quality.
A car insurer who cannot observe how carefully the policyholder drives.
questions.explain: A principal–agent problem needs (i) one party acting on behalf of another and (ii) a hidden action or attribute that cannot be written into an enforceable contract. The shopper observes the good before buying and pays a price for it — a straightforward market exchange with no hidden action. The other three all involve unobservable effort or care: lending, corporate governance and insurance are the classic textbook cases alongside employment.

questions.q: Eva earns 280 CZK an hour, values the disutility of her effort at 45 CZK an hour, and would receive the equivalent of 135 CZK an hour if she lost her job. She expects a spell of unemployment to last 18 weeks at 40 hours a week. What is her employment rent, in CZK?
questions.explain: Rent per hour $= 280 - 45 - 135 = 100$ CZK. Expected duration $= 18 \times 40 = 720$ hours. Rent $= 100 \times 720 = 72\,000$ CZK. Both components matter: the flow advantage of the job and how long the loss would last. This is why the same wage disciplines workers much more strongly in a recession, when spells are long.

questions.q: A firm currently pays 250 CZK/h and gets effort 0.50. It is considering 300 CZK/h, which would raise effort to 0.57. What should it do, and why?
options: Raise the wage: effort rises, so output per worker rises.
Keep the wage at 250: cost per unit of effort would rise from 500 to 526 CZK.
Cut the wage: the firm always minimises its wage bill.
It cannot be decided without knowing the firm's fixed costs.
questions.explain: The firm minimises $w/e$, not $w$ and not $e$. Now: $250/0.50 = 500$ CZK per unit of effort. After: $300/0.57 = 526.3$ CZK. The wage would rise 20 % but effort only 14 %, so the elasticity of effort with respect to the wage is $0.7 \lt 1$ — the firm is already past the tangency point. Fixed costs are irrelevant to this margin.

questions.q: A firm faces demand $P = 200 - 4Q$ and has marginal cost $MC = 20 + 2Q$. What is the profit-maximising price $P^*$?
questions.explain: $MR = 200 - 8Q$ (same intercept, twice the slope). Setting $MR = MC$: $200-8Q = 20+2Q \Rightarrow 180 = 10Q \Rightarrow Q^* = 18$, so $P^* = 200 - 72 = 128$. Setting the demand curve equal to MC instead gives $Q = 30$ and $P = 80$ — that is the efficient outcome, not the firm's choice, and it is the most common error on this question.

questions.q: A firm reports a markup of 40 % of its price over marginal cost. What is the price elasticity of demand it faces at its chosen price?
questions.explain: The markup rule is $(P-MC)/P = 1/\varepsilon$, so $\varepsilon = 1/0.4 = 2.5$. Note that $\varepsilon$ must exceed 1 at any profit-maximising point: if it were below 1 the firm could raise the price, sell less, increase revenue and cut costs at the same time — so no optimum ever lies on the inelastic part of demand.

questions.q: For the same firm ($P = 200 - 4Q$, $MC = 20 + 2Q$, profit-maximising at $Q = 18$, $P = 128$), compute the deadweight loss.
questions.explain: Efficient quantity: $200-4Q = 20+2Q \Rightarrow Q = 30$. At the firm's quantity of 18 the vertical gap between demand and MC is $128 - (20+36) = 128-56 = 72$, and it closes to zero at $Q = 30$. So $DWL = \frac12 \times (30-18) \times 72 = \frac12 \times 12 \times 72 = 432$.
