Remember this is surplus that disappears — the part of consumer surplus captured by the firm is a transfer, not a deadweight loss.

questions.q: In the market for coffee, a frost destroys part of the Brazilian harvest. Which statement describes the situation correctly?
options: Supply shifts left; demand does not shift — there is a movement along the demand curve; price rises and quantity falls.
Supply shifts left and demand shifts left, because people buy less at the higher price.
Demand shifts left; supply does not move.
There is a movement along both curves, because only the price changed.
questions.explain: Exactly one curve moves for one shock. The frost is a supply-side event, so supply shifts left. Buyers then respond to the higher price by moving along an unchanged demand curve — 'quantity demanded falls', not 'demand falls'. Option B is the classic double-counting error. Note the diagnostic: price up and quantity down in opposite directions is the signature of a supply shock.

questions.q: A market has $Q^D = 600 - 10P$ and $Q^S = 20P - 150$. The government imposes a tax of 6 CZK per unit on sellers. By how many CZK does the price received by sellers fall relative to the no-tax equilibrium?
questions.explain: No-tax equilibrium: $600-10P = 20P-150 \Rightarrow 750 = 30P \Rightarrow P = 25$, $Q = 350$. With the tax, $Q^S = 20(P-6)-150 = 20P-270$, so $600-10P = 20P-270 \Rightarrow 870 = 30P \Rightarrow P_{buyer} = 29$ and $P_{seller} = 23$. Sellers therefore lose 2 CZK and buyers pay 4 CZK more. Check with elasticities at $(25,350)$: $\varepsilon_D = 0.714$, $\varepsilon_S = 1.429$, buyers' share $= 1.429/2.143 = 2/3$, and $\frac23 \times 6 = 4$ ✔. Demand is the more inelastic side, so buyers bear more.

questions.q: Which of the following are true of a perfectly competitive market in long-run equilibrium, but not of a firm with market power?
options: Price equals marginal cost.
There is no deadweight loss from the pricing decision.
The individual firm faces a horizontal demand curve.
The firm maximises profit by setting marginal revenue equal to marginal cost.
The markup over marginal cost is positive.
questions.explain: A price-taker's marginal revenue equals the price, so $MR = MC$ implies $P = MC$ (A), which leaves no unrealised mutually beneficial trade and therefore no deadweight loss (B); the individual firm's demand curve is horizontal because it can sell any quantity at the market price (C). Option D is true of both — every profit-maximising firm sets $MR = MC$; only what MR equals differs. Option E is true of the firm with market power, not the competitive one, whose markup is zero.

questions.q: You have 8 000 CZK now and expect 16 500 CZK in a year. The interest rate is 10 %. What is the maximum you could consume now, in CZK?
questions.explain: Discount the future income and add today's: $8\,000 + \frac{16\,500}{1.10} = 8\,000 + 15\,000 = 23\,000$ CZK. The other endpoint of the feasible frontier is $8\,000(1.10) + 16\,500 = 25\,300$ CZK of consumption later, and the frontier joining the two has slope $-1.10$. Discounting, not compounding, is what you do to future income when you move it to the present.

questions.q: Vaccination protects the person vaccinated and also reduces the chance that others catch the disease. What does an unregulated market do, and what is the appropriate remedy?
options: Too much vaccination; a Pigouvian tax.
Too little vaccination; a Pigouvian subsidy or free provision.
The efficient amount, since people care about their own health.
Too little vaccination; a quota capping the number of doses.
questions.explain: This is a positive externality: the social marginal benefit exceeds the private marginal benefit, because the decision-maker ignores the protection she gives others (herd immunity). Individuals equate private benefit with cost, which stops short of the social optimum, so the market under-provides. The mirror image of the pollution case: the remedy is a subsidy equal to the marginal external benefit — in practice, free or mandatory vaccination programmes. A quota would make things worse.

questions.q: A Czech e-bike maker has to solve two problems at once. (a) Its workers' best response function is: wage 160 CZK/h → effort 0.30; 200 → 0.50; 240 → 0.64; 280 → 0.68. Find the profit-maximising wage and the cost per unit of effort, and state the general condition characterising the optimum. (b) Its marginal cost is $MC = 12\,000 + 40Q$ (CZK per bike) and the demand it faces is $P = 30\,000 - 80Q$. Find $Q^*$, $P^*$, the markup and the elasticity at the optimum, and verify the markup rule. (c) Explain what the two problems have in common and what each leaves behind that a perfectly competitive market would not.
questions.solution:
(a) The wage decision.

The firm minimises the cost per unit of effort $w/e$, not the wage:

$160/0.30 = 533.3$;   $200/0.50 = 400$;   $240/0.64 = \mathbf{375}$;   $280/0.68 = 411.8$.

The minimum is at $w^* = 240$ CZK/h with $e^* = 0.64$ and a cost of 375 CZK per unit of effort.

Check with the elasticity test: from 200 to 240 the wage rises 20 % and effort rises 28 %, an elasticity of 1.4 > 1, so keep raising; from 240 to 280 the wage rises 16.7 % and effort only 6.25 %, an elasticity of 0.375 < 1, so stop. The general condition is that the flattest isocost ray through the origin is tangent to the best response curve, i.e. the elasticity of effort with respect to the wage equals 1.

(b) The price decision.

$MR = 30\,000 - 160Q$ (same intercept as demand, twice the slope).

$MR = MC:\ 30\,000-160Q = 12\,000+40Q \Rightarrow 18\,000 = 200Q \Rightarrow Q^* = 90$ bikes.

$P^* = 30\,000 - 80(90) = \mathbf{22\,800}$ CZK.

$MC(90) = 12\,000 + 3\,600 = 15\,600$ CZK, so the markup is $\frac{22\,800-15\,600}{22\,800} = 0.3158 = \mathbf{31.6\,\%}$.

Elasticity: $\frac{dQ}{dP} = -\frac{1}{80}$, so $\varepsilon = \frac{1}{80}\cdot\frac{22\,800}{90} = \frac{22\,800}{7\,200} = 3.167$. And $1/\varepsilon = 0.3158$ ✔ — the markup rule holds exactly.

(c) What the two problems share.

Both are tangency problems: the firm pushes onto the best curve it can reach given a constraint set by the other side's behaviour. In the labour market the constraint is the workers' best response curve and the firm chooses the point where the flattest isocost ray touches it. In the product market the constraint is the demand curve and the firm chooses the point where the highest isoprofit curve touches it. In both, the optimum is characterised by an elasticity condition.

Both also arise from the same source: an asymmetry that gives the firm no way to get what it wants at a competitive price. It cannot buy effort directly, so it must overpay for hours; it cannot sell to each customer at that customer's willingness to pay, so it must set one price for all.

What each leaves behind. The wage decision leaves an employment rent — workers are paid strictly more than their reservation wage, and because every firm does this, the labour market does not clear: involuntary unemployment persists in equilibrium. The pricing decision leaves a markup, so $P \gt MC$, and the units between $Q^* = 90$ and the efficient quantity (where $30\,000-80Q = 12\,000+40Q \Rightarrow Q = 150$) are never produced: a deadweight loss of $\frac12(150-90)(22\,800-15\,600) = \frac12(60)(7\,200) = 216\,000$ CZK per month. A perfectly competitive market would have neither: zero markup, $P = MC$, no deadweight loss, and no rent above the reservation wage.

questions.tag: L15 · full market analysis with a tax
questions.q: A market has $Q^D = 600 - 10P$ and $Q^S = 20P - 150$ ($P$ in CZK, $Q$ in thousands of units per week). (a) Find the equilibrium and the consumer, producer and total surplus. (b) A tax of 6 CZK per unit is imposed on sellers. Find the new quantity, both prices, tax revenue and the deadweight loss. (c) Show that the incidence is what the elasticity formula predicts, and explain why it would make no difference if the tax were legally levied on buyers. (d) Total surplus falls by more than the tax revenue raised. Explain exactly where the difference goes.
questions.solution:
(a) Equilibrium and surplus.

$600-10P = 20P-150 \Rightarrow 750 = 30P \Rightarrow P^* = 25$ CZK, $Q^* = 600-250 = 350$ (supply check: $500-150 = 350$ ✔).

Inverse demand: $P = 60 - Q/10$, so the choke price is 60. Inverse supply: $P = 7.5 + Q/20$, so the lowest reservation price is 7.5.

$CS = \tfrac12(350)(60-25) = \tfrac12(350)(35) = 6\,125$.

$PS = \tfrac12(350)(25-7.5) = \tfrac12(350)(17.5) = 3\,062.5$.

Total surplus $= \mathbf{9\,187.5}$ (thousands of CZK per week).

(b) The tax.

Sellers keep $P-6$, so $Q^S = 20(P-6)-150 = 20P-270$.

$600-10P = 20P-270 \Rightarrow 870 = 30P \Rightarrow P_{buyer} = 29$ CZK; $P_{seller} = 23$ CZK; $Q = 600-290 = \mathbf{310}$.

Tax revenue $= 6 \times 310 = \mathbf{1\,860}$.

$DWL = \tfrac12 \times \text{tax} \times \Delta Q = \tfrac12 \times 6 \times (350-310) = \tfrac12 \times 6 \times 40 = \mathbf{120}$.

(c) Incidence.

Buyers pay 4 CZK more (25 → 29); sellers receive 2 CZK less (25 → 23). Split: two thirds on buyers, one third on sellers.

Elasticities at the original equilibrium: $\varepsilon_D = 10\cdot\frac{25}{350} = 0.714$ and $\varepsilon_S = 20\cdot\frac{25}{350} = 1.429$.

Buyers' share $= \frac{\varepsilon_S}{\varepsilon_S+\varepsilon_D} = \frac{1.429}{2.143} = 0.667$, and $0.667 \times 6 = 4$ CZK ✔. Demand is the more inelastic side, and the more inelastic side always bears more, because it has fewer ways to escape by changing behaviour.

Why legal incidence is irrelevant. The tax inserts a fixed wedge of 6 CZK between what buyers pay and what sellers keep. The market then settles at the quantity where the vertical distance between the demand and supply curves is exactly 6. Nothing in that condition refers to who hands the money to the tax office. Formally: with the tax on buyers, $Q^D = 600-10(P_s+6) = 540-10P_s$, and $540-10P_s = 20P_s-150 \Rightarrow P_s = 23$, $P_b = 29$, $Q = 310$ — identical in every number.

(d) Where the missing surplus goes.

New $CS = \tfrac12(310)(60-29) = \tfrac12(310)(31) = 4\,805$; new $PS = \tfrac12(310)(23-7.5) = \tfrac12(310)(15.5) = 2\,402.5$. Private surplus $= 7\,207.5$, plus government revenue $1\,860$ gives $9\,067.5$.

The fall in total surplus is $9\,187.5 - 9\,067.5 = 120$ — exactly the deadweight loss computed in (b) ✔.

So of the $9\,187.5 - 7\,207.5 = 1\,980$ that buyers and sellers lose, $1\,860$ is a transfer to the government (which can be spent on something valuable, so it is not destroyed), and only $120$ actually disappears. That 120 is the surplus on the 40 thousand units that were worth more to buyers than they cost sellers to produce, but which the tax wedge prevented from being traded at all. This distinction between a transfer and a deadweight loss is the whole point of the diagram: a tax redistributes a lot and destroys comparatively little, and the amount it destroys is smaller the more inelastic the two sides are.

questions.q: A chemical plant's output causes water pollution. Demand for the chemical is $P = 150 - 3Q$, the plant's private marginal cost is $MPC = 30 + 2Q$, and each unit imposes an external cost of 25 on downstream users ($Q$ in thousand tonnes per year, $P$ in thousand CZK per tonne). (a) Find the market and the efficient quantity and price. (b) Compute the deadweight loss. (c) Design a Pigouvian tax and verify it works; state the revenue. (d) Suppose there is a single identifiable downstream victim. Show that a Coase bargain exists and give the range of payments that would make both sides better off. (e) State two conditions under which the Coase solution would fail, with an example.
questions.solution:
(a) Market and efficient outcomes.

Market: the plant ignores the damage and equates price with private cost.

$150-3Q = 30+2Q \Rightarrow 120 = 5Q \Rightarrow Q_m = 24$, and $P = 150-72 = 78$.

Social marginal cost: $MSC = MPC + 25 = 55+2Q$.

Efficient: $150-3Q = 55+2Q \Rightarrow 95 = 5Q \Rightarrow Q_e = 19$, and the marginal willingness to pay there is $P = 150-57 = 93$.

The market produces 5 thousand tonnes too much — the standard result for a negative externality.

(b) Deadweight loss.

Over the excess output, social cost exceeds the value to buyers. At $Q = 24$ the gap is $MSC(24) - P(24) = (55+48) - 78 = 103-78 = 25$; at $Q = 19$ it is zero.

$DWL = \tfrac12 \times (24-19) \times 25 = \tfrac12 \times 5 \times 25 = \mathbf{62.5}$ million CZK per year.

(c) Pigouvian tax.

Set the tax equal to the marginal external cost: $t = 25$ per tonne. The plant's private cost becomes $30+2Q+25 = 55+2Q = MSC$, so its profit-maximising choice now coincides with the social optimum.

Verify: $150-3Q = 55+2Q \Rightarrow Q = 19$ ✔. Revenue $= 25 \times 19 = \mathbf{475}$ million CZK per year.

Note that the tax does not eliminate pollution — the efficient level of pollution is positive, because cutting output below 19 would destroy more value than the damage it avoids.

(d) The Coase bargain.

Consider moving from $Q = 24$ to $Q = 19$.

Gain to the victim: damage avoided $= 25 \times 5 = \mathbf{125}$ million CZK.

Loss to the plant and its customers: the surplus given up on those units is

$\int_{19}^{24}\big[(150-3Q)-(30+2Q)\big]dQ = \int_{19}^{24}(120-5Q)\,dQ = \big[120Q - 2.5Q^2\big]_{19}^{24} = (2\,880-1\,440)-(2\,280-902.5) = 1\,440-1\,377.5 = \mathbf{62.5}$ million CZK.

Because 125 > 62.5, there is a net gain of 62.5 million — exactly the deadweight loss — available to be shared. Any payment $X$ from the victim to the plant with

$$62.5 \lt X \lt 125$$

makes both parties strictly better off. If the property right ran the other way (the downstream user has a right to clean water), the plant would instead pay the victim for the right to pollute up to 19, and the efficient quantity would still be reached. That is Coase's point: the allocation of the right determines who pays whom, not the efficient quantity.

(e) When Coase fails.

1. Many parties / high transaction costs. With thousands or billions of affected people, negotiating and enforcing an agreement is impossible and each individual has an incentive to free-ride on others' bargaining. Example: global CO₂ emissions — no bargain between eight billion people is conceivable, which is why climate policy uses carbon taxes and the EU ETS.

2. Property rights not defined or not enforceable, or damage not attributable. If nobody owns the river, or the harm cannot be traced to a particular emitter, there is nothing to bargain over and no court to enforce the deal. Example: antibiotic resistance — the damage is diffuse, delayed and impossible to attribute to a single prescription, so regulation (prescription-only rules, stewardship programmes) is used instead.

(Other acceptable answers: asymmetric information about the true size of the damage, which invites strategic exaggeration; and victims who cannot bargain at all, such as future generations.)

final.sub: Final exam for 4ES104 Principles of Economics: Theory and Data I. Twenty questions, 50 points, 90 minutes, covering all five blocks of the course: growth and inequality, models and costs, constrained choice, games and institutions, firms and markets. This paper mirrors the real final test, which is worth 40 % of your grade and which you must pass with at least 50 % to complete the course.
final.rules:
• No calculator is needed. Every number in this paper is built so that it works out in your head or on the margin of the paper. If you find yourself needing a calculator, you have probably taken a wrong turn.
  • Draw the diagram on paper. Indifference curves, feasible frontiers, isocosts, supply and demand, the externality diagram — sketch each one before you write a sentence. Half of the mistakes in this subject disappear once the axes are labelled.
  • This paper mirrors the real 40 % final test: same length (90 minutes), same balance across the five blocks, same mix of multiple choice, numerical and open questions. Remember that you need at least 50 % on the final test to pass the course, whatever your presentation and midterm scores are.
  • Open questions are marked for the economic reasoning, not for the final number. Always state the model you are using, define the variables, and finish with one sentence that answers the question in plain English.
  • Budget roughly 1.5 minutes per point: about 4 minutes for a 2-point question, about 8 minutes for a 5-point open question. Do the multiple choice first, then come back to the open questions.
  • The exam is in English. Use the English terms — if you write only the Czech term you may not get the point. Check the glossary before the exam.

questions.q: GDP per capita in Britain was almost flat for six centuries and then, from roughly 1750 onwards, started to rise at a few per cent a year and never stopped — the famous hockey stick. Which explanation is consistent with the data and with the model used in the course?
options: Population fell sharply, so the same output was divided among fewer people; the hockey stick is a measurement artefact.

A permanent technological revolution raised labour productivity, and the institutions of the time allowed the innovators to keep part of the gains, so improvement became continuous rather than one-off.
Countries that grew simply had more natural resources than the rest of the world; the hockey stick maps exactly onto coal and iron deposits.
The hockey stick shows a rise in total output, not in output per person, so living standards were in fact unchanged.
questions.explain: The hockey stick is drawn in GDP per capita, so option D is simply wrong, and population actually rose during the Industrial Revolution, which kills option A. Resources matter, but they cannot explain a permanent growth rate: Britain had coal for centuries before 1750, and resource-rich countries such as Nigeria have no hockey stick, which kills option C. What changed was the combination of continuous technological progress (each innovation raising output per hour of labour) with institutions — secure property rights, patents, competitive markets — that made innovating privately profitable. Technology alone gives you a one-off jump; technology plus incentives to keep innovating gives you a permanently positive growth rate, which is exactly what an upward-sloping line on a ratio (log) scale means.

questions.q: A small economy has four households with monthly disposable incomes of 10, 20, 30 and 60 thousand CZK. Compute the Gini coefficient of this distribution. Give your answer as a decimal number between 0 and 1 (a fraction such as 1/3 is also accepted).
questions.explain:
Build the Lorenz curve first. Total income is $10+20+30+60=120$, so the cumulative population shares are 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 1 and the cumulative income shares are $10/120=1/12$, $30/120=1/4$, $60/120=1/2$, $1$.

The area under the Lorenz curve is a sum of four trapezoids of width $0.25$:

$A=0.25\cdot\left[\frac{0+1/12}{2}+\frac{1/12+1/4}{2}+\frac{1/4+1/2}{2}+\frac{1/2+1}{2}\right]=0.25\cdot\frac{1}{2}\left[\tfrac{1}{12}+\tfrac{1}{3}+\tfrac{3}{4}+\tfrac{3}{2}\right]=0.125\cdot\tfrac{8}{3}=\tfrac13$.

Gini $=1-2A=1-\frac23=\frac13\approx0{,}333$.

Quick check with the ranked formula $G=\frac{2\sum_i i\,y_i}{n\sum_i y_i}-\frac{n+1}{n}$ (incomes sorted ascending): $\sum i\,y_i=1\cdot10+2\cdot20+3\cdot30+4\cdot60=380$, so $G=\frac{2\cdot380}{4\cdot120}-\frac54=\frac{760}{480}-1{,}25=1{,}5833-1{,}25=0{,}3333$. Same answer — always cross-check a Gini with the second formula, it takes twenty seconds.

questions.q: A farm produces grain with land fixed and only the number of workers varying. Total output (tonnes) is: 1 worker → 20, 2 workers → 36, 3 workers → 48, 4 workers → 56, 5 workers → 60. Which statement describes this production function correctly?
options: There are increasing returns, because total output keeps rising as workers are added.
The marginal product of labour falls by 4 tonnes with every extra worker, so output rises but at a decreasing rate — the production function is concave.
Output falls after the fourth worker, which is what diminishing returns means.
The average product of labour is constant at 20 tonnes per worker, so the technology has constant returns.
questions.explain:
Marginal products are $20,\,16,\,12,\,8,\,4$ — falling by exactly 4 each time. Average products are $20,\,18,\,16,\,14,\,12$ — also falling, and always above MP from the second worker on (the average is dragged down by the weaker marginal contributions).

Option A is the classic error: total output rising is not increasing returns. What matters is whether each additional worker adds more or less than the previous one. Option C confuses diminishing marginal product (MP falling but still positive) with negative marginal product (total output actually falling) — the latter never happens here. Option D just misreads the table. The economic meaning: with land fixed, each new worker gets less land and less equipment to work with, so the extra output shrinks — the same logic behind the concave feasible frontier for study hours and grades.

questions.tag: production function · MP, AP and technology
questions.q:
Marie studies for an exam. Her grade as a function of daily study hours $h$ is: $h=1\to28$, $h=2\to48$, $h=3\to62$, $h=4\to70$, $h=5\to74$ points.
(a) Compute the marginal product and the average product of the fourth hour, and of study in general.
(b) Explain in economic terms why this function is concave and what concavity implies for how Marie should allocate her time.
(c) Marie learns a better study technique that raises her grade by 20 % at every number of hours. Draw (describe) what happens to the production function and to the marginal product, and say whether she will necessarily study more.
questions.solution:
(a) Marginal and average product.

Marginal product $MP(h)=G(h)-G(h-1)$:

$MP(1)=28$, $MP(2)=48-28=20$, $MP(3)=62-48=14$, $MP(4)=70-62=8$, $MP(5)=74-70=4$.

Average product $AP(h)=G(h)/h$:

$AP(1)=28$, $AP(2)=24$, $AP(3)\approx20{,}7$, $AP(4)=17{,}5$, $AP(5)=14{,}8$.

So the fourth hour has $MP=8$ points and $AP=17{,}5$ points per hour. Note $MP<AP$ everywhere after the first hour — that is exactly why the average keeps falling.

(b) Why concave.

Concavity means diminishing marginal product: each extra hour adds less than the one before. The economics: Marie studies the highest-value material first (the core definitions, the model, the worked examples). By hour four she is re-reading things she already knows, and she is also more tired — attention is the fixed factor that the extra hours have to share, exactly as land is the fixed factor in the farm example.

Implication for her choice: since the pay-off from the marginal hour keeps shrinking while the value of the free time she gives up keeps rising, she should not push study to the maximum. She should stop at the hour where the extra grade points just stop being worth the lost free time — formally where the marginal rate of transformation equals her marginal rate of substitution. Corner solutions (0 hours or all hours) are almost never optimal with a concave frontier and convex preferences.

(c) Better technology.

The whole function shifts upward and becomes steeper: the new grades are $33{,}6$; $57{,}6$; $74{,}4$; $84$; $88{,}8$, and each marginal product is multiplied by 1.2 ($33{,}6$; $24$; $16{,}8$; $9{,}6$; $4{,}8$). It is still concave — better technology raises productivity, it does not repeal diminishing returns.

Will she study more? Not necessarily. There are two opposing forces, exactly as with a wage increase:

  • Substitution effect: an hour of study now buys more grade points, so free time has become more expensive — this pushes towards more study.
  • Income effect: she can now reach her old grade with fewer hours, and being better off she wants more of everything including free time — this pushes towards less study.

Which dominates depends on her preferences. A defensible answer must mention both effects; an answer that says only more study, or only less, does not get full marks.

questions.q: Alena is deciding whether to open an e-shop. She would invest 200 000 CZK of her own savings, which are currently in a deposit paying 4 % a year (8 000 CZK), and she would quit a job paying 480 000 CZK a year. Over the first year the e-shop brings in revenue minus all out-of-pocket costs of 500 000 CZK. What is her economic profit — the economic rent from running the e-shop rather than taking her next best option?
options: 500 000 CZK, because that is what the business earns after paying its bills.
20 000 CZK, because she gives up the 480 000 CZK salary.
12 000 CZK, because she gives up both the 480 000 CZK salary and the 8 000 CZK of interest.
492 000 CZK, because only the forgone interest is a genuine economic cost.
questions.explain:
Economic profit = revenue − all opportunity costs, explicit and implicit: $500\,000-480\,000-8\,000=12\,000$ CZK.

Option A is accounting profit — it ignores every implicit cost. Option B is the single most common exam error: remembering the forgone wage but forgetting the forgone return on the capital she ties up. Option D does the reverse.

Interpretation: 12 000 CZK is the economic rent of the e-shop — the amount by which the best available action beats the next best alternative. It is positive but small, which tells you two things: the project is worth doing, but it is only barely worth doing, and if other people can copy it the rent will be competed away.

questions.q:
Two countries each have 100 worker-years available. In one worker-year, Czechia can produce 8 units of software or 16 tonnes of wheat; Slovakia can produce 2 units of software or 8 tonnes of wheat.
(a) Who has the absolute advantage in each good?
(b) Compute the opportunity cost of one unit of software and of one tonne of wheat in each country.
(c) Who should specialise in what, and why is your answer not the same as the answer to (a)?
(d) Both countries start with workers split 50/50. Find a reallocation of workers that leaves world wheat output unchanged and raises world software output, and state by how much.
(e) At which prices (tonnes of wheat per unit of software) will both countries want to trade?
questions.solution:
(a) Absolute advantage. Czechia produces more of both goods per worker-year ($8>2$ software, $16>8$ wheat). Czechia has the absolute advantage in both goods; Slovakia in neither.

(b) Opportunity costs. Opportunity cost = what you give up.

  • Czechia: one worker-year makes 8 software or 16 wheat, so 1 software costs $16/8=\mathbf{2}$ tonnes of wheat; 1 tonne of wheat costs $8/16=\mathbf{0{,}5}$ software.
  • Slovakia: 1 software costs $8/2=\mathbf{4}$ tonnes of wheat; 1 tonne of wheat costs $2/8=\mathbf{0{,}25}$ software.

(c) Specialisation. Czechia's opportunity cost of software (2 wheat) is lower than Slovakia's (4 wheat), so Czechia has the comparative advantage in software. Slovakia's opportunity cost of wheat (0,25 software) is lower than Czechia's (0,5 software), so Slovakia has the comparative advantage in wheat. Czechia specialises in software, Slovakia in wheat.

This differs from (a) because absolute advantage compares productivity levels across countries, while comparative advantage compares ratios of productivities within each country. Gains from trade come from the ratios: what matters is not that Czechia is better at wheat than Slovakia, but that Czechia is relatively even better at software. A country can be worse at everything and still be the cheap producer of something.

(d) A reallocation that makes the world richer. Starting point (50 workers on each good):

  • Czechia: $50\cdot8=400$ software, $50\cdot16=800$ wheat.
  • Slovakia: $50\cdot2=100$ software, $50\cdot8=400$ wheat.
  • World: 500 software, 1 200 wheat.

Now move 10 Czech workers from wheat to software and 20 Slovak workers from software to wheat:

  • Czechia: software $+10\cdot8=+80$; wheat $-10\cdot16=-160$.
  • Slovakia: software $-20\cdot2=-40$; wheat $+20\cdot8=+160$.
  • World: software $+80-40=\mathbf{+40}$; wheat $-160+160=\mathbf{0}$.

The world gets 40 extra units of software with exactly the same amount of wheat — a Pareto improvement is available at no cost in resources, purely from letting each country do what it is relatively good at. (New world totals: 540 software, 1 200 wheat.)

(e) Terms of trade. Czechia will only sell software if it gets more than its own opportunity cost, i.e. more than 2 tonnes of wheat per unit. Slovakia will only buy software if it pays less than 4 tonnes, its own cost of making it. So any price $p$ with

$2 < p < 4$ tonnes of wheat per unit of software

makes both countries better off. Where inside that interval the price ends up is a question about bargaining power and institutions, not about technology; the closer to 2, the larger Slovakia's share of the gain.

questions.q: A firm can produce 100 units of output with one of three technologies (labour in worker-days, energy in units): A = 20 L, 10 E; B = 14 L, 20 E; C = 8 L, 40 E. Energy costs 50 CZK per unit. Initially the wage is 100 CZK per worker-day; then the wage doubles to 200 CZK while the energy price is unchanged. Which technology does a cost-minimising firm use before and after the wage increase?
options: B before, B after — the ranking of technologies does not depend on prices, only on the technology set.
B before, C after — the isocost lines get steeper, so the firm substitutes energy for labour.
A before, A after — A always uses the fewest inputs in total (30 units).
C before, A after — a higher wage makes the labour-intensive technology relatively cheaper.
questions.explain:
Compute the cost of each technology at both wages.

At $w=100$: A $=20\cdot100+10\cdot50=2\,500$; B $=14\cdot100+20\cdot50=\mathbf{2\,400}$; C $=8\cdot100+40\cdot50=2\,800$. B is cheapest.

At $w=200$: A $=4\,000+500=4\,500$; B $=2\,800+1\,000=3\,800$; C $=1\,600+2\,000=\mathbf{3\,600}$. C is cheapest.

The diagram version: with labour on the horizontal axis and energy on the vertical, an isocost line $C=wL+pE$ has slope $-w/p$. The slope goes from $-100/50=-2$ to $-200/50=-4$ — the lines become steeper, so the lowest isocost line touching the technology set now touches the energy-intensive point C. Option A is wrong precisely because the cheapest technology is a joint property of technology and relative prices; option C adds up units of different things, which is meaningless.

questions.q: Which statement about indifference curves over two goods (both of which the person likes) is correct?
options: Curves further from the origin represent lower utility, because they require more spending.
Two indifference curves may intersect if the person's preferences are unusual.

The slope of an indifference curve at a point is the marginal rate of substitution: how much of the good on the vertical axis the person is willing to give up for one more unit of the good on the horizontal axis, staying equally happy.
Indifference curves are convex to the origin because of diminishing marginal returns in production.
questions.explain:
C is the definition of the MRS: it is a statement about willingness to trade at constant utility, read off the slope of one curve, and it is measured in units of the vertical good per unit of the horizontal good.

A reverses the ranking — with goods (not bads) more is better, so curves further out are higher utility. B is impossible: if two curves crossed, the bundle at the intersection would belong to two different utility levels at once, which contradicts transitivity. D mixes up two different concavities: indifference curves bend because of a diminishing MRS in preferences (the more of a good you already have, the less of the other you will give up for it), whereas diminishing marginal returns is a property of a production function. Both give you curved lines, but they are different objects on different diagrams.

questions.q:
A student chooses between free time (hours per day) and her exam grade. Her feasible frontier is: free time 20 → grade 40; 18 → 52; 16 → 62; 14 → 70; 12 → 76; 10 → 80.
(a) Compute the marginal rate of transformation (MRT) on each segment and say what its behaviour tells you about the frontier.
(b) State the optimality condition for her choice and explain what it means in words.
(c) At 16 hours of free time her marginal rate of substitution is 3 grade points per hour. Is she at her optimum? If not, in which direction should she move, and roughly where does she stop?
(d) The university introduces free tutoring that raises the grade by 6 points at every level of free time. Explain, using income and substitution effects, why her study time may go either up or down.
questions.solution:
(a) MRT on each segment. The MRT is the number of grade points given up per extra hour of free time — the absolute slope of the frontier.

  • 20 ← 18: $(52-40)/2=\mathbf{6}$ points per hour
  • 18 ← 16: $(62-52)/2=\mathbf{5}$
  • 16 ← 14: $(70-62)/2=\mathbf{4}$
  • 14 ← 12: $(76-70)/2=\mathbf{3}$
  • 12 ← 10: $(80-76)/2=\mathbf{2}$

The MRT falls as free time falls, i.e. the frontier is concave: the first hours of study are very productive, later ones much less. This is diminishing marginal product of study time, seen from the frontier side.

(b) Optimality condition. The best feasible bundle is the point where the highest attainable indifference curve is tangent to the feasible frontier, i.e.

$MRS = MRT$

In words: at the optimum, the number of grade points she would be willing to give up for one more hour of free time (MRS, from preferences) equals the number of grade points she would actually have to give up (MRT, from technology). If the two differ, there is a trade with herself that makes her better off.

(c) Is 16 hours optimal? No. At 16 hours of free time, giving up one hour of free time buys her about 4 extra grade points (the MRT on the segment towards 14), while she only requires 3 points to be compensated for that lost hour (her MRS). The gain exceeds the compensation she needs, so she should give up free time and study more.

As she moves left, the MRT falls (4, then 3) while the MRS rises (the less free time she has, the more grade points she demands for another hour of it). They meet at around 13–14 hours of free time, i.e. a grade of roughly 70–73. That is her optimum. Note that $MRT>MRS$ always means move towards more of the good on the vertical axis (grade); $MRT<MRS$ means the opposite.

(d) Free tutoring. The frontier shifts up by 6 points at every level of free time. Two effects pull in opposite directions:

  • Substitution effect: if the tutoring also makes study hours more productive at the margin, an hour of free time now costs more grade points, so free time is relatively more expensive → study more.
  • Income effect: she is better off at every choice; if free time is a normal good, being better off makes her want more of it → study less. In the extreme case here, where the frontier merely shifts up by a constant 6 points and its slope is unchanged, the substitution effect is zero and only the income effect operates, so she unambiguously takes more free time and still ends up with a better grade than before.

General conclusion: a better technology raises attainable well-being, but the effect on effort is ambiguous and depends on the balance of the two effects — exactly the same logic as a wage increase and hours of work.

questions.tag: income and substitution effects · labour supply
questions.q: The hourly wage of a worker who freely chooses her hours rises from 200 to 300 CZK. Which of the following statements are correct? (Free time is a normal good.)
options: The substitution effect pushes towards less free time and more hours of work, because free time has become more expensive.
The income effect pushes towards more free time, because the worker is better off and free time is a normal good.
Labour supply must be upward sloping, because a higher wage always makes working more attractive.
Over the last century, hours worked per year fell in rich countries while wages rose, which suggests that in the long run the income effect dominated.
The substitution effect is measured by moving to the new budget line and simultaneously to a new indifference curve.
questions.explain:
A and B are the two standard effects: the wage is the price of free time, so a higher wage raises the opportunity cost of an hour off (substitution → work more), while it also expands the feasible set (income → consume more of everything, including free time → work less).

C is false — this is one of the most common exam claims and it is exactly what the model denies. If the income effect is larger, the labour supply curve bends backwards and higher wages reduce hours.

D is the empirical counterpart: annual hours worked in Western Europe fell from roughly 3 000 to around 1 500–1 700 while real wages rose many times over. Consistent with a dominant income effect (plus institutional changes such as the eight-hour day and statutory holidays).

E is false by construction: the substitution effect is defined at constant utility — you slide along the original indifference curve to the point where its slope equals the new wage. Moving to a new curve at the same time is the total effect, not the substitution effect.

questions.q: Two neighbouring farmers each choose a pest-control method: Terminator (T, a cheap chemical that drifts onto the neighbour's field) or Integrated Pest Control (I). Payoffs are (row player, column player): (T,T) = (2, 2); (T,I) = (4, 1); (I,T) = (1, 4); (I,I) = (3, 3). What is the Nash equilibrium?
options: (I, I) with payoffs (3, 3), because it gives the highest total payoff.
(T, T) with payoffs (2, 2), because T is a dominant strategy for both players.
(T, I) with payoffs (4, 1), because the row player prefers it.
There is no Nash equilibrium in this game.
questions.explain:
Check best responses. If the column player plays T, the row player gets 2 from T and 1 from I → play T. If the column player plays I, the row player gets 4 from T and 3 from I → play T again. So T is a dominant strategy; by symmetry the same holds for the column player. The only cell where neither player wants to deviate unilaterally is (T, T).

This is a prisoners' dilemma: (I, I) gives both players more (3 > 2), so the Nash equilibrium is Pareto-dominated. That is precisely the point — option A is wrong because a Nash equilibrium is defined by the absence of a profitable unilateral deviation, not by being the best outcome. Option C is not an equilibrium because the column player would switch from I to T and gain 1.

questions.q: In a public goods experiment, four players each receive 10 tokens. Whatever is put into the common project is multiplied by 1.6 and split equally among all four players, regardless of who contributed. The other three players contribute their full 10 tokens each. By how many tokens does the fourth player's own payoff rise if she contributes nothing rather than all 10 tokens?
questions.explain:
If she contributes all 10: the pot is $40\cdot1{,}6=64$, split four ways → she gets 16 and keeps nothing privately.

If she contributes nothing: the pot is $30\cdot1{,}6=48$, split four ways → 12 each, plus the 10 tokens she kept → 22.

Difference: $22-16=\mathbf{6}$ tokens.

The general logic: each token contributed returns $1{,}6/4=0{,}4$ to the contributor but costs her 1, so the private net return is $-0{,}6$ per token — free-riding is a dominant strategy. Yet each token contributed creates 1,6 tokens of value for the group, so full contribution is socially efficient. Nash equilibrium: everyone contributes 0 and each gets 10. Efficient outcome: everyone contributes 10 and each gets 16. That gap is the social dilemma, and it is why experiments find contributions starting around half the endowment and decaying towards zero — unless punishment or communication is allowed.

questions.q:
Overfishing of a shared fishing ground is often described as a social dilemma.
(a) Model it: what are the strategies, why is the Nash equilibrium inefficient, and in what sense is it a prisoners' dilemma?
(b) Public goods experiments show contributions falling towards zero over ten rounds without punishment, but staying high when peer punishment is allowed. Describe both patterns and explain them.
(c) Name and explain three mechanisms — from experiments or from real institutions — that can sustain cooperation, and say what each one changes in the game.
questions.solution:
(a) The model. Each of $n$ fishing crews chooses restraint (small catch) or overfish (large catch). One crew's extra catch raises its own income but reduces the stock available to everyone — a negative externality. For each crew, overfishing pays more whatever the others do: if others restrain, you get a large catch from a healthy stock; if others overfish, restraining just means you get nothing from a stock that will collapse anyway. So overfishing is a dominant strategy and the Nash equilibrium is everyone overfishing.

That equilibrium is Pareto-inefficient: the all-restraint outcome gives every crew a higher long-run income. Individually rational behaviour produces a collectively irrational result — the defining structure of the prisoners' dilemma. The reason is that each crew bears only $1/n$ of the cost it imposes on the stock.

(b) The experimental evidence.

  • Without punishment: in the standard public goods game contributions start at roughly 40–60 % of the endowment — people are not purely self-interested — but they decline round by round towards very low levels. The usual interpretation is conditional cooperation: most subjects are reciprocators who contribute if others do. When they see some free-riding, they lower their contribution, which triggers further reductions — cooperation unravels not from greed alone but from the reaction of the willing to the unwilling.
  • With peer punishment: when subjects can pay a small cost to reduce a free-rider's payoff, contributions rise and stay high, often near the maximum. Punishment is costly to the punisher and gives no private benefit — it is altruistic punishment — but by making free-riding unprofitable it changes the payoffs of the game, so cooperation becomes an equilibrium. Cross-country versions of the experiment show the effect is strongest where there is a shared norm that punishment is legitimate.

(c) Three mechanisms.

  1. Repeated interaction with reputation. If crews meet again and again and remember what others did, a strategy such as tit-for-tat becomes viable: the threat of losing future cooperation adds to the cost of defecting today. What changes: the payoffs, because the one-shot gain is weighed against a stream of future losses.
  2. Peer punishment / social norms. Fines, exclusion from the harbour, ostracism, or simple disapproval make defecting expensive. What changes: the payoffs again, but the enforcement is decentralised and rests on people's willingness to pay to punish unfairness — the same preference we observe in the ultimatum game.
  3. Formal rules — quotas, property rights, taxes. Individual transferable quotas or a tax per tonne landed make each crew face the cost it imposes on the others. What changes: the game itself, i.e. the rules and the feasible strategies, which is why institutions are called the rules of the game. Elinor Ostrom's field work shows that community-managed commons with clear boundaries, local monitoring and graduated sanctions can do this without a central authority.

A fourth acceptable answer: communication. Simply letting participants talk before choosing raises contributions substantially, because it allows a shared norm to be stated and a promise to be made — even though talk is cheap and changes no payoff directly.

questions.q: Which statement about Pareto efficiency is correct?
options: An allocation is Pareto efficient only if no one is much poorer than anyone else.
An allocation in which one person owns everything and the others own nothing can be Pareto efficient.
If an allocation is Pareto efficient, no other allocation gives anyone a higher payoff.
Every Pareto improvement makes the distribution of income more equal.
questions.explain:
Pareto efficiency says only that no one can be made better off without making someone else worse off. It says nothing about how the pie is divided. Taking anything away from the sole owner in option B makes him worse off, so that extreme allocation passes the test — which is exactly why efficiency and fairness are separate criteria and you need both to judge an outcome.

A and D smuggle a fairness requirement into an efficiency concept. C confuses efficiency with maximising one person's payoff: there are usually many Pareto-efficient allocations (the whole Pareto frontier), and each of them gives different people more. Moving along the frontier makes someone better off and someone else worse off; only moves towards the frontier are Pareto improvements.

questions.q: In the ultimatum game a Proposer offers a split of 1 000 CZK and a Responder either accepts (the split is implemented) or rejects (both get nothing). Which statements are correct?
options: If both players are purely self-interested and this is common knowledge, the prediction is that the Proposer offers the smallest positive amount and the Responder accepts.
In experiments across many countries, offers typically cluster around 40–50 % and offers below about 20 % are frequently rejected.
Rejecting a positive offer shows that people are willing to pay a personal cost to punish behaviour they see as unfair.
Because a rejection destroys money, rejections prove that subjects do not understand the game and the experiment tells us nothing about real economies.
Institutions merely redistribute a fixed pie; they cannot change how large the pie is.
questions.explain:
A is the self-interest benchmark: any positive amount beats zero, so a purely self-interested Responder accepts anything, and the Proposer anticipating this offers the minimum. B and C are the robust experimental findings that contradict that benchmark: modal offers are close to half, and low offers are routinely rejected — a costly act that is only rational if the Responder's preferences include fairness or reciprocity.

D is wrong: rejection rates fall only slightly with experience and with much larger stakes, and the same behaviour appears in real settings such as wage bargaining and strikes. Calling it a misunderstanding is a way of refusing to update the model.

E is wrong and is one of the central claims of Block 4: the rules of the game change both who gets what and how much there is. Compare the ultimatum game with a version where the Responder cannot reject (the dictator game) — offers collapse. Institutions that enforce contracts, protect property or allow punishment expand the set of mutually beneficial deals that can actually be made.

questions.q: A firm producing a differentiated soft drink has a constant marginal cost of 60 CZK per crate. At its profit-maximising output the price elasticity of demand is 4 (in absolute value). What price does the firm set, in CZK per crate?
questions.explain:
The markup rule (the Lerner condition) says that at the profit-maximising point

$\dfrac{P-MC}{P}=\dfrac{1}{\varepsilon}$

With $\varepsilon=4$ the markup is $1/4=25\,\%$ of the price, so $P-60=0{,}25P$, hence $0{,}75P=60$ and $P=\mathbf{80}$ CZK.

Equivalently $P=\dfrac{MC}{1-1/\varepsilon}=\dfrac{60}{0{,}75}=80$.

Two things to notice. First, the markup is a share of the price, not of cost — dividing by MC gives 33 %, a different (and here wrong) number. Second, the more elastic the demand, the smaller the markup: with $\varepsilon=2$ the price would be 120, with $\varepsilon\to\infty$ (perfect competition) the price falls to marginal cost. A firm that raises its price is telling you something about the elasticity it faces.

questions.tag: labour discipline · wage setting and the minimum wage
questions.q:
(a) Explain why a profit-maximising firm sets a wage above the worker's reservation wage, using the ideas of incomplete contracts and the principal–agent problem.
(b) Define the employment rent and compute it for a worker earning 30 000 CZK a month whose next best option is 22 000 CZK, given that a job loss means on average 6 months without work.
(c) Evaluate the claim: an increase in the minimum wage always reduces employment. Use both the competitive model and the wage-setting model, and refer to the evidence.
questions.solution:
(a) Why the wage exceeds the reservation wage.

A labour contract is incomplete: the firm can buy the worker's time, but effort, care and honesty are not verifiable in court, so they cannot be written into an enforceable contract. This creates a principal–agent problem: the firm (principal) wants high effort, the worker (agent) prefers low effort, and their interests diverge in a dimension the contract cannot cover.

The firm's remedy is not a rule but an incentive: pay more than the worker could get elsewhere, and monitor imperfectly. Then being caught shirking and dismissed costs the worker something real. If the firm paid exactly the reservation wage, dismissal would cost the worker nothing and no effort would be forthcoming at any level of monitoring. The wage is therefore chosen where the extra effort bought by one more koruna just equals that koruna — the point where the isocost line for effort is tangent to the best response function, i.e. where effort per unit of wage is maximised. This is the efficiency wage: it is set unilaterally by the firm, and at it the labour market does not clear — there is involuntary unemployment, which is itself part of the discipline mechanism.

(b) The employment rent.

The employment rent is the economic rent of holding the job: the value of the job over the next best alternative, over the expected duration of the loss.

Monthly rent $=30\,000-22\,000=8\,000$ CZK. With an expected 6 months of unemployment after dismissal,

cost of job loss $\approx6\times8\,000=\mathbf{48\,000}$ CZK,

plus the disutility of effort saved while unemployed (which reduces the rent slightly) and any loss of non-wage benefits (which raises it). The larger this number, the more effort the firm can extract at a given level of monitoring. Note the two levers: a higher wage and a longer expected spell of unemployment both raise the rent — which is why worker discipline is stronger when unemployment is high.

(c) Does a minimum wage always cut employment?

The competitive model says yes: with a horizontal supply of labour to each firm and a downward-sloping labour demand curve, a binding minimum wage above the market-clearing wage moves firms up their demand curve; employment falls and a queue of unemployed workers appears. Clean, and it is the right first answer.

But the assumptions matter. Three qualifications from the wage-setting model:

  • Firms have wage-setting power. If a firm faces an upward-sloping labour supply (workers cannot costlessly switch employers — a monopsony), it holds the wage below the value of the marginal product. A minimum wage between the two can raise both the wage and employment, because it removes the firm's incentive to restrict hiring in order to keep the wage down.
  • Effort responds to the wage. In the labour-discipline model a higher wage raises the employment rent and therefore effort and productivity, so unit labour costs rise by less than the wage — sometimes much less. Turnover and recruitment costs fall for the same reason.
  • Demand feeds back. Low-paid workers have a high propensity to consume, so the wage bill partly returns as demand for the firms' products.

The evidence. The classic Card and Krueger study of fast-food restaurants in New Jersey and Pennsylvania found no employment loss after a minimum wage increase; the large modern literature finds effects clustered near zero for moderate increases, with clearer negative effects when the minimum is high relative to the median wage (roughly above 55–60 %) or when it bites hard in poorer regions. The Czech minimum wage has risen fast in the last decade with employment at record highs, though that period also had very tight labour markets.

Conclusion. The correct answer is conditional, not absolute: a minimum wage that is moderate relative to the median wage typically raises pay with little or no employment loss; one set well above the productivity of the least-skilled workers will reduce employment. Anyone who answers always or never is asserting a conclusion the models do not deliver.

questions.tag: market power · surplus and deadweight loss
questions.q:
A firm is the sole producer of a good. Inverse demand is $P=100-Q$ (price in CZK, quantity in thousands of units) and marginal cost is constant at $MC=20$.
(a) Find the price and quantity a price-taking competitive industry would produce, and the resulting total surplus.
(b) Find the monopolist's price and quantity, its markup, and consumer and producer surplus.
(c) Compute the deadweight loss and explain precisely what it is — and why it is not the same thing as the transfer from consumers to the firm.
questions.solution:
(a) The competitive benchmark. Price-taking firms produce where $P=MC$:

$100-Q=20\Rightarrow Q^*=80$, $P^*=20$.

Total surplus is the triangle between the demand curve and the MC line: $\tfrac12\cdot80\cdot(100-20)=\tfrac12\cdot80\cdot80=\mathbf{3\,200}$. All of it is consumer surplus; producer surplus is zero because price equals marginal cost.

(b) The monopolist. With linear inverse demand $P=100-Q$, total revenue is $R=100Q-Q^2$ and marginal revenue is

$MR=100-2Q$ (twice the slope of the demand curve — worth memorising).

Set $MR=MC$: $100-2Q=20\Rightarrow Q^m=\mathbf{40}$, and from the demand curve $P^m=100-40=\mathbf{60}$.

  • Markup: $(P-MC)/P=(60-20)/60=2/3\approx67\,\%$. Consistency check with the markup rule: at this point the elasticity is $\varepsilon=\frac{P}{Q}\cdot\frac{1}{|\text{slope}|}=\frac{60}{40}\cdot1=1{,}5$, and $1/\varepsilon=2/3$ — it matches.
  • Consumer surplus: $\tfrac12\cdot40\cdot(100-60)=\mathbf{800}$.
  • Producer surplus (= profit, since MC is constant): $(60-20)\cdot40=\mathbf{1\,600}$.
  • Total surplus: $800+1\,600=2\,400$.

(c) Deadweight loss.

$DWL=3\,200-2\,400=\mathbf{800}$.

Directly as a triangle: $\tfrac12\cdot(P^m-MC)\cdot(Q^*-Q^m)=\tfrac12\cdot40\cdot40=800$. Same number, as it must be.

What it is. The deadweight loss is the surplus on the 40 thousand units that are not produced even though every one of them is valued by some consumer at more than it costs to make. Those trades are mutually beneficial and they simply do not happen, because producing them would force the monopolist to cut the price on all the units it is already selling. The monopoly outcome is therefore Pareto inefficient.

Why it is not a transfer. Compare with the rectangle $(60-20)\times40=1\,600$: that is surplus which used to belong to consumers and now belongs to the firm. It has changed hands, but it has not disappeared — from the point of view of total surplus it nets out to zero, and whether you dislike it is a question about fairness, not efficiency. The 800 of deadweight loss belongs to nobody: it is destroyed, not moved. Writing that the firm gains the deadweight loss triangle is one of the most costly errors in this part of the course.

questions.tag: supply and demand · shifts vs movements
questions.q: Electricity is a major input in industrial baking. Over a year, the price of electricity falls sharply while consumers' incomes and tastes are unchanged. What happens in the competitive market for bread?
options: The demand curve shifts right because bread has become cheaper, so both price and quantity rise.
The supply curve shifts right; the equilibrium price falls and the equilibrium quantity rises, with buyers moving along an unchanged demand curve.
The supply curve shifts left because firms now produce with cheaper inputs and can afford to supply less.
Both curves shift right, so the quantity rises and the effect on price is ambiguous.
questions.explain:
A fall in an input price lowers marginal cost, so at every price firms are willing to supply more: the supply curve shifts right. Nothing has happened to buyers' incomes, tastes, or the prices of substitutes, so the demand curve does not move; buyers respond to the lower price by moving along their unchanged demand curve. The new equilibrium has a lower price and a higher quantity.

Option A is the single most common error in this whole block: a change in the price of the good itself never shifts that good's demand curve; it is a movement along it. Option C has the sign backwards. Option D invents a demand shift that has no cause in the story. Rule of thumb: ask what changed. If it is the price of this good, you move along a curve; if it is anything else, a curve shifts.

questions.q: A chemical plant emits a pollutant that harms downstream farmers. Its private marginal cost lies below the social marginal cost by a constant amount of 30 CZK per tonne of output. Which policy restores efficiency?
options: A tax of 30 CZK per tonne of output, which makes the firm's private marginal cost equal to the social marginal cost and cuts output to the efficient level.
A tax high enough to shut the plant down, since any pollution is inefficient.
A subsidy of 30 CZK per tonne to the farmers, which compensates them and therefore removes the inefficiency.
Nothing: the market outcome is already Pareto efficient because both parties trade voluntarily.
questions.explain:
A Pigouvian tax equal to the marginal external cost at the efficient quantity internalises the externality: the firm now faces $MC_{private}+30=MC_{social}$ and voluntarily cuts output to where price equals social marginal cost. The deadweight loss from over-production disappears.

B is wrong because the efficient level of pollution is generally positive, not zero — you stop where the marginal benefit of another tonne of output equals its marginal social cost, and abating the last tonne usually costs more than the harm it does. C compensates the victims but leaves the firm's incentives untouched, so output stays inefficiently high — compensation and efficiency are different goals. D ignores the fact that the farmers are affected by a transaction they are not party to; that is exactly what an external effect is. (If the parties are few and property rights are clear, Coase bargaining could also reach the efficient outcome — but that changes who pays, not what the efficient quantity is.)

extras.title: Study plan
extras.sub: Week by week — how to get through the course and the final test.
extras.html:
This is a working plan for 4ES104 written for exactly your situation: it is the end of July 2026, the winter semester starts in mid-September, and this is the course that will teach you to think like an economist for the rest of the degree. Below you get a summer warm-up, a 13-week table matched to the syllabus, a 10-day exam-period plan, a section on how to study economics (which is not how you studied maths at grammar school), and a section on the 20 % presentation. At the bottom there is a checklist the site remembers for you.

🎯What this plan is for
  • So that the first lecture is not the first time you hear the words opportunity cost and marginal.
  • So that you never fall behind in a course where every block builds on the previous one (you cannot do constrained choice without production functions, and you cannot do the firm without constrained choice).
  • So that the exam period is revision, not first contact — because the final test is 40 % of the grade and you need at least 50 % on it to pass, whatever else you have collected.
📌The one sentence to remember

4ES104 is not a memorisation course and it is not a calculation course. It is a course in using a handful of models to answer questions about real data. The exam rewards a correct diagram plus three sentences of correct reasoning far more than it rewards a remembered definition.

Phase A · The summer before (August – mid-September)

You have roughly six weeks. The goal is not to pre-learn the whole course; that never works and it is not necessary. The goal is narrower: arrive in September with the vocabulary, the arithmetic and the first block already familiar, so that lectures feel like a second pass rather than a first.

⚠The real reason people struggle in 4ES104

It is almost never the maths — the maths here is slopes, percentages and areas of triangles. It is that students read the text, nod, and never draw the diagram or say the argument out loud. Then in the exam they are asked what happens to equilibrium bread prices when electricity gets cheaper and they cannot produce a supply and demand diagram from memory. Every hour of this plan is designed to prevent that.

Summer schedule

WeekWhat to doTimeWhere you should be at the end
S1
3–9 Aug		 Tool check, not economics. Percentages and percentage points, growth rates, ratio (log) scales, reading a slope off a graph, area of a triangle and a rectangle, weighted averages, simple linear equations such as $100-Q=20$. Then read Lesson 1 and do its quiz. 6–8 h You can compute a growth rate in your head and explain why a straight line on a log scale means a constant growth rate. L01 done.
S2
10–16 Aug		 L02 production functions and L03 inequality. Draw a concave production function ten times until the shape is automatic. Compute one Gini by hand from four incomes. 6–8 h You can distinguish total, average and marginal product without looking, and draw a Lorenz curve from a table. Then take the Block 1 test.
S3
17–23 Aug		 L04 opportunity cost and rent, L05 comparative advantage. Comparative advantage is the topic that separates people who understand the course from people who recite it — spend the extra hour here. 6–8 h You can explain to a non-economist why a country that is worse at everything still gains from trade, using numbers you invented yourself.
S4
24–30 Aug		 L06 technology choice and isocosts and the Block 2 test. Read the CORE Economy Unit 2 end-of-unit questions and answer them in writing. 6–8 h Given a wage and an input price you can rank three technologies by cost and say which way the isocost tilts when the wage rises.
S5
31 Aug – 6 Sep		 Start Block 3: L07 preferences and L08 constrained choice. This is the geometric core of the course; do not rush it. Learn the cheat sheet sections on MRS and MRT. 6–8 h You can draw a feasible frontier with an indifference curve tangent to it, label both axes, and state MRS = MRT in your own words.
S6
7–13 Sep		 Buffer and vocabulary. Go through the glossary and mark every English term you cannot define in one sentence. Skim common mistakes. Do not start Block 4 — leave something for the semester. 4–6 h Blocks 1–2 solid, Block 3 begun, terminology under control, rested.
💡If you only have two weekends

Then do this and nothing else: L01, L02, L04, L05, plus the glossary sections on growth and on models and costs. Blocks 1 and 2 are the ones the lectures move through fastest, and they are the ones everything else stands on.

Phase B · During the semester (13 weeks)

The syllabus has 10 units (following CORE The Economy), spread over 13 teaching weeks starting the week of 14 September. The midterm test — 30 % of your grade — lands around week 7, just after the block on constrained choice. Read the row for the coming week before the seminar, not after.

WeekLecture topic (syllabus)Read / do hereWatch out for
W1
14–20 Sep		 Unit 1 · The capitalist revolution. The hockey stick, income differences between countries, capitalism as an economic system. L01 + quiz. Look up Czech GDP per capita on a ratio scale in Our World in Data. Growth rates versus growth levels. A country can be rich and growing slowly. Learn to read a log scale now, it comes back all semester.
W2
21–27 Sep		 Unit 2 · Technology, population, growth. The production function, marginal and average product, diminishing returns, the Malthusian trap. L02 + quiz. Draw the MP and AP curves under the total product curve. Do not confuse total output rising with increasing returns. MP falling while total output rises is the normal case.
W3
28 Sep – 4 Oct		 Unit 1/5 · Measuring inequality. Lorenz curve, Gini coefficient, income shares, inequality between and within countries. L03 + quiz, then the Block 1 test. Find the Czech Gini in the Eurostat SILC data. 28 September is a public holiday — check whether your seminar is cancelled and catch up. Also: two very different distributions can share a Gini.
W4
5–11 Oct		 Unit 2 · Models, opportunity cost, economic rent; then specialisation and comparative advantage. L04 and L05 + quizzes. Compute the opportunity cost of your own studies in CZK. Opportunity cost includes forgone earnings and forgone interest, not just money spent. And absolute ≠ comparative advantage.
W5
12–18 Oct		 Unit 2 · Technology choice, isocost lines, relative prices, innovation rents. Presentations usually start this week. L06 + quiz, Block 2 test. Pick your presentation topic (see below). The isocost slope is $-w/p$. Which input goes on which axis decides whether the slope looks steep or flat — always label first.
W6
19–25 Oct		 Unit 3 · Scarcity, work and choice. Preferences, indifference curves, the feasible set and the feasible frontier. L07 and L08 + quizzes. Indifference curves never cross and never touch the axes for goods you like. Feasible frontier = technology; indifference curve = preferences. Different objects, same picture.
W7
26 Oct – 1 Nov		 Midterm test (30 %) — typically covers Units 1–3. Lecture continues with the constrained choice optimum, MRS = MRT. Revise with the cheat sheet and common mistakes. Redo the Block 1 and 2 tests until you are over 85 %. 28 October is a public holiday. Do not leave midterm revision to the long weekend before it — the calendar is against you here.
W8
2–8 Nov		 Unit 3 · Income and substitution effects, the choice of working hours, historical trends in hours worked. L09 + quiz, then the Block 3 test. The two effects go in opposite directions. Never claim a higher wage always means more hours — the whole point is that it need not.
W9
9–15 Nov		 Unit 4 · Social interactions. Payoff matrices, dominant strategies, Nash equilibrium, the prisoners' dilemma. L10 + quiz. Solve five 2×2 games by underlining best responses. A Nash equilibrium is defined by no profitable unilateral deviation, not by being the best outcome for the players.
W10
16–22 Nov		 Unit 4 · Social dilemmas, public goods, experimental evidence, altruistic punishment, conditional cooperation. L11 + quiz. Read the public goods experiment results carefully — numbers get examined. 17 November is a public holiday. Learn the two experimental patterns (decay without punishment, persistence with punishment) as facts, with roughly correct magnitudes.
W11
23–29 Nov		 Unit 5 · Property and power. The rules of the game, bargaining, Pareto efficiency, fairness, the ultimatum game. L12 + quiz, then the Block 4 test. Efficiency and fairness are two separate criteria. Practise saying which one you are using in a given sentence.
W12
30 Nov – 6 Dec		 Units 6 and 7 · The firm and its employees (principal–agent, effort, wage setting, minimum wage); the firm and its customers (costs, elasticity, markup). L13 and L14 + quizzes. Two heavy lessons in one week — start on the weekend before. The markup depends on elasticity, and elasticity is defined with percentage changes, not absolute ones.
W13
7–13 Dec		 Units 8, 10, 12 · Supply and demand, equilibrium and surplus, deadweight loss; credit markets, intertemporal choice; externalities and market failure. Last presentations. L15 and L16 + quizzes, then the Block 5 test. The last week is always compressed and the material is heavily examined. Do not let Unit 12 (externalities) be something you first read in January.
⚠The 10 % of LMS assignments

They are small, they have deadlines, and they are the cheapest points in the course. Losing them because you forgot is the same as walking into the final needing four extra percentage points. Put every deadline in a calendar in week 1 and treat them as non-negotiable.

Phase C · The exam period — the last 10 days

The final test is 90 minutes, worth 40 %, and needs at least 50 % on its own. Ten days of honest work is enough if you have been doing the lessons during the semester. If you have not, start twenty days out and accept that some of it will be first contact.

DayProgrammeOutput
D-10Blocks 1 and 2 revision: L01–L06. Read the summaries, then close the page and reproduce the hockey stick, the concave production function and the isocost diagram from memory.Three diagrams drawn from memory, no notes.
D-9Redo the Block 1 and Block 2 tests under time. Write out every question you got wrong with a one-line reason.Both tests over 80 %. An error list started.
D-8Block 3: L07–L09. Draw the constrained-choice optimum and then the income/substitution decomposition four times, with the axes labelled and the compensating budget line dashed.You can do the decomposition without hesitating about which line is which.
D-7Block 3 test under time; then re-read the parts you missed. Practise one numerical Gini and one comparative advantage problem to keep Blocks 1–2 warm.Block 3 test over 80 %.
D-6Block 4: L10–L12. Solve six payoff matrices. Write out, in five sentences, why a social dilemma has an inefficient equilibrium and what fixes it.Nash equilibria found by underlining best responses, automatically.
D-5Block 4 test. Then read the common mistakes page in full — at this stage it is worth more than new material.Block 4 test over 80 %. Error list updated.
D-4Block 5, part one: L13 and L14. Employment rent, best response curve, wage setting; then costs, elasticity, markup, deadweight loss. Compute one full monopoly surplus problem end to end.You can go from $P=100-Q$ and $MC=20$ to the deadweight loss in under five minutes.
D-3Block 5, part two: L15 and L16 plus the Block 5 test. Supply and demand shifts, intertemporal budget constraint, externalities, Pigouvian tax.The shift table from the cheat sheet reproduced from memory.
D-2Full mock: the final exam, 90 minutes, timed, no notes, on paper. Then mark yourself honestly against the model solutions.A score and a list of the three weakest topics.
D-1Only the three weakest topics plus your error list and the cheat sheet. Redraw all the key diagrams once. Stop by early evening.Nothing new learned, everything shaky repaired. Sleep.
💡How to mark your own mock

For each open question, check three things separately: (1) did you name the model and define the variables, (2) is the diagram or the arithmetic right, (3) is there a final sentence in plain English that actually answers the question. Most lost points in this course come from missing (1) and (3), not from (2).

How to study economics (it is not like maths at grammar school)

1 · Draw every diagram from memory

Blank paper, no notes, axes labelled with units. If you cannot produce the indifference-curve tangency, the supply and demand cross and the externality diagram from an empty page, you do not know them yet. Recognising a diagram in a textbook is not the same skill as producing one under time pressure.

2 · Explain the model out loud

Take one model a day and explain it aloud in 90 seconds to an imaginary non-economist: what the axes are, what the agent chooses, what constrains them, what the result is. The moment you start hesitating is the moment you have found the hole. This is also exactly what the presentation and the open exam questions test.

3 · Always ask what the data say

Every model in this course has a matching empirical fact: the hockey stick, the fall in hours worked, contributions in public goods experiments, offers in the ultimatum game, minimum-wage studies. For every model, learn one number or one graph. Answers that combine a model with a fact score visibly higher than answers with only one of the two.

4 · Do the CORE end-of-unit questions

At the end of every unit of The Economy there are discussion and exercise questions. Write short answers, in English, in full sentences. They are the closest thing to the real exam's open questions that exists, and they force you to produce language rather than recognise it.

5 · Learn the vocabulary as vocabulary

The exam is in English and the terms are technical: marginal rate of substitution, reservation price, deadweight loss, incomplete contract. Use the glossary like a language course — cover the English column, produce it from the Czech one, and back.

6 · Never read passively

Reading a lesson without drawing anything or answering anything has close to zero effect on your exam score. The minimum unit of study in this course is: read a section → close it → write down the model in three lines and one diagram → check.

📊Why this matters for data analysis

You are on a data-analysis programme, so the payoff of this course is specific: economics gives you the causal stories that make a regression interpretable. A correlation between the minimum wage and employment means nothing until you know the two models that predict opposite signs. When you later fit models in R, the difference between a good analyst and a spreadsheet operator is exactly the ability to say which mechanism the coefficient is supposed to be measuring.

The presentation (20 % of the grade)

A fifth of your mark comes from a presentation, and it is the part students most often improvise the night before. It is also the easiest 20 % to score highly on, because the criteria are predictable.

Picking a topic

  • Pick a question, not a subject. Not inequality in the Czech Republic but has income inequality in the Czech Republic risen since 2010, and does the Gini tell the same story as the top-10 % income share? A question has an answer; a subject just has material.
  • Pick something with data you can actually get. ČSÚ, Eurostat (SILC, LFS), Our World in Data, OECD.Stat, the Czech National Bank ARAD database. Two or three good charts beat twenty slides of text.
  • Pick something a course model applies to. The best topics are ones where you can put a model on a slide: minimum wage and the wage-setting model, congestion charges and externalities, streaming subscriptions and markup pricing, the Czech housing market and supply and demand, tragedy of the commons in fishing quotas.
  • Avoid topics that are only opinion (should the state do X) with no measurable quantity. You will have nothing to defend.

Structure that works (10–12 minutes)

PartTimeContent
1 · The question1 minOne slide, one sentence, and why anyone should care. State up front what you will conclude.
2 · The data3 minSource, period, what is measured, and one or two charts. Say explicitly what the chart shows before you interpret it.
3 · The model3 minThe course model that organises the facts, on one diagram. Name it, state its assumptions, show what it predicts.
4 · Confrontation3 minDoes the data match the prediction? Where does it not, and what might be missing from the model? This is where the marks are.
5 · Answer and limits1–2 minAnswer your question in one sentence, then name two limitations honestly. Never end on a bullet list of platitudes.

Defending it

  • Prepare answers to the three questions you will certainly be asked: where do the data come from, what are the assumptions of your model, and what would change your conclusion.
  • Know every number on your slides, including the units and the year. A number you cannot explain is worse than no number.
  • If you are asked something you do not know, say what you would need to answer it. That reads as competence; inventing an answer does not.
  • Rehearse out loud, timed, at least twice. Presentations that overrun get cut, and the part that gets cut is your conclusion.
⚠The two ways presentations lose marks

First: a wall of text read from the slide. Second: describing data without ever using a model, so the presentation could have been given by anyone from any faculty. This is an economics course — the model has to appear, by name, on a slide.

Progress checklist

Tick a lesson when you have read it, done its quiz at 80 % or more, and can draw its main diagram from memory. Tick a block test when you have passed it at 70 % or more.

Block 1 · Growth and inequality

  • L01 — The economic way of thinking and the hockey stick
  • L02 — Production functions and diminishing returns
  • L03 — Inequality: Lorenz curve and Gini coefficient
  • Block 1 test passed (70 %+)

Block 2 · Models, costs and specialisation

  • L04 — Models, opportunity cost and economic rent
  • L05 — Comparative advantage and gains from specialisation
  • L06 — Technology choice and isocost lines
  • Block 2 test passed (70 %+)

Block 3 · Preferences and constrained choice

  • L07 — Preferences and indifference curves
  • L08 — Feasible set and constrained choice, MRS = MRT
  • L09 — Income and substitution effects, working hours
  • Block 3 test passed (70 %+)

Block 4 · Games, dilemmas and institutions

  • L10 — Game theory: payoff matrices and Nash equilibrium
  • L11 — Social dilemmas and experimental evidence
  • L12 — Rules of the game, Pareto efficiency and fairness
  • Block 4 test passed (70 %+)

Block 5 · Firms and markets

  • L13 — The firm and its employees: principal–agent, wage setting, minimum wage
  • L14 — The firm and its customers: costs, elasticity, markup, deadweight loss
  • L15 — Supply and demand, equilibrium and surplus
  • L16 — Credit markets and externalities
  • Block 5 test passed (70 %+)

Final preparation

  • Glossary gone through, both directions
  • Cheat sheet printed and annotated
  • Common mistakes page read in full
  • Presentation prepared, rehearsed and delivered
  • All LMS assignments submitted on time
  • Midterm test written
  • Final exam written as a timed mock, at least 70 %
📌Takeaways
  • Six summer weeks are enough to arrive with Blocks 1–2 done — that is the whole difference between comfortable and desperate in December.
  • The midterm is around week 7 and covers Units 1–3; the heaviest material (Units 6–8, 10, 12) arrives in the last two weeks, so do not run out of energy in November.
  • The final test is 40 % of the grade and a 50 % hurdle. Treat the 10 % LMS points and the 20 % presentation as free insurance against a bad exam day — but they cannot save you if you miss the hurdle.
  • Draw every diagram from memory, explain every model out loud, and pair every model with one number from real data.

extras.title: Glossary EN ↔ CZ
extras.sub: Every key term in English with the Czech equivalent and a one-line definition.
extras.html:
Every term you need for 4ES104, in both languages, with a one-line definition. The tables are grouped by block and sorted alphabetically by the English term, so you can jump straight to the section you are revising or use Ctrl+F (⌘+F) to find a term anywhere on the page. Around 150 entries — everything the lectures, the seminars and the exam use.

💡Why both languages, when the exam is in English

The exam is written and answered in English, so the English term is what earns the point: if you write ztráta mrtvé váhy instead of deadweight loss, the examiner cannot give you credit for a term you did not use. But the Czech equivalent is what makes you actually understand the concept — alternativní náklady immediately tells you that opportunity cost is about the alternative you gave up, which the English phrase hides. So learn both, and use the English one.
