How to drill it: cover the English column and produce it from the Czech one; then cover the Czech and produce the definition from the English. Anything you cannot do in three seconds goes on a separate list. Do this twice — once in November, once two days before the exam.

📌A warning about false friends

Three traps that cost points every year. Rent in economics is not nájem but ekonomická renta — a surplus over the next best option. Capital is not kapitál in the accounting sense but the stock of productive equipment. Efficiency (Pareto efficiency) says nothing about fairness, unlike the everyday Czech efektivnost, which often carries an approving tone.

1 · Growth and inequality (Block 1 — L01–L03)

English termČeský ekvivalentDefinition
average product (AP)průměrný produktTotal output divided by the quantity of the input used: $AP=Q/L$.
ceteris paribusza jinak stejných podmínekReasoning that holds every other variable constant while one is varied.
concave functionkonkávní funkceA function whose slope decreases as the input rises — the graphical form of diminishing returns.
deciledecilOne of ten equal groups of the population ranked by income; the tenth decile is the richest 10 %.
diminishing marginal returnsklesající mezní výnosyEach additional unit of a variable input adds less output than the previous one, other inputs fixed.
disposable incomedisponibilní příjemIncome after taxes and transfers — what a household can actually spend or save.
economic growthhospodářský růstA sustained rise in output per person, usually measured as an annual percentage change.
GDP per capitaHDP na obyvateleTotal value of goods and services produced in a country divided by its population.
Gini coefficientGiniho koeficientInequality measure from 0 (everyone equal) to 1 (one person has everything); twice the area between the Lorenz curve and the 45° line.
growth ratetempo růstuProportional change per period: $(x_t-x_{t-1})/x_{t-1}$, normally expressed in per cent.
hockey stickhokejka (hokejkový graf)The shape of GDP per capita over the last millennium: flat for centuries, then sharply rising after about 1750.
income distributionrozdělení příjmůHow total income is divided among the individuals or households of a population.
income sharepříjmový podílThe fraction of total income received by a given group, e.g. the top 10 %.
Industrial Revolutionprůmyslová revoluceThe cluster of technological and institutional changes from the late 18th century that started permanent growth.
labour productivityproduktivita práceOutput per hour or per worker; the main proximate driver of living standards.
line of perfect equalitylinie dokonalé rovnostiThe 45° diagonal in a Lorenz diagram, where every population share receives the same income share.
Lorenz curveLorenzova křivkaPlot of the cumulative share of income against the cumulative share of the population, ranked from poorest.
Malthusian trapmalthusiánská pastSituation where higher productivity raises population rather than income per head, so living standards stagnate.
marginal product (MP)mezní produktExtra output obtained from one more unit of an input, other inputs held constant.
nominal valuenominální hodnotaA quantity measured at current prices, without correcting for inflation.
production functionprodukční funkceRelationship showing the maximum output obtainable from given quantities of inputs.
purchasing power parity (PPP)parita kupní sílyConversion of incomes at rates that equalise the cost of the same basket of goods across countries.
ratio (logarithmic) scalepoměrové (logaritmické) měřítkoVertical axis on which equal distances mean equal proportional changes; a straight line means a constant growth rate.
real valuereálná hodnotaA quantity corrected for price changes, so that it measures actual purchasing power.
technological progresstechnologický pokrokA change in technology that allows more output from the same inputs.
wealthbohatství (majetek)The stock of assets a household owns minus its debts — distinct from income, which is a flow.

2 · Models, costs and specialisation (Block 2 — L04–L06)

English termČeský ekvivalentDefinition
absolute advantageabsolutní výhodaProducing more of a good than another producer using the same amount of inputs.
accounting profitúčetní ziskRevenue minus explicit (out-of-pocket) costs only.
assumptionpředpokladA simplification deliberately built into a model so that the essential mechanism becomes visible.
capital-intensive technologykapitálově náročná technologieA technology using a high ratio of capital or energy to labour.
comparative advantagekomparativní výhodaProducing a good at a lower opportunity cost than another producer, even if you are absolutely worse at everything.
cost minimisationminimalizace nákladůChoosing the input combination that produces a given output at the lowest total cost, i.e. the lowest isocost line touching the technology.
economic profitekonomický ziskRevenue minus all opportunity costs, explicit and implicit; equals the economic rent of the activity.
economic rentekonomická rentaThe amount by which the pay-off of an action exceeds the pay-off of the next best alternative.
endogenous variableendogenní proměnnáA variable whose value is determined inside the model.
exogenous variableexogenní proměnnáA variable taken as given from outside the model.
explicit costexplicitní nákladyCosts involving an actual payment to someone else.
factor of productionvýrobní faktorAn input used in production: labour, capital, land, energy, materials.
gains from tradezisky z obchodu (ze směny)The extra output or utility obtained when parties specialise according to comparative advantage and then trade.
implicit costimplicitní nákladyThe value of a resource you already own and use up — forgone wages, forgone interest, forgone time.
innovation rentinovační rentaTemporary economic profit earned by a first adopter of a new technology, competed away as others imitate.
isocost lineizonákladová přímkaAll input combinations costing the same total amount; slope $-w/p$ with labour on the horizontal axis.
labour-intensive technologypracovně náročná technologieA technology using a high ratio of labour to capital or energy.
modelmodelA deliberately simplified description of reality that isolates the mechanism you want to study.
opportunity costalternativní náklady (náklady obětované příležitosti)The value of the best alternative you give up when you choose something.
production possibility frontierhranice produkčních možnostíAll combinations of two goods an economy can produce when its resources are fully used; its slope is the opportunity cost.
relative pricerelativní cenaThe price of one good expressed in units of another; what determines substitution decisions.
reservation optionrezervační možnostThe next best alternative available if you say no to the deal on the table.
specialisationspecializaceConcentrating production on the goods in which you have a comparative advantage.
sunk costutopené nákladyA cost already incurred that cannot be recovered; irrelevant to any forward-looking decision.
terms of tradesměnné relaceThe rate at which one good exchanges for another; must lie between the two parties' opportunity costs for trade to be mutually beneficial.

3 · Choice, preferences and constrained optimisation (Block 3 — L07–L09)

English termČeský ekvivalentDefinition
backward-bending labour supply curvezpět zahnutá křivka nabídky práceLabour supply that falls at high wages, because the income effect outweighs the substitution effect.
budget constraintrozpočtové omezeníThe equation describing all bundles a person can just afford given prices and income.
constrained choiceomezená (podmíněná) volbaChoosing the most preferred bundle from the feasible set — the basic problem of the whole course.
consumptionspotřebaGoods and services actually used by a household in a period.
convex preferenceskonvexní preferencePreferences for which averages are preferred to extremes; they generate indifference curves bowed towards the origin.
diminishing marginal rate of substitutionklesající mezní míra substituceThe more of a good you already have, the less of the other good you will sacrifice for one more unit of it.
feasible frontierhranice dosažitelných možnostíThe boundary of the feasible set — the best combinations technology and resources allow.
feasible setmnožina dosažitelných možnostíAll bundles a person can obtain given the constraints they face.
free timevolný časTime not spent in paid work; treated as a good with a price equal to the wage.
income effectdůchodový efektThe change in demand caused by a price change making the person richer or poorer overall.
indifference curveindiferenční křivkaAll bundles among which a person is indifferent, i.e. that give the same utility.
indifference mapmapa indiferenčních křivekThe whole family of a person's indifference curves; curves further from the origin mean higher utility.
inferior goodméněcenný (inferiorní) statekA good of which a person buys less when income rises.
labour supply curvekřivka nabídky práceRelationship between the wage and the number of hours a worker chooses to work.
marginal rate of substitution (MRS)mezní míra substituceThe absolute slope of an indifference curve: how much of one good a person will give up for one more unit of the other, utility constant.
marginal rate of transformation (MRT)mezní míra transformaceThe absolute slope of the feasible frontier: how much of one good must actually be given up to get one more unit of the other.
normal goodnormální statekA good of which a person buys more when income rises.
optimum (best feasible bundle)optimum (nejlepší dosažitelná kombinace)The point where the highest attainable indifference curve is tangent to the feasible frontier, so that MRS = MRT.
preferencespreferenceA consistent ranking of bundles telling us what a person likes, independent of what they can afford.
reservation wagerezervační mzdaThe lowest wage at which a person is willing to accept a job rather than stay out of work.
substitution effectsubstituční efektThe change in demand caused purely by the change in relative prices, holding utility constant.
tangency conditionpodmínka tečnostiMRS = MRT — the slopes of preferences and of the constraint are equal at the optimum.
utilityužitekA numerical index representing preferences; higher utility simply means more preferred.

4 · Games, dilemmas and institutions (Block 4 — L10–L12)

English termČeský ekvivalentDefinition
altruistic punishmentaltruistické trestáníPaying a personal cost to punish someone who behaved unfairly, with no private benefit in return.
bargaining powervyjednávací sílaThe extent to which one party can secure a larger share of the mutual gains from an exchange.
best responsenejlepší odpověďThe strategy giving a player the highest pay-off, given what the other players do.
conditional cooperationpodmíněná spolupráceContributing to a public good if, and only if, others are seen to contribute too.
dominant strategydominantní strategieA strategy that is the best response to everything the other player might do.
dominated strategydominovaná strategieA strategy that is worse than some other strategy whatever the opponent does.
fairness — proceduralprocedurální spravedlnostJudging an outcome by how it came about (voluntary exchange, equal rules) rather than by the result.
fairness — substantivevěcná spravedlnostJudging an outcome by the resulting distribution itself, e.g. by how unequal it is.
free ridingčerné pasažérstvíBenefiting from a public good or a common effort without contributing to it.
institutionsinstituceThe written and unwritten rules governing how people interact — laws, contracts, norms, property rights.
Nash equilibriumNashova rovnováhaA combination of strategies in which each player's choice is a best response to the others', so nobody wants to deviate alone.
Pareto efficiencyparetovská efektivnostA state in which nobody can be made better off without making someone else worse off.
Pareto frontierparetovská hraniceThe set of all Pareto-efficient allocations; moving along it helps one party at the expense of another.
Pareto improvementparetovské zlepšeníA change that makes at least one person better off and nobody worse off.
payoff matrixvýplatní maticeTable showing each player's pay-off for every combination of strategies.
playerhráčA decision maker in a game whose pay-off depends also on what others do.
prisoners' dilemmavězňovo dilemaA game where defecting is dominant for both players, so the Nash equilibrium is worse for both than mutual cooperation.
public goodveřejný statekA good that is non-rival and non-excludable, so private provision is typically too small.
reciprocityreciprocitaThe preference to be kind to those who are kind to you and to punish those who are not.
rules of the gamepravidla hryWho can do what, who gets what, and who decides — the institutional setting that determines the outcome as much as preferences do.
social dilemmasociální dilemaA situation in which individually rational actions produce a collectively inferior outcome.
social normsociální normaA shared expectation about how one ought to behave, enforced by approval and disapproval.
strategystrategieA complete plan of action a player can choose in a game.
tragedy of the commonstragédie obecní pastvinyOveruse of a shared resource because each user ignores the cost imposed on the others.
ultimatum gameultimátní hraExperiment where a Proposer offers a split and a Responder can reject, destroying the money — evidence on fairness preferences.

5 · Firms, workers, customers and markets (Block 5 — L13–L15)

English termČeský ekvivalentDefinition
asymmetric informationasymetrická informaceOne party to a transaction knows something relevant that the other cannot verify.
average cost (AC)průměrné nákladyTotal cost divided by output: $AC=TC/Q$.
best response curve (effort)křivka nejlepší odpovědi (úsilí)How much effort a worker chooses at each wage, given monitoring and the risk of dismissal.
consumer surplusspotřebitelský přebytekTotal willingness to pay minus what consumers actually pay; the area under demand and above price.
deadweight lossztráta mrtvé váhySurplus destroyed because mutually beneficial trades do not take place; the triangle between demand and MC over the missing units.
demand curvepoptávková křivkaQuantity buyers wish to purchase at each price, everything else held constant.
differentiated productdiferencovaný produktA product buyers see as distinct from rivals', which gives the seller a downward-sloping demand curve.
economies of scaleúspory z rozsahuAverage cost falls as output rises.
efficiency wageefektivnostní mzdaA wage set above the reservation wage in order to motivate effort, chosen where the wage per unit of effort is minimised.
elastic demandelastická poptávkaElasticity greater than 1: quantity responds more than proportionally to price, so cutting price raises revenue.
employment rentrenta ze zaměstnáníThe value of keeping the job over the next best alternative, multiplied by the expected duration of unemployment — the cost of job loss.
equilibriumrovnováhaA situation self-perpetuating in the absence of an outside shock; in a market, where quantity supplied equals quantity demanded.
excess demandpřevis poptávkyQuantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied at the prevailing price, which pushes the price up.
fixed costfixní nákladyCosts that do not vary with output in the short run.
incomplete contractneúplná smlouvaA contract that cannot specify everything that matters (e.g. effort or care), because it is not verifiable in court.
inelastic demandneelastická poptávkaElasticity below 1: quantity responds less than proportionally to price, so raising price raises revenue.
involuntary unemploymentnedobrovolná nezaměstnanostPeople willing to work at the going wage who cannot find a job — an equilibrium feature of the labour-discipline model.
isoprofit curveizozisková křivkaAll price–quantity combinations giving a firm the same profit.
marginal cost (MC)mezní nákladyThe increase in total cost from producing one more unit.
marginal revenue (MR)mezní příjemThe increase in total revenue from selling one more unit; for a linear demand curve it falls twice as fast as price.
market powertržní sílaThe ability to set a price above marginal cost without losing all customers.
markuppřirážka (marže)$(P-MC)/P$, the share of the price that is not marginal cost; equals $1/\varepsilon$ at the profit-maximising point.
minimum wageminimální mzdaA legal floor on the hourly or monthly wage an employer may pay.
monopsonymonopsonA market with wage-setting power on the employer side, because workers cannot costlessly switch jobs.
moral hazardmorální hazardTaking a hidden action that harms the other party once the contract is signed, because it cannot be observed.
price ceilingcenový stropA legal maximum price; if binding, it creates excess demand and rationing.
price elasticity of demandcenová elasticita poptávkyPercentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in price, usually reported in absolute value.
price floorcenová podlahaA legal minimum price; if binding, it creates excess supply.
price takercenový příjemceA buyer or seller with no influence on the price, facing a horizontal demand or supply curve.
principal–agent problemproblém zmocnitele a zmocněnceOne party (principal) wants another (agent) to act in their interest, but cannot write an enforceable contract on that action.
producer surplusvýrobcův přebytekRevenue minus the cost of producing each unit; the area above the supply/MC curve and below price.
reservation pricerezervační cenaThe highest price a buyer will pay, or the lowest a seller will accept.
shift of a curveposun křivkyThe whole curve moves because something other than the good's own price changed.
supply curvenabídková křivkaQuantity sellers wish to sell at each price; in a competitive market it is the marginal cost curve.
total cost (TC)celkové nákladyFixed plus variable costs of producing a given output.
total surpluscelkový přebytekConsumer surplus plus producer surplus; maximised where price equals marginal cost.
variable costvariabilní nákladyCosts that rise with the quantity produced.
wage-setting curvekřivka stanovení mezdThe wage firms must pay to elicit effort at each level of employment; rises as unemployment falls.
willingness to pay (WTP)ochota platitThe maximum amount a consumer would give up for a unit of the good; the height of the demand curve.

6 · Credit markets and market failure (Block 5 — L16)

English termČeský ekvivalentDefinition
borrowerdlužníkSomeone who moves consumption from the future to the present by taking a loan.
cap and tradeobchodovatelné emisní povolenkyPolicy setting a total quantity of emissions and letting firms trade permits, so abatement happens where it is cheapest.
Coase bargainingCoaseovo vyjednáváníPrivate negotiation that can reach the efficient outcome when property rights are clear and bargaining costs are low.
collateralzástava (kolaterál)An asset pledged to the lender and forfeited on default; it reduces the lender's risk and widens access to credit.
consumption smoothingvyhlazování spotřebyUsing borrowing and saving to keep consumption steadier than income over time.
credit constraintúvěrové omezeníBeing able to borrow only on unfavourable terms, or less than one would want, because of limited wealth or collateral.
credit rationingracionování úvěruLenders refusing to lend at all to some borrowers rather than charging them a higher rate.
discountingdiskontováníConverting a future amount into its value today by dividing by $(1+r)$ for each period.
externalityexternalitaA cost or benefit falling on someone who is not party to the transaction and is not compensated or charged for it.
interest rateúroková míraThe price of moving purchasing power from the future to the present, per unit borrowed per period.
intertemporal budget constraintmezičasové rozpočtové omezeníThe line showing all combinations of present and future consumption available at the interest rate; slope $-(1+r)$.
lendervěřitelSomeone who moves consumption from the present to the future by saving or lending.
market failuretržní selháníA situation in which market outcomes are not Pareto efficient, e.g. because of externalities, market power or missing information.
negative externalitynegativní externalitaAn uncompensated cost imposed on others, so the market produces too much of the activity.
Pigouvian taxPigouova daňA tax equal to the marginal external cost, which makes private marginal cost equal social marginal cost.
positive externalitypozitivní externalitaAn uncompensated benefit conferred on others, so the market produces too little of the activity.
present valuesoučasná hodnotaToday's equivalent of a future payment: $PV=X/(1+r)^t$.
principal (of a loan)jistinaThe amount borrowed, on which interest is calculated.
private marginal costmezní soukromé nákladyThe cost of one more unit borne by the decision maker alone.
property rightsvlastnická právaLegally enforceable rights to use, exclude others from and sell an asset — the precondition for markets and for Coase bargaining.
rate of time preferencemíra časové preferenceHow strongly a person prefers consumption now over consumption later, shown by the slope of indifference curves at equal consumption.
social marginal costmezní společenské nákladyPrivate marginal cost plus the marginal external cost imposed on everyone else.
tax incidencedopad (incidence) daněHow the burden of a tax is shared between buyers and sellers, determined by the relative elasticities.
⚠Terms that are constantly confused
  • MRS vs MRT — preferences versus technology. MRS is the slope of an indifference curve, MRT the slope of the feasible frontier. They are equal only at the optimum.
  • Absolute vs comparative advantage — productivity levels versus opportunity costs. Only the second one drives specialisation.
  • Accounting vs economic profit — the second subtracts implicit costs as well, which is why a profitable business can have zero economic profit.
  • Deadweight loss vs transfer — the triangle is surplus destroyed; the rectangle is surplus that changed owner.
  • Pareto efficient vs fair — the first is about whether anything is being wasted, the second about who gets what. Neither implies the other.
  • Shift vs movement along — a change in the good's own price moves you along the curve; anything else shifts it.
📌How to use this page in the last week

Go section by section, cover the middle column, and speak the Czech term aloud. Then cover the third column and produce the definition. Any term where you hesitate goes on paper. On the day before the final exam, that paper list plus the cheat sheet is all you should be reading.

extras.title: Cheat sheet
extras.sub: All the models, curves and formulas on one printable page.
extras.html:
Every model, curve, formula and decision rule of 4ES104 on one page, grouped by block. This is a reference sheet, not a text to read from start to finish — it is what you look at when you cannot remember whether the markup is $1/\varepsilon$ or $\varepsilon$, or which way the isocost tilts when the wage rises. Print it, annotate it, and take it to every seminar.

💡How to use this sheet
  • Cover the right-hand columns and reproduce them from the formula alone. What you cannot reproduce, circle and repeat tomorrow.
  • The three diagrams below are the exam. If you can redraw the tangency picture, the supply-and-demand cross and the externality diagram from a blank page with the axes labelled, you have most of the marks in the drawing questions.
  • Every formula here should be attached to one worked number you did yourself. A formula you have never used will not come back under time pressure.
  • Notation: $Q$ output/quantity, $L$ labour, $w$ wage, $P$ price, $r$ interest rate, $\varepsilon$ price elasticity of demand (absolute value).

1 · Growth and the hockey stick (L01)

FormulaMeaningWhen you use it
$g=\dfrac{x_t-x_{t-1}}{x_{t-1}}$Growth rate over one period.Any question asking by how many per cent something rose.
$x_t=x_0(1+g)^t$Compound growth over $t$ periods.Projecting GDP per capita forward; comparing two countries' catch-up.
Rule of 70: $t\approx\dfrac{70}{g\,[\%]}$Years needed to double.Fast mental check: 2 % growth doubles income in ~35 years.
Straight line on a ratio (log) scaleConstant growth rate, not constant increment.Reading any long-run GDP chart; the hockey stick becomes an upward-sloping line.

What the hockey stick shows

GDP per capita roughly flat for six centuries, then permanent growth from about 1750 in Britain, later elsewhere. It is a graph of output per person, so it is a statement about living standards, not about the size of the economy.

Why it happened

Permanent technological progress (each innovation raising labour productivity) plus institutions that made innovating privately profitable: secure property rights, competitive markets, patents, and a labour market that let people move. Technology alone gives a one-off jump; technology plus incentives gives a growth rate.

2 · Production function, MP and AP (L02)

FormulaMeaningWhen you use it
$Q=f(L)$Maximum output from $L$ units of the variable input, other inputs fixed.Every Block 1 and Block 3 diagram: farm output, study hours and grades.
$MP=\dfrac{\Delta Q}{\Delta L}$ (discrete) $=f'(L)$Extra output from one more unit of input; the slope of the production function.Tables of output — compute differences between consecutive rows.
$AP=\dfrac{Q}{L}$Output per unit of input; the slope of the ray from the origin to the point.Productivity comparisons; the AP/MP relationship.
$MP<AP\Rightarrow AP$ falling
$MP>AP\Rightarrow AP$ rising		The average is pulled towards the marginal.Checking your table: AP peaks exactly where $MP=AP$.
Concave $f$ ⇔ $MP$ decreasingDiminishing marginal returns.Justifying the shape of every feasible frontier in the course.
⚠Three things concavity does NOT mean

It does not mean output falls (that would be negative MP). It does not mean AP is constant. And it does not mean the technology is bad — better technology shifts the whole function up and still has diminishing returns.

3 · Lorenz curve and Gini coefficient (L03)

FormulaMeaningWhen you use it
Lorenz curveCumulative income share (vertical) against cumulative population share (horizontal), ranked from poorest.Drawing inequality; the 45° line is perfect equality.
$G=\dfrac{A}{A+B}=1-2B$$A$ = area between the 45° line and the Lorenz curve, $B$ = area under the Lorenz curve.The definition. Since $A+B=\tfrac12$, computing $B$ is enough.
$B=\sum_k \dfrac{(y_{k-1}+y_k)}{2}\cdot\Delta p$Area under the Lorenz curve as a sum of trapezoids of width $\Delta p=1/n$.Hand computation from a small table of incomes.
$G=\dfrac{2\sum_{i} i\,y_i}{n\sum_i y_i}-\dfrac{n+1}{n}$Direct formula, incomes $y_i$ sorted ascending, $i=1\ldots n$.The fastest exam method — and the cross-check on the trapezoid method.
$G=0$ / $G\to1$Perfect equality / one person has everything.Sanity check: a Gini outside $[0,1]$ is always an error.

Worked mini-example

Incomes 10, 20, 30, 60 (total 120). $\sum i\,y_i = 10+40+90+240=380$. $G=\dfrac{2\cdot380}{4\cdot120}-\dfrac54=1{,}5833-1{,}25=\dfrac13$.

What the Gini cannot tell you

Two very different distributions can have the same Gini — one with a poor tail, one with a rich tail. Always pair it with an income share (top 10 %, bottom 40 %) or a 90/10 ratio. Also: it is scale-invariant, so doubling everyone's income leaves it unchanged.

4 · Opportunity cost, rent and comparative advantage (L04, L05)

Formula / ruleMeaningWhen you use it
Opportunity cost = explicit + implicit costMoney paid out plus the value of what you gave up (forgone wage, forgone interest, forgone time).Any "should I do X" question, any profit calculation.
Economic profit = revenue − all opportunity costsAccounting profit minus implicit costs.Deciding whether an activity beats the next best alternative.
Economic rent = pay-off of action − pay-off of next best optionThe surplus that makes an action worth taking.Innovation rent, employment rent, rent in bargaining.
Sunk costs are irrelevantAlready spent and unrecoverable, so they do not enter any decision.Whenever the question mentions money already invested.
OC of 1 unit of A $=\dfrac{\text{output of B per worker}}{\text{output of A per worker}}$How much B you give up for one A.Comparative advantage tables.
Comparative advantage rule: specialise in the good with the lower opportunity costNot the good you produce most of — the good you sacrifice least for.Every trade question. Absolute advantage is a distraction.
$OC_{\text{A, country 1}} < p < OC_{\text{A, country 2}}$Range of terms of trade at which both parties gain."At which prices will they trade?"
💡The two-line comparative advantage routine

Write a 2×2 table of output per worker. For each country divide across the row both ways — that gives four opportunity costs. Compare the two numbers for the same good across countries; the lower one specialises. Never compare a country to itself.

5 · Technology choice and isocost lines (L06)

FormulaMeaningWhen you use it
$C=wL+pE$Total cost of a technology using $L$ labour at wage $w$ and $E$ energy at price $p$.Ranking technologies — just compute the number for each.
$E=\dfrac{C}{p}-\dfrac{w}{p}L$Isocost line with $L$ horizontal, $E$ vertical.Drawing the diagram.
Slope $=-\dfrac{w}{p}$The relative price of labour in terms of energy.Predicting substitution: higher $w$ ⇒ steeper isocost ⇒ move to a more energy-intensive technology.
Cost minimisationChoose the technology touched by the lowest isocost line.Every technology-choice question.

The one-sentence prediction

When an input becomes relatively more expensive, firms move towards technologies that use less of it. This is why rising wages historically drove mechanisation, and why the carbon price is expected to change technology, not just output.

Exam trap

The cheapest technology is a joint property of technology and prices. A technology that uses fewer units in total can easily be the expensive one. Always compute $wL+pE$, never count units.

6 · Preferences, MRS and the feasible frontier (L07, L08)

ConceptDefinition / formulaDiagram property
Indifference curveAll bundles giving the same utility.Downward sloping, convex to the origin, never crosses another, higher curve = higher utility.
MRS$MRS=\left|\dfrac{\Delta y}{\Delta x}\right|_{U\ \text{const}}=\dfrac{MU_x}{MU_y}$Absolute slope of the indifference curve. Falls as you move right (diminishing MRS).
Feasible setAll bundles the constraints allow.The area under the frontier.
Feasible frontierBoundary of the feasible set, from the production function or the budget.Concave when technology has diminishing returns; a straight line when the trade-off is constant (budget line).
MRTAbsolute slope of the feasible frontier; for a budget line $MRT=P_x/P_y$.How much of $y$ you must actually give up for one more $x$.
Optimum$\boxed{MRS = MRT}$Tangency of the highest attainable indifference curve with the frontier.
ΣThe adjustment rule you can use without any algebra

If $MRT > MRS$: giving up one unit of $x$ buys you more $y$ than you require in compensation ⇒ move left (less $x$, more $y$). If $MRT < MRS$: move right. You stop where they are equal. This single rule answers most "is she at the optimum, and which way should she move?" questions.

7 · Income and substitution effects (L09)

EffectWhat causes itDirection after a wage riseHow you draw it
Substitution effectFree time became relatively more expensive (its price is the wage).Less free time, more hours worked.Slide along the original indifference curve to where its slope equals the new wage — utility held constant.
Income effectThe person can now afford more of everything.More free time, fewer hours worked (free time is a normal good).Shift from the compensating (dashed) line out to the real new budget line, slope unchanged.
Total effectBoth together.Ambiguous — either sign is possible.From the old optimum straight to the new optimum.

Backward-bending labour supply

If the income effect dominates at high wages, hours fall as the wage rises and the labour supply curve bends backwards. The long-run fact matches this: annual hours in Western Europe fell from about 3 000 to roughly 1 500–1 700 while real wages multiplied.

Pure effects

An unearned income (lottery win, inheritance, unconditional transfer) shifts the budget line without changing its slope ⇒ pure income effect, no substitution effect. A change in relative prices with compensation ⇒ pure substitution effect. Exam questions love these two limiting cases.

8 · Games: payoff matrix, dominance, Nash (L10, L11)

ConceptDefinitionHow you find it on the matrix
Best responseThe strategy with the highest pay-off given the other player's choice.Fix the opponent's column, compare the row player's numbers, underline the larger.
Dominant strategyBest response to everything the opponent might do.The same row is underlined in every column.
Nash equilibriumEvery player is playing a best response to the others.The cell where both numbers are underlined.
Prisoners' dilemmaBoth have a dominant strategy to defect; the equilibrium is Pareto-dominated by mutual cooperation.The underlined cell is worse for both than another cell.
Social dilemmaIndividually rational actions ⇒ collectively worse outcome.Public goods, overfishing, climate, congestion.
ΣStandard prisoners' dilemma matrix (row, column)
Column: defectColumn: cooperate
Row: defect(2, 2) ← Nash(4, 1)
Row: cooperate(1, 4)(3, 3) ← Pareto-better

A Nash equilibrium is a statement about stability, not about goodness. Here (2,2) is stable and (3,3) is not, even though both players prefer (3,3).

Public goods game arithmetic

$n$ players, endowment $e$, multiplier $m$ (with $1<m<n$). Each token contributed returns $m/n < 1$ to the contributor but $m > 1$ to the group. So free riding is dominant and full contribution is efficient. With $n=4$, $m=1{,}6$: private return per token $0{,}4$, net $-0{,}6$.

What raises cooperation

Repeated interaction and reputation · peer (altruistic) punishment · communication before choosing · social norms and reciprocity · formal rules: quotas, taxes, property rights. Each one works by changing the pay-offs or the rules, not by asking people to be nicer.

9 · Pareto efficiency, fairness and institutions (L12)

ConceptDefinitionWhat it does not say
Pareto improvementSomeone gains, nobody loses.Nothing about how the gain is split.
Pareto efficiencyNo Pareto improvement is available.Nothing about fairness — an allocation where one person owns everything can be efficient.
Pareto frontierAll efficient allocations; moving along it helps one and hurts the other.It does not select a point — that is a question of bargaining power and institutions.
Substantive fairnessJudging the outcome (how unequal it is).—
Procedural fairnessJudging how the outcome came about (rules, consent, equal treatment).—
InstitutionsRules of the game: who can do what, who gets what, who decides.They change both the size of the pie and its division — not only the division.

10 · The firm and its employees (L13)

Formula / conceptMeaningWhen you use it
Incomplete contractEffort cannot be written into an enforceable contract, because it is not verifiable.The starting point of the whole model.
Principal–agent problemThe firm wants effort, the worker prefers less; interests diverge in a dimension the contract cannot cover.Explaining why wages exceed the reservation wage.
Employment rent $\approx (w-w_{res})\times$ expected months of unemploymentThe cost to the worker of losing the job.Numerical questions on the cost of job loss; explaining effort.
Best response curveEffort chosen by the worker at each wage — rising, then flattening.The vertical axis of the wage-setting diagram.
Efficiency wage: maximise $\dfrac{\text{effort}}{w}$Tangency of the flattest ray from the origin with the best response curve.Finding the wage the firm actually sets.
Involuntary unemploymentAn equilibrium outcome, because the wage is deliberately above market clearing.Why the labour market does not clear in this model.

Minimum wage — the competitive answer

A binding floor above the market-clearing wage moves firms up a downward-sloping labour demand curve: employment falls, unemployment appears. This is the correct first answer and you should always state it.

Minimum wage — the qualifications

With monopsony (employer wage-setting power) a moderate floor can raise wages and employment. With effort responding to the wage, unit labour costs rise less than the wage. Evidence (Card–Krueger and the later literature) finds effects near zero for moderate increases, clearly negative when the minimum is high relative to the median.

11 · Costs, elasticity, markup (L14)

FormulaMeaningWhen you use it
$TC=FC+VC$Total cost.Any cost table.
$AC=\dfrac{TC}{Q}$Average cost — the slope of the ray from the origin to the total cost curve.Economies of scale (AC falling).
$MC=\dfrac{\Delta TC}{\Delta Q}$Marginal cost — the slope of the total cost curve.Supply decisions; $MC$ cuts $AC$ at its minimum.
$\varepsilon=\left|\dfrac{\%\Delta Q}{\%\Delta P}\right|=\left|\dfrac{\Delta Q}{\Delta P}\cdot\dfrac{P}{Q}\right|$Price elasticity of demand.Every markup and revenue question. Always use percentage changes with a consistent base.
$\varepsilon>1$ elastic · $\varepsilon<1$ inelasticElastic: cutting the price raises revenue. Inelastic: raising the price raises revenue."What happens to revenue if the price changes?"
$MR=P\left(1-\dfrac1\varepsilon\right)$; for $P=a-bQ$: $MR=a-2bQ$Marginal revenue; falls twice as fast as a linear demand curve.Finding the profit-maximising quantity.
$MR=MC$Profit maximisation.The starting equation of every monopoly problem.
$\boxed{\dfrac{P-MC}{P}=\dfrac{1}{\varepsilon}}$Markup rule. The markup is a share of the price.Going from elasticity to price: $P=\dfrac{MC}{1-1/\varepsilon}$.
💡Two mental checks on the markup

More elastic demand ⇒ smaller markup ($\varepsilon\to\infty$ gives $P=MC$, perfect competition). And the profit-maximising point always lies in the elastic part of the demand curve: if $\varepsilon\le1$, raising the price would raise revenue and cut costs at once, so you cannot be optimising.

12 · Surplus and deadweight loss (L14, L15)

ConceptHow to compute itOn the diagram
Willingness to payThe height of the demand curve at that unit.Demand = marginal benefit.
Consumer surplus$\sum(WTP-P)$; for a linear demand, $\tfrac12\cdot Q\cdot(P_{max}-P)$.Triangle under demand, above price.
Producer surplus$\sum(P-MC)$; with constant $MC$, $(P-MC)\cdot Q$.Area above supply/MC, below price.
Total surplusCS + PS; maximised where $P=MC$.Triangle between demand and MC up to the competitive quantity.
Deadweight loss$\tfrac12\cdot(P^m-MC)\cdot(Q^{comp}-Q^m)$ for linear curves.Triangle between demand and MC over the units not traded.
⚠Triangle vs rectangle

The rectangle $(P^m-MC)\cdot Q^m$ is surplus transferred from consumers to the firm — it still exists, it just changed owner, and disliking it is a fairness judgement. The triangle is surplus destroyed: trades worth more than they cost that simply do not happen. Only the triangle is the efficiency loss.

📐The standard monopoly computation, once

$P=100-Q$, $MC=20$. Competitive: $P=MC\Rightarrow Q=80$, total surplus $\tfrac12\cdot80\cdot80=3200$. Monopoly: $MR=100-2Q=20\Rightarrow Q=40$, $P=60$; $CS=\tfrac12\cdot40\cdot40=800$, $PS=40\cdot40=1600$, total $2400$. $DWL=3200-2400=800=\tfrac12\cdot40\cdot40$. Markup $=40/60=2/3$, and $\varepsilon=\tfrac{60}{40}=1{,}5$, so $1/\varepsilon=2/3$ — consistent.

13 · Supply and demand (L15)

What changesWhich curveDirectionEffect on P and Q
Price of the good itselfNeitherMovement along the curvesNo shift at all — this is the classic error.
Consumers' income rises (normal good)DemandRight$P\uparrow$, $Q\uparrow$
Price of a substitute risesDemandRight$P\uparrow$, $Q\uparrow$
Price of a complement risesDemandLeft$P\downarrow$, $Q\downarrow$
Tastes turn against the goodDemandLeft$P\downarrow$, $Q\downarrow$
Input price (energy, wages) fallsSupplyRight$P\downarrow$, $Q\uparrow$
Better production technologySupplyRight$P\downarrow$, $Q\uparrow$
Tax per unit on sellersSupplyLeft (up by the tax)$P\uparrow$ for buyers, $Q\downarrow$
Number of sellers fallsSupplyLeft$P\uparrow$, $Q\downarrow$
Demand right and supply rightBoth—$Q\uparrow$ certainly, $P$ ambiguous
Demand right and supply leftBoth—$P\uparrow$ certainly, $Q$ ambiguous

Price ceiling and price floor

A binding ceiling (below equilibrium) creates excess demand, queues and rationing. A binding floor (above equilibrium) creates excess supply. Both create a deadweight loss because the traded quantity is below the efficient one.

Tax incidence

The burden falls mostly on the less elastic side of the market: whoever has fewer alternatives cannot escape the tax. It does not matter legally on whom the tax is levied — the economic incidence is the same.

14 · Credit markets and intertemporal choice (L16)

FormulaMeaningWhen you use it
$PV=\dfrac{X}{(1+r)^t}$Present value of a future amount.Comparing money at different dates. Never add amounts from different periods without discounting.
$c_2=(y_1-c_1)(1+r)+y_2$Intertemporal budget constraint: what you do not consume today grows at $1+r$.Drawing the two-period diagram with $c_1$ horizontal, $c_2$ vertical.
Slope $=-(1+r)$One unit of consumption given up today buys $1+r$ units tomorrow.The MRT of the credit market.
Optimum: $MRS=1+r$Rate of time preference equals the market interest rate.Deciding whether the person borrows or lends.
Borrower / lenderChooses $c_1>y_1$ / $c_1<y_1$.Read off which side of the endowment point the optimum lies.
Collateral, credit rationingWealth reduces the lender's risk; without it, borrowers face higher rates or are excluded.Explaining why the poor pay more for credit — a source of persistent inequality.

15 · Externalities and Pigouvian taxes (L16)

ConceptRuleConsequence
Negative externality$MSC=MPC+MEC$, with $MEC>0$.Market produces too much; DWL triangle between $Q^*$ and $Q^{market}$.
Positive externality$MSB=MPB+MEB$.Market produces too little; a subsidy is the corrective policy.
Pigouvian taxTax $=MEC$ evaluated at the efficient quantity $Q^*$.Firms' private cost becomes the social cost; output falls to $Q^*$ and the DWL disappears.
Coase bargainingClear property rights + low bargaining costs ⇒ private negotiation reaches $Q^*$.Who pays depends on who holds the right; the efficient quantity does not.
Cap and tradeFix the total quantity, let permits trade.Abatement happens where it is cheapest; the price emerges from the market instead of being set.
Efficient pollutionGenerally positive, not zero.Stop where marginal benefit of output equals marginal social cost — eliminating all pollution is usually inefficient.
📌The five things to check before you hand in
  • Are both axes labelled, with units?
  • Did you use a percentage change (not an absolute one) in every elasticity?
  • Is the deadweight loss a triangle, and did you keep it separate from the transfer rectangle?
  • Did every "should they do X" answer subtract the implicit costs as well?
  • Does each open answer end with one plain-English sentence that answers the question asked?

extras.title: Common mistakes
extras.sub: The exact errors that cost points in the CORE final test.
extras.html:
These are not general study tips. They are twenty specific errors that examiners see in almost every batch of 4ES104 papers — errors made by students who understand the model but state it wrongly, and who therefore lose marks they had already earned. Read this page before every block test and again the day before the final exam.

🎯How to use this page
  • Each mistake is ✗ Wrong (what students actually write) versus ✓ Right, plus one sentence explaining why.
  • They are grouped by block, so you can read only the part you are being tested on.
  • Most of them come with a three-second check in italics — a habit that catches the error before you hand in.
  • If you find yourself recognising one of these as something you would have written, mark it and come back to it. Recognition is not correction.

Block 1 · Growth, production and inequality

⚠Mistake 1 · Total output rising is called increasing returns

✗ Wrong

Output goes 20, 36, 48, 56, 60 as workers are added, so the farm has increasing returns — output keeps growing.

✓ Right

Marginal products are 20, 16, 12, 8, 4 — falling. Output rises at a decreasing rate: this is diminishing marginal returns and a concave production function.

Why: Returns are a statement about the marginal unit, not about the total. Total output can rise while every extra worker contributes less than the last. Check: before saying anything about returns, write the row of differences between consecutive outputs.

⚠Mistake 2 · Reading the Gini as if it described the distribution

✗ Wrong

Country A and country B both have a Gini of 0.33, so income is distributed in the same way in both.

✓ Right

The same Gini is consistent with very different distributions — one with a long poor tail, one with a small very rich group. Report the Gini together with an income share (top 10 %, bottom 40 %) or a 90/10 ratio.

Why: The Gini compresses an entire Lorenz curve into one number, and different curves can enclose the same area. Check: if a question gives you two distributions with the same Gini, it is asking you to say exactly this.

Block 2 · Opportunity cost, specialisation, technology

⚠Mistake 3 · Confusing absolute and comparative advantage

✗ Wrong

Czechia produces more software and more wheat per worker than Slovakia, so Czechia should produce both and there are no gains from trade.

✓ Right

Compare opportunity costs: 1 software costs 2 wheat in Czechia and 4 wheat in Slovakia, so Czechia specialises in software and Slovakia — despite being worse at everything — in wheat.

Why: Absolute advantage compares productivity across countries; comparative advantage compares ratios within each country, and only the second one determines who should produce what. Check: a country can never have a comparative advantage in both goods — if your answer says it does, you have divided the wrong way.

⚠Mistake 4 · Forgetting forgone earnings (and forgone interest) in opportunity cost

✗ Wrong

The e-shop earns 500 000 CZK after paying its bills, so its profit is 500 000 CZK — or, one step better, 20 000 CZK after subtracting the 480 000 CZK salary she gave up.

✓ Right

Economic profit $=500\,000-480\,000$ (forgone wage) $-\,8\,000$ (forgone interest on her own 200 000 CZK) $=\mathbf{12\,000}$ CZK.

Why: Opportunity cost includes everything you gave up, and own capital is not free — it could have earned a return elsewhere. Check: for every decision ask two questions — what else could this person have done with their time, and what else with their money.

⚠Mistake 5 · Counting sunk costs in a forward-looking decision

✗ Wrong

We have already spent 3 million on the project, so we must finish it, otherwise the 3 million is wasted.

✓ Right

The 3 million is gone either way. Compare only the additional cost of finishing with the additional benefit; if that comparison fails, stop.

Why: A cost that cannot be recovered is identical under every option, so it cannot distinguish between them. Check: if a number in the question refers to something already paid and unrecoverable, cross it out before you start.

⚠Mistake 6 · Choosing a technology without prices, and tilting the isocost the wrong way

✗ Wrong

Technology A uses 20 workers + 10 energy = 30 units, technology C uses 8 + 40 = 48 units, so A is cheaper.

And when the wage rises, labour is dearer, so the isocost gets flatter and the firm hires more workers.

✓ Right

Compute the cost: at $w=200$, $p=50$, A costs $20\cdot200+10\cdot50=4\,500$ while C costs $8\cdot200+40\cdot50=3\,600$ — C is cheaper.

With labour on the horizontal axis the slope is $-w/p$, so a higher $w$ makes the isocost steeper and the firm moves to the labour-saving, energy-intensive technology.

Why: Workers and units of energy are different things with different prices, so adding them up is meaningless — the cheapest technology depends on the relative price $w/p$, and when an input gets dearer the tangency always moves away from it. Check: a technology ranking that contains no price is always wrong, and a more expensive input is never used more.

Block 3 · Preferences and constrained choice

⚠Mistake 7 · Drawing indifference curves that cross

✗ Wrong

Two indifference curves drawn intersecting at a point, "because preferences can change".

✓ Right

Indifference curves never intersect. The bundle at the crossing point would have to give two different utility levels at once, which contradicts a consistent (transitive) ranking.

Why: The whole indifference map is one person's ranking at one moment; a bundle has exactly one place in that ranking. Check: also make sure the curves slope downwards and bow towards the origin — for goods a person likes, both are compulsory.

⚠Mistake 8 · Mixing up MRS and MRT

✗ Wrong

The MRS is the slope of the feasible frontier, and it tells us how many grade points an extra hour of study produces.

✓ Right

MRS = slope of the indifference curve = what she is willing to trade (preferences). MRT = slope of the feasible frontier = what she can trade (technology/constraint). They coincide only at the optimum.

Why: The whole model works because two different objects — a preference and a constraint — meet on the same diagram; if you call them by the same name, the tangency condition becomes empty. Check: say out loud which curve you are on before writing a slope.

⚠Mistake 9 · Claiming a higher wage always means more hours worked

✗ Wrong

Wages rose, so people work more — labour supply is upward sloping, that is what the model says.

✓ Right

The substitution effect pushes towards more work (free time is dearer), the income effect towards less (the worker is richer and free time is normal). The net effect is ambiguous; when the income effect dominates the labour supply curve bends backwards, which is what long-run data on hours worked suggest.

Why: A wage change alters both the price of free time and the worker's real income, and those two channels pull in opposite directions. Check: any answer containing the word "always" in this topic is almost certainly wrong.

⚠Mistake 10 · Measuring the substitution effect on the wrong indifference curve

✗ Wrong

Substitution effect = the move from the old optimum to the new optimum on the new budget line.

✓ Right

Substitution effect = the move along the original indifference curve to the point where its slope equals the new relative price (drawn with a dashed, compensating budget line). The remaining jump to the new optimum is the income effect.

Why: The substitution effect is defined at constant utility — it isolates the pure price change; adding the shift to a new curve gives you the total effect. Check: your decomposition must have three points and two lines, one of them dashed. If the picture has only two points, you have not decomposed anything.

Block 4 · Games, dilemmas and institutions

⚠Mistake 11 · Calling the Nash equilibrium the best outcome

✗ Wrong

Mutual cooperation gives (3, 3), which is the highest total, so that is the Nash equilibrium.

✓ Right

The Nash equilibrium is (2, 2) — the only cell where neither player gains by deviating alone. It is Pareto-dominated by (3, 3), and that gap is the entire point of the prisoners' dilemma.

Why: Nash equilibrium is a stability concept (no profitable unilateral deviation), not a welfare ranking. Check: find it mechanically — underline each player's best response in every cell and look for the cell with two underlines. Never choose it by which numbers look nicest.

⚠Mistake 12 · Claiming that Pareto efficient means fair

✗ Wrong

The allocation is Pareto efficient, so it is a good and fair outcome and there is nothing to object to.

✓ Right

Pareto efficiency only says nothing is being wasted. An allocation where one person owns everything is efficient too. Efficiency and fairness are two independent criteria, and a full answer applies both.

Why: There are usually infinitely many efficient allocations (the whole Pareto frontier), and choosing among them is a distributional question that efficiency cannot settle. Check: whenever you write "efficient", ask yourself whether the question was actually about who gets what.

⚠Mistake 13 · Dismissing the experimental evidence

✗ Wrong

People reject positive offers in the ultimatum game and contribute in public goods games — that is irrational, so the experiments tell us nothing.

✓ Right

The behaviour is consistent and predictable: offers cluster at 40–50 %, low offers are rejected, contributions start near half the endowment and decay without punishment but persist with it. This is evidence of social preferences — fairness, reciprocity, conditional cooperation — not of confusion.

Why: Rational means acting consistently on your preferences, and the results show that those preferences include more than own money. Check: when data contradict a model, the exam wants you to amend the model's assumptions, not to dismiss the data.

Block 5 · Firms, markets and market failure

⚠Mistake 14 · Using an inconsistent base in an elasticity calculation

✗ Wrong

Price falls from 100 to 80 and quantity rises from 40 to 50: $\varepsilon=\dfrac{10}{20}=0{,}5$ — quantity changed by less than price, so demand is inelastic.

✓ Right

Elasticity uses percentage changes on a consistent base: $\%\Delta Q=10/40=25\,\%$, $\%\Delta P=-20/100=-20\,\%$, so $\varepsilon=25/20=\mathbf{1{,}25}$ — demand is elastic.

Why: Absolute changes depend on the units (crates versus bottles, CZK versus EUR); only percentages make quantity and price comparable. Check: if your elasticity would change when you switch from litres to hectolitres, you have not used percentages.

⚠Mistake 15 · Treating the markup as independent of elasticity — or as a share of cost

✗ Wrong

With $MC=60$ and a 25 % markup the price is $60\cdot1{,}25=75$; and anyway the firm just adds whatever margin it likes.

✓ Right

$\dfrac{P-MC}{P}=\dfrac{1}{\varepsilon}$. With $\varepsilon=4$: $P=\dfrac{MC}{1-1/4}=\dfrac{60}{0{,}75}=\mathbf{80}$. The markup is a share of the price, and its size is dictated by the elasticity the firm faces.

Why: The markup is not a choice of business policy but the solution of $MR=MC$; the more elastic the demand, the smaller the markup, until $P=MC$ under perfect competition. Check: a firm's profit-maximising point always lies where $\varepsilon>1$ — if your answer implies inelastic demand at the optimum, redo it.

⚠Mistake 16 · Treating the deadweight loss triangle as a transfer

✗ Wrong

The deadweight loss of 800 is what consumers lose and the monopolist gains.

✓ Right

The rectangle $(60-20)\cdot40=1\,600$ moves from consumers to the firm — a transfer, a fairness issue. The triangle $\tfrac12\cdot40\cdot40=800$ goes to nobody: it is the surplus on units that were worth making and are not made.

Why: Efficiency losses and distributional shifts are different things, and only the first one reduces total surplus. Check: if you can name who receives the amount, it is a transfer, not a deadweight loss.

⚠Mistake 17 · Confusing consumer surplus with profit

✗ Wrong

Consumer surplus is the area between price and marginal cost, which is what the firm earns from consumers.

✓ Right

Consumer surplus = willingness to pay − price, i.e. the area under the demand curve and above the price — it belongs to buyers. Producer surplus (profit) = price − marginal cost, the area above the MC curve and below the price.

Why: The two surpluses are measured from opposite sides of the same price line and accrue to opposite sides of the market. Check: label the price line first and then ask which area is above it and which below.

⚠Mistake 18 · Saying the minimum wage always reduces employment

✗ Wrong

A minimum wage is a price floor above equilibrium, so employment always falls. End of answer.

✓ Right

In the competitive model, yes — and you should say so first. But with monopsony a moderate floor can raise wages and employment, and with effort responding to the wage, unit labour costs rise by less than the wage. Empirically, moderate increases show effects near zero (Card–Krueger and the later literature); clearly negative effects appear when the minimum is high relative to the median wage.

Why: The competitive prediction rests on assumptions — price-taking employers, effort independent of the wage — that the wage-setting model of this course explicitly relaxes. Check: a full-mark answer names the model, states its prediction, names the assumption that could fail, and cites one piece of evidence.

⚠Mistake 19 · Shifting a curve when you should move along it

✗ Wrong

Electricity gets cheaper, so bread is cheaper, so demand rises and the demand curve shifts to the right.

✓ Right

Cheaper electricity lowers marginal cost, so the supply curve shifts right. Price falls and quantity rises, and buyers move along an unchanged demand curve — nothing happened to their income or tastes.

Why: A change in the good's own price is always a movement along the curve; only a change in something else (income, tastes, the price of another good, input costs, technology, taxes) shifts a curve. Check: ask what changed. If the answer is "the price of this good", nothing shifts.

⚠Mistake 20 · Claiming the efficient level of pollution is zero

✗ Wrong

Pollution is a negative externality, so the efficient policy is a tax high enough to eliminate it entirely.

✓ Right

The efficient quantity is where marginal benefit equals social marginal cost — generally with pollution still positive. The corrective Pigouvian tax equals the marginal external cost at that quantity, not whatever it takes to shut production down.

Why: Abatement itself has costs, and eliminating the last unit of pollution usually costs more than the harm it does. Check: draw the diagram — the efficient point is an intersection of two curves, never the origin.

📌The five checks that catch most of these
  • Marginal or total? Returns, products, costs and revenues are almost always about the marginal unit.
  • Which curve am I on? Preferences (indifference curve, MRS) or constraint (frontier, budget, MRT)?
  • Percentages, not levels. Every elasticity, every growth rate, every markup share.
  • Destroyed or moved? Deadweight loss versus transfer; efficiency versus fairness.
  • What changed? The good's own price ⇒ movement along; anything else ⇒ shift.
💡Before the exam

Read this page once, then close it and write down from memory the five mistakes you are personally most likely to make. Keep that list next to you while you revise with the cheat sheet and while you write the final exam as a timed mock. Recognising an error on this page is easy; not producing it under time pressure is the actual skill.
